scoring.rule: Five statements, each true or false, 1 point each. The student checks the statements they believe are true. A statement scores 1 point if it is checked and true, or unchecked and false; otherwise 0.

questions.stem: Candidates for a game-programming job are asked what the words scene, level and map mean in the three big engines. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In Unity, "scene" means a reusable object that is instanced many times, in the way a prefab is.
statements.explanation: A Unity scene is a container of GameObjects for a level or screen; the reusable, instanced object is the prefab.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A Godot scene can be a single weapon, a character or a whole level, so "scene" does not mean "one screen of the game".
statements.explanation: A Godot scene is any saved tree of nodes, which is why one mechanism serves for small objects and whole levels.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In Unity, more than one scene can be loaded at the same time, which is called additive loading.
statements.explanation: Unity can load a scene on top of the scenes already open (additive loading), which is how levels are built from several parts.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In Unreal, a level is a saved map that holds the Actors placed in one part of the world.
statements.explanation: In Unreal the level (map) file stores the Actors placed in it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Godot, "level" has no special meaning to the engine; a level is a scene, often one that instances other scenes.
statements.explanation: Godot has no separate level type; any scene can serve as a level, and a level scene usually contains instances of smaller scenes.

questions.stem: Engines package a reusable game object once and then place many copies of it. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In Unity, a prefab is an asset that serves as a template, and each copy placed in a scene is a prefab instance that stays linked to that asset.
statements.explanation: The prefab asset is the template; instances in scenes are linked copies of it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In Unity, a prefab instance in a scene and the prefab asset are one object, so deleting the instance from the scene also deletes the asset file.
statements.explanation: The instance is a separate object in the scene; removing it leaves the asset untouched.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In Unity, a scene and a prefab are the same kind of asset stored in the same file type, so loading a prefab replaces the current level.
statements.explanation: Scenes and prefabs are different asset types; opening a prefab does not replace the level.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In Godot, a saved scene can be instantiated inside another scene, so one mechanism covers both a whole level and a reusable object such as an enemy.
statements.explanation: In Godot a scene file is both the level format and the reusable-object format, and scenes can be nested.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Unreal, a Blueprint class is an asset that defines a custom Actor type, and each Actor placed in a level from it is an instance of that class.
statements.explanation: A Blueprint class is the definition; each placed copy is an instance of that class.

questions.source: Translating engine words in an instruction
questions.stem: A developer working in a Godot project types this to a coding agent: "Make the coin a prefab and spawn ten of them along the track." (Prefab is a Unity word.) Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Once instantiate has been called, the coin appears and runs in the game, without a parent node being needed.
statements.explanation: An instance only becomes part of the running game after it is added as a child of a node in the scene tree.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Instantiating the coin's loaded scene ten times yields ten separate node trees that can each be given a different position.
statements.explanation: Each call to instantiate produces a fresh, independent tree of nodes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A Godot scene plays the role a prefab plays in Unity, so the agent can reasonably read "prefab" as "a saved scene that is instanced".
statements.explanation: A saved Godot scene is the reusable template that Unity calls a prefab, so the word can be translated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Godot has a built-in prefab file type, and the agent must create one before it can spawn anything in the level.
statements.explanation: Godot has no prefab file type; the scene file is the mechanism.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Spawning ten coins means creating one coin node and ten references to it, so all ten share a single position and move together.
statements.explanation: Each instance is a separate node with its own position; references to one node would be the same object.

questions.stem: A prefab-style asset (a Unity prefab, an Unreal Blueprint class or a Godot scene) for an enemy is instanced 50 times in a level. On 3 of the instances the developer changes the move speed to a different value in the instance only. Later the developer edits the move speed default in the asset itself. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Adding a new child object or component to the asset normally shows up in all 50 instances without editing them one by one.
statements.explanation: Structural changes made to the template, such as an added child node or component, appear in its instances.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Instances are independent copies made at placement time, so later edits to the asset do not reach them.
statements.explanation: Instances stay linked to the asset in all three engines; that link is what lets edits flow to them.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The 47 instances whose speed was left unchanged pick up the new default.
statements.explanation: Properties an instance has not overridden keep following the asset's value.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Editing the asset once is less work and less error-prone than editing 50 copies by hand, which is the main reason for the asset and instance split.
statements.explanation: Central editing of a shared template is the practical benefit of instancing instead of copy-and-paste.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The 3 instances that carry their own speed value keep it, because an instance-level override wins over the asset's default.
statements.explanation: An override is a value stored on the instance, so it is not replaced when the default changes.

questions.stem: A candidate is asked how objects get behaviour in each of the three engines. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In Unreal, an Actor can be placed in a level or spawned during play, and its location, rotation and scale come from its root component.
statements.explanation: An Unreal Actor has no transform of its own; it takes one from its root component.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In Unity, a GameObject has a Transform, and features such as rendering, physics and scripts are added to it as components.
statements.explanation: Every GameObject has a Transform; other behaviour comes from components.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In Godot, the idiom for giving one object several unrelated abilities is to attach several components to a single node, as with Unity's GameObjects.
statements.explanation: Godot combines behaviour by arranging nodes in a tree and instancing scenes; its own documentation says its nodes do not work like components in some other engines.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In Unity, a GameObject that only holds scripts can exist without a Transform, because the Transform is added only when something needs a position.
statements.explanation: A GameObject cannot exist without a Transform.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Unreal, the base Actor Component type carries a transform and can be attached to other components in a hierarchy.
statements.explanation: The transform and attachment belong to Scene Components; the plain Actor Component is not tied to a place in the world.

questions.stem: Games need labels so that code can find or filter objects such as enemies. Engines give those labels different rules. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Adding a group or tag to an object only helps code look it up; by itself it changes neither how the object looks nor how it moves.
statements.explanation: A label has no built-in effect on rendering or physics.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In Godot, a group is a collision rule that decides which objects physically touch each other, so adding a node to a group changes what it can hit.
statements.explanation: Collision filtering uses layers and masks; groups are lookup labels.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In Unity, a GameObject has exactly one tag, so one object cannot carry the tags "Enemy" and "Flying" at the same time.
statements.explanation: Unity gives each GameObject a single tag (and a single layer).

statements.label: D
statements.text: In Godot, a node can belong to several groups at once, and the scene tree can list the members of a group or call a method on all of them.
statements.explanation: Groups work like tags with many allowed per node, and the scene tree can list a group's members or call a method on all of them.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Unity, a GameObject's tag and its layer are two names for the same property, so setting one also sets the other.
statements.explanation: Tags and layers are separate properties; layers are used for filtering such as rendering and physics, tags for lookup.

questions.stem: In a 2D game a parent object sits at world position (200, 50) with no rotation and a scale of 1. A child object has a local position of (100, 0), meaning 100 units along the parent's own x axis. Assume the engine builds the child's world position by scaling its local position by the parent's scale, then rotating it by the parent's rotation, then adding the parent's position. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the parent moves to (500, 50) and nothing else changes, the child's local position becomes (400, 0) so that the child stays in place in the world.
statements.explanation: A local position is stored relative to the parent and does not change when the parent moves; the child's world position becomes (600, 50).

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the parent is scaled to 2 on both axes and the child's local position is left unchanged, the child's world position is (400, 50).
statements.explanation: Scaling doubles the offset to (200, 0), and adding the parent's position gives (400, 50).

statements.label: C
statements.text: Setting the child's local position to (0, 0) puts the child at the world origin.
statements.explanation: A local position of (0, 0) is the parent's own origin, so the child sits at the parent's world position (200, 50).

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the parent is rotated 90 degrees so that its own x axis points along the world's +y direction, with no scaling, the child's world position becomes (300, 150).
statements.explanation: The local offset (100, 0) is turned into (0, 100), so the child's world position is (200, 150), not (300, 150).

statements.label: E
statements.text: With the parent unrotated and unscaled, the child's world position is (300, 50).
statements.explanation: The world position is the parent's position plus the local offset: (200 + 100, 50 + 0).

questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: "Raise the platform by 100 units." The agent must edit position values in three different engines. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In Unreal, positive z points up, so raising an Actor means adding to its z.
statements.explanation: Unreal is z-up, so adding to z raises the Actor.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In Unity the vertical axis is y with positive y pointing up, so subtracting 100 from a GameObject's y raises it.
statements.explanation: In Unity positive y is up, so subtracting from y lowers the object.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In Godot's 2D space the y axis points down the screen, so raising a 2D node by 100 pixels means subtracting 100 from its y position.
statements.explanation: Godot 2D uses screen-style coordinates in which y grows downward, so "up" means a smaller y.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A distance of 100 units is the same real-world length in Unity and Unreal by default, because both treat one unit as one metre.
statements.explanation: Unity's convention is one unit per metre, but Unreal's unit is a centimetre, so 100 units is 100 cm in Unreal.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Unreal, y is the vertical axis, so raising an Actor means adding 100 to its y.
statements.explanation: Unreal's vertical axis is z, not y.

questions.stem: A 2D game draws into a viewport that is 640 pixels wide and 360 pixels high. The camera is centred on world position (1000, 500), is not rotated, and shows one world unit per viewport pixel (zoom 1). Screen position (0, 0) is the top-left corner of the viewport, and y grows downward in both screen space and world space. A developer tells a coding agent: "Move the player to where I click." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The agent can use the raw click position as the player's target, because screen coordinates and world coordinates are the same thing.
statements.explanation: Screen coordinates are measured in the viewport; world coordinates are positions in the game world, and the camera relates them.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A click at screen position (0, 0) corresponds to world position (680, 320).
statements.explanation: The viewport's top-left corner is half a viewport (320, 180) away from the camera centre, so it is (1000 - 320, 500 - 180) = (680, 320).

statements.label: C
statements.text: A click at the centre of the viewport, screen position (320, 180), corresponds to world position (320, 180).
statements.explanation: The viewport centre is where the camera looks, which is world (1000, 500).

statements.label: D
statements.text: After the camera zooms in by a factor of 2, so that objects appear twice as large, a click at screen position (0, 0) corresponds to world position (840, 410).
statements.explanation: At zoom 2 the viewport covers 320 by 180 world units, so the top-left corner is (1000 - 160, 500 - 90) = (840, 410).

statements.label: E
statements.text: A precise instruction asks the agent to convert the click from screen coordinates to world coordinates using the camera, and then move the player to that world position.
statements.explanation: Naming the two spaces and the conversion removes the guess that would otherwise put the player at the wrong place.

questions.stem: Check each statement about frames, ticks and delta time.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The delta passed to a per-frame callback is a fixed 1/60 s, because 60 frames per second is the standard rate that games are built to run at.
statements.explanation: The per-frame delta varies with how long each frame took on that machine.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A tick is one update step of a subsystem such as physics, while a frame is one pass of the main loop ending in a rendered image, so the counts can differ.
statements.explanation: Physics ticks and rendered frames are counted separately and need not be equal in number.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Frame rate is the number of fixed physics steps that run each second, which is why the two numbers match.
statements.explanation: Frame rate counts rendered frames per second; the fixed-step rate is a separate setting and the two need not be equal.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Delta time is the time elapsed since the previous call of the update callback, usually measured in seconds.
statements.explanation: Delta is the elapsed time between consecutive calls, which lets movement be scaled by real time.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Godot, the delta passed to the physics callback follows the fixed physics rate, so it does not stretch when a rendered frame takes longer than usual.
statements.explanation: Godot's physics callback runs at a fixed rate and its delta follows that rate rather than the length of the last rendered frame.

questions.stem: A developer asks a coding agent: "Make the enemy move right 5 pixels every frame." The agent writes position.x += 5 in the per-frame update function. The game is then tested on one screen where the loop runs at 60 frames per second and on another where it runs at 144 frames per second. Use these figures. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: At 60 frames per second the enemy moves 300 pixels per second, and at 144 frames per second it moves 720 pixels per second.
statements.explanation: 5 pixels times 60 frames is 300 per second, and 5 times 144 is 720 per second.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The enemy moves more slowly on the 144 frames-per-second screen, because each frame lasts a shorter time and so the 5-pixel step covers less time.
statements.explanation: More frames per second means more 5-pixel steps per second, so the enemy is faster, 2.4 times as fast.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Asking for "move right at 300 pixels per second" and writing position.x += 300 * delta gives the same on-screen speed at 60 and at 144 frames per second.
statements.explanation: A speed in pixels per second multiplied by the elapsed time per frame covers the same distance per second at any frame rate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Running position.x += 5 in a fixed-step callback that runs 60 times per second gives 300 pixels per second on both screens.
statements.explanation: The fixed-step callback runs 60 times per second regardless of display rate, so 5 pixels per step is 300 per second everywhere.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Replacing the step with 5 * delta gives 300 pixels per second at 60 frames per second and 720 at 144, because delta makes the step scale with the frame rate.
statements.explanation: Each frame moves 5 * delta pixels, and the deltas of the frames in one second add up to one second, so the enemy covers only 5 pixels per second at either rate.

questions.stem: An interviewer asks why movement that involves the physics engine belongs in the engine's fixed-step callback (Unity's FixedUpdate, Godot's _physics_process) rather than in the per-frame callback (Update, _process). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The physics engine advances the world in fixed-size steps, so forces and velocities applied in the callback tied to that step line up with the simulation.
statements.explanation: Fixed-size steps keep the simulation's time unit constant and match the rate at which the engine integrates motion.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In Godot, the physics callback is the right place for purely cosmetic effects such as a flickering light, because it runs more often than the per-frame callback.
statements.explanation: The physics callback runs at a fixed rate that can be lower or higher than the frame rate; it is not "more often", and cosmetic effects belong in the per-frame callback.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Physics driven by the variable per-frame delta depends on how fast the machine renders, so the same input can give different results on different machines.
statements.explanation: A varying step makes collisions and jump heights less repeatable between machines.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Putting movement in the fixed-step callback makes the on-screen frame rate constant, because the physics step no longer varies from frame to frame.
statements.explanation: Frame rate depends on rendering and load; the fixed step only decouples physics from it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The per-frame callback is forbidden from changing any object's position, so all movement code has to live in the fixed-step callback.
statements.explanation: Nothing forbids moving objects in the per-frame callback; it is simply the wrong place for physics-driven motion.

questions.stem: A game's fixed-step callback is set to run 50 times per second, so one step is 20 ms. Rendering is not capped, and the engine catches up by running extra steps when a frame is long. Use these figures. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: At 100 rendered frames per second, the fixed-step callback runs once per rendered frame.
statements.explanation: At 100 frames per second a frame lasts 10 ms, half a step, so the fixed step runs on about every second frame.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A single frame that takes 60 ms to render is followed by about 3 fixed steps to catch up.
statements.explanation: 60 ms of elapsed time divided by the 20 ms step is 3 steps.

statements.label: C
statements.text: At 100 rendered frames per second, the step length shrinks to 10 ms so that each fixed step lines up with one frame.
statements.explanation: The step length is a fixed setting and does not change with the frame rate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: At 25 rendered frames per second, the fixed-step callback runs 25 times per second, once per rendered frame.
statements.explanation: The fixed step still runs 50 times per second, which is about 2 steps per frame at 25 frames per second.

statements.label: E
statements.text: When three catch-up steps run after a 60 ms frame, each call of the fixed-step callback receives a delta of 60 ms.
statements.explanation: Each call receives the step length, 20 ms; running it three times covers the 60 ms.

questions.stem: A scene contains 2000 enemies. Each enemy's per-frame update function takes 0.01 ms of CPU time, and one frame at 60 frames per second has a budget of 16.67 ms. Use these figures. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Halving the enemy count to 1000 would still leave the enemy updates above the 16.67 ms budget.
statements.explanation: 1000 enemies cost 10 ms, which is below 16.67 ms.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The enemies' update functions alone take 20 ms per frame, which exceeds the 16.67 ms budget.
statements.explanation: 2000 times 0.01 ms is 20 ms.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Reacting to an event when something changes, instead of checking each frame, removes the per-frame cost for objects that are idle.
statements.explanation: An event-driven design only runs code when something happens, so idle objects cost nothing per frame.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the enemy updates were the only cost, the game could run at no more than 50 frames per second.
statements.explanation: 20 ms per frame corresponds to 1000 / 20 = 50 frames per second at best.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Switching off the per-frame callback on the 1500 enemies that are idle would leave 5 ms of enemy work per frame.
statements.explanation: 500 remaining enemies times 0.01 ms is 5 ms.

questions.stem: Most engines give an object a hook that runs once when it is ready to be used (Godot's _ready, Unity's Start, Unreal's BeginPlay) and a hook that runs repeatedly (Godot's _process, Unity's Update, Unreal's Tick). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In Unity, Start is called before the script's first frame update, and only if the script instance is enabled.
statements.explanation: Unity's reference says Start is called before the first frame update only if the script instance is enabled.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Because a start hook runs only once, it cannot be used to begin repeating behaviour such as a looping timer.
statements.explanation: A once-only hook can start a timer or any repeating process; it simply starts it once.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A per-frame hook is the right place to build the player's starting inventory, because it keeps retrying until it succeeds.
statements.explanation: Setup placed in a per-frame hook is repeated every frame or needs a guard flag; setup belongs in the once-only hook.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In Godot, _ready is called again each time a node is removed from the scene tree and added back.
statements.explanation: _ready is called only once per node unless request_ready is used.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Godot, a parent's _ready runs after the _ready of its children, so the parent can rely on its children being set up.
statements.explanation: Godot's documentation says children's _ready callbacks are triggered first and the parent's afterwards.

questions.stem: Godot calls it a signal, Unity programmers use C# events or UnityEvent, and Unreal has delegates and Event Dispatchers. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In all three, the code that announces an event does not need to name the objects that react to it.
statements.explanation: Listeners register themselves, so the announcer stays unaware of who is listening.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A callback is a function that a listener hands over so that the announcing object can call it when the event happens.
statements.explanation: The callback is the function passed to the signal, event or delegate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Signals, events and delegates hold the message in a queue until each listener checks it once per frame.
statements.explanation: Listeners are called by the announcer when the event happens; by default a Godot signal calls its connected functions immediately, and deferring is an option the connection must request.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In Godot, emitting a signal that nothing is connected to is not an error; it calls nothing.
statements.explanation: Godot's documented error case for emitting is an unknown signal, not an empty list of listeners.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Godot, a listener can connect to a signal on any node it can get a reference to; a parent and child relationship is not required.
statements.explanation: A connection links a signal to a callable on any object; the tree layout does not restrict it.

questions.source: Signals versus polling and direct calls
questions.stem: A developer wants the health bar (HUD) to redraw when the player takes damage. The requirements for the coding agent are that the player's code must not need to know the HUD exists and that the HUD must not check the player every frame. Check each statement that is true: a statement is true only if the request it quotes meets both requirements.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Give the player a reference to the HUD and have the player call the HUD's redraw function when it takes damage."
statements.explanation: The player must hold a reference to the HUD, which breaks the first requirement.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "In the HUD's per-frame update function, read the player's health and redraw if it changed."
statements.explanation: This polls the player every frame, which breaks the second requirement.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Have the player emit a health-changed signal, and have the HUD connect to it and redraw in the handler."
statements.explanation: The player only announces the change and the HUD listens, so neither requirement is broken.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Have the HUD declare a signal, and have the player connect to it and emit it whenever health changes."
statements.explanation: The player has to reference the HUD to connect to and emit its signal, which breaks the first requirement.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Store health in a global variable that the player writes and the HUD reads in its per-frame update function."
statements.explanation: The HUD still reads the shared value on every frame, which breaks the second requirement.

questions.stem: A Unity script subscribes one of its methods to a C# event on a long-lived manager object. The script's GameObject is later destroyed without the script unsubscribing. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Event systems keep only weak references to subscribers, so a long-lived emitter drops a destroyed subscriber without needing an unsubscribe call.
statements.explanation: A C# event holds a normal reference to each subscriber, so a missing unsubscribe causes stale calls and keeps the object reachable.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The manager's list of subscribers still holds the destroyed script's method, so the next time the event is raised the call can be made on an object that no longer exists.
statements.explanation: A C# event keeps a reference to each subscribed method, so a stale subscription stays in the list.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The engine queues the event until the start of the next frame, by which time the destroyed object has been cleaned up and no error follows.
statements.explanation: A C# event calls its subscribers in the line that raises it; nothing is queued.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The usual remedy is symmetrical: subscribe when the object is enabled and unsubscribe when it is disabled or destroyed.
statements.explanation: Pairing subscribe and unsubscribe with the object's enable and disable (or destroy) is the standard discipline.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Godot, when a node whose method is connected to a signal is freed, the engine removes that connection, so the emitter does not keep calling the freed node.
statements.explanation: Godot removes the connections of a freed object, as both emitter and receiver.

questions.stem: A studio interview asks why engines offer input actions instead of letting game code read raw keys. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because game code asks about the action, a player can rebind the key without any game code changing.
statements.explanation: Rebinding changes the mapping, not the code that reads the action.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Hard-coding a check for the Space key in the movement code is the preferred way to support rebinding, since the key is then easy to find.
statements.explanation: A hard-coded key defeats rebinding and ties the code to one device.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An input action is a named intent, such as "jump", that is mapped to one or more physical inputs like a keyboard key or a gamepad button.
statements.explanation: The action is the game-level meaning, and bindings tie it to devices.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Unity's Input System actions, Unreal's Enhanced Input actions and Godot's Input Map actions are three engine-specific forms of this same idea.
statements.explanation: Each engine maps named actions to bindings, under different names and tools.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Polling asks for an action's current state on each update, while an event callback is called once for each input event as it arrives.
statements.explanation: Polling reads state when asked; an event callback is pushed to the code when the input happens.

questions.stem: Developers use "asset" and "resource" loosely. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An asset, in the everyday sense, is a file in the project folder such as a PNG, a WAV or a mesh, which the engine imports before using it.
statements.explanation: Source files are imported by the editor, and the engine uses the imported form at runtime.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Unity's ScriptableObject and Unreal's Data Asset fill a similar role: a data-only asset that many objects can read, independent of any object in a level.
statements.explanation: Both are data assets that exist independently of objects in a level, though they are not identical features.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A Godot Resource is a data container that does nothing on its own; nodes use resources to do their work.
statements.explanation: Godot's documentation calls resources data containers that do nothing on their own.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In Godot, loading the same resource path twice returns two independent copies, because each load reads the file again, so changing one does not affect the other.
statements.explanation: Godot's documentation says loading a resource that is already in memory returns the same copy every time.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Godot, a Resource and a Node are interchangeable: both can be placed in the scene tree and both receive the per-frame callback.
statements.explanation: Only nodes live in the scene tree and get per-frame callbacks; a resource is just data.

questions.stem: A game keeps the player's inventory in one globally reachable object: a singleton in Unity, an autoload in Godot, or an object held by the persistent Game Instance in Unreal. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In Godot, replacing the current scene also frees the autoload nodes, which are then recreated for the new scene along with its nodes.
statements.explanation: Godot's documentation says autoloads are always loaded, no matter which scene is running.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Such an object is useful mainly because it outlives any one scene or level, so what it stores survives scene changes.
statements.explanation: Lifetime beyond the current scene is the reason to put shared state in such an object.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Registering a script as an autoload makes the engine refuse to create a second copy of it, which is what makes it a true singleton.
statements.explanation: Godot's documentation says an autoload can still be instanced more than once if the user wants.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because any code can reach it, a function that quietly reads the global is harder to test alone than one handed the inventory as a parameter.
statements.explanation: A hidden dependency on a global makes a function depend on state its signature does not show.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Unity, a manager object that sits in the first scene stays alive when another scene is loaded in its place, because manager objects are kept across scene loads by default.
statements.explanation: Unity destroys the objects of the scene being replaced unless they are explicitly marked to survive the load.

questions.stem: A developer asks a coding agent for "a global score counter" in a Godot game that has a title scene, a level scene and a game-over scene. The agent puts the counter in a script on the root node of the level scene. When the game reaches the game-over scene, the score reads zero. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Registering the script as an autoload would keep it alive from startup through each scene change.
statements.explanation: An autoload is a node placed under the root before the main scene and kept through scene changes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Marking the variable with @export keeps its value when the game switches scenes.
statements.explanation: @export exposes a variable to the editor and saves its value in the scene; it does not extend its lifetime.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The score variable was freed along with the level scene's nodes when the game switched to another scene.
statements.explanation: A variable in a script lives only as long as the node it belongs to, and the level scene's nodes were removed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The cause is that GDScript resets number variables to zero when a new scene is loaded.
statements.explanation: GDScript does not reset variables; the object holding the variable was removed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A way to avoid a global is to pass the score along to the next scene as the scenes are switched.
statements.explanation: The vague word "global" hid a design choice; handing the value to the next scene is a legitimate alternative to a global.

questions.stem: Check each statement about the editor, a running game and a built (exported or packaged) game.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A game that runs correctly when started from the editor will also run correctly in a built version, so testing the build adds little.
statements.explanation: Builds can differ from editor runs in included files, platform settings and performance, so a successful editor run does not replace testing the build.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Code written to extend the editor, such as Unity code that uses the UnityEditor namespace, cannot be used in a built player.
statements.explanation: Editor-only code does not exist in the player, so it must be kept out of the built game.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Producing a standalone game is a separate step from running it in the editor, and engines give that step different names, such as export, build or package.
statements.explanation: Running in the editor and producing a standalone game are different steps, and each engine names the second one in its own way.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In Unity, edits made to scene objects while the editor is in Play mode are kept when Play mode stops.
statements.explanation: Changes made to scene objects in Play mode are discarded when Play mode ends.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Godot, the editor on its own is enough to export a project to another platform; no separately installed runtime files for that platform are needed.
statements.explanation: Godot's documentation says export templates, the prebuilt runtime for each target platform, must be installed before a project can be exported.

questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: "Ship the game to my tester." The agent starts the project from the command line, sees it run, and reports that it is done. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Ship" is precise enough, because it is the engines' own name for the export step and the tester's platform can be taken to match the developer's.
statements.explanation: The engines call the step export, build or packaging, not "ship", and the tester's platform is not stated, so the word leaves the target open.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Because the game ran on the agent's machine, the agent has already produced a standalone file that the tester can open without the engine installed.
statements.explanation: Running from the command line launches the project with the engine; it creates no standalone game.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The tester's machine needs the editor installed to run the result of an export, because the exported game is opened through the editor.
statements.explanation: A built game is meant to run without the editor.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The exported game is made from the same project folder, so any file the game loads when run from the editor is also present in the build.
statements.explanation: The editor run reads the project folder directly, while an export includes only the files its settings select (Godot, for example, leaves out files whose names begin with a period), so a file can load in the editor and be missing from the build.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Running the project from the editor or command line is not a build, so the instruction should name the export step and the target platform.
statements.explanation: Running a project and exporting it are different steps, and an exported build needs a chosen target.

questions.stem: A studio connects a language-model assistant to a scene editor through Model Context Protocol (MCP). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: MCP is the model that predicts the next words in the assistant's reply.
statements.explanation: Inference belongs to the language model, not the integration protocol.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Installing MCP trains the assistant on the project's assets.
statements.explanation: Connecting a service does not update model weights.

statements.label: C
statements.text: MCP supplies the engine's rendering pipeline.
statements.explanation: Rendering remains an engine responsibility.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The MCP server replaces the project's gameplay scripts.
statements.explanation: The server exposes operations; gameplay still needs its implementation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: MCP defines an interface through which the assistant application can access external capabilities.
statements.explanation: The protocol connects applications to tools and context.

questions.stem: An assistant application contains an MCP connector that calls a service exposing a game editor. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The connector plays the client role.
statements.explanation: The client communicates with the MCP server on the host's behalf.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The assistant application plays the host role.
statements.explanation: The host contains the user interaction and integration machinery.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The user-written gameplay character is the MCP client in this arrangement.
statements.explanation: The client is the integration connector, not an in-game character.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The editor-facing service plays the server role.
statements.explanation: It supplies the external capabilities.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The server role implies that the service runs in a cloud data center.
statements.explanation: A server can be a local process.

questions.stem: A hypothetical editor server exposes a spawn operation, a readable scene manifest and a reusable review template. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The spawn operation fits the tool primitive.
statements.explanation: A tool invokes an operation with inputs.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Reading the manifest can inform a later spawn request.
statements.explanation: Context can guide a subsequent action.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The review template fits the prompt primitive.
statements.explanation: Prompts provide reusable messages or workflows.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The scene manifest fits a resource if the server exposes it as URI-addressed content.
statements.explanation: Resources supply context that a client can read.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Retrieving the review template is evidence that the scene passed review.
statements.explanation: Obtaining instructions does not execute or satisfy them.

questions.stem: An agent knows a tool name from a tutorial, but the connected editor does not advertise that tool. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The missing tool proves that the scene file is corrupt.
statements.explanation: Tool availability and scene integrity are different questions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A familiar tutorial name is a sufficient substitute for the live tool schema.
statements.explanation: Names and arguments may differ across integrations.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The agent should inspect the connected server's available tools before constructing a call.
statements.explanation: Discovery grounds the operation in the actual integration.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Renaming a scene object to the missing tool name registers that tool.
statements.explanation: Object names do not implement server operations.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The installed integration may expose a different operation for the same goal.
statements.explanation: Tool catalogs are implementation-specific.

questions.stem: A hypothetical move tool accepts an object identifier and a numeric distance. The schema does not specify units or coordinate space. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The agent needs the tool contract or an inspected example to determine coordinate space.
statements.explanation: Local and world coordinates can produce different changes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A schema-valid request establishes that the target object is the intended one.
statements.explanation: Identity must be checked separately.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Reading back the final transform checks the effect of the operation.
statements.explanation: Observed state can reveal semantic mistakes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Using a number proves that the intended unit was used.
statements.explanation: The same number may mean meters, centimeters or another unit.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A numeric argument can pass schema validation while expressing the wrong distance.
statements.explanation: Type correctness does not establish units.

questions.stem: An MCP trace contains JSON-RPC requests and replies while several editor operations are being investigated. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A notification's lack of a reply is sufficient evidence of a broken connection.
statements.explanation: No reply is expected for a notification.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A JSON-RPC notification has no request identifier and receives no JSON-RPC response.
statements.explanation: Notifications do not provide request-response acknowledgment.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The identifier is the index of the target Actor in the level.
statements.explanation: Protocol correlation is separate from engine identity.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A response identifier associates a reply with its request.
statements.explanation: Correlation uses the request's identifier.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A syntactically valid JSON message proves that the requested edit succeeded.
statements.explanation: Message syntax says nothing about the operation's result.

questions.stem: Two integrations carry MCP messages using stdio and Streamable HTTP respectively. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: HTTP can be used for a service on the same machine.
statements.explanation: HTTP does not imply a remote cloud service.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A transport fault can prevent a valid tool request from reaching the editor.
statements.explanation: Delivery can fail before execution.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Changing the transport translates Unity components into Unreal components.
statements.explanation: A transport does not convert engine data models.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Stdio can connect a client to a subprocess through standard streams.
statements.explanation: It is a process communication transport.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The transport and the engine operation are separate layers.
statements.explanation: Message delivery does not define scene-editing semantics.

questions.stem: A hypothetical tool reports that its request was received but the named scene object could not be found. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Changing the network port repairs an obsolete object identifier.
statements.explanation: Port selection does not restore object identity.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Reinstalling the model is the first diagnosis supported by this evidence.
statements.explanation: There is no evidence of a model installation fault.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The next investigation should include object identity and current scene state.
statements.explanation: The error concerns the operation's target.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Receiving a structured reply means that the object was successfully modified.
statements.explanation: The reply explicitly reports a failure.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A successful network exchange can carry an unsuccessful editor operation.
statements.explanation: Transport success and domain success differ.

questions.stem: A client and server were developed against different MCP revisions. Both claim to support MCP, but their first exchange fails. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The applicable specification and implementation documentation should guide discovery and setup.
statements.explanation: Lifecycle details should be checked for the deployed revision.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The supported protocol revisions are relevant diagnostic evidence.
statements.explanation: The same protocol family can have incompatible revision requirements.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A small read-only interoperability check is useful before authorizing scene edits.
statements.explanation: It isolates communication without risking scene changes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A tutorial's initialization sequence is sufficient evidence of the current protocol's requirements.
statements.explanation: Protocol lifecycle rules evolve.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The MCP name establishes that the two implementations support the same revision.
statements.explanation: A product label is not a compatibility guarantee.

questions.stem: A resource returned a list of lights. A designer then deleted one of those lights before the agent prepared its edit. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The earlier list is a snapshot that may now be stale.
statements.explanation: Editor changes can invalidate read context.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Resource content is locked against later editor changes once read.
statements.explanation: Reading context does not freeze the scene.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Reusing the old list proves that the deleted light still exists.
statements.explanation: A cached observation is not current evidence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The agent should resolve the target again before changing it.
statements.explanation: A fresh lookup checks continued existence and identity.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The deletion changes the historical resource response into a protocol error.
statements.explanation: The earlier response can have been valid when produced.

questions.stem: Two engine servers both expose a tool described as creating an object. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An identical tool description proves identical side effects.
statements.explanation: Contracts and observed behavior must also be checked.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A reusable agent can share high-level intent while using different adapters.
statements.explanation: Portability can live above engine-specific operations.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Their created objects may have different engine-specific semantics.
statements.explanation: An Actor and a GameObject are not interchangeable serialized objects.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A shared protocol makes their asset files mutually loadable.
statements.explanation: Asset formats are outside that guarantee.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Their argument schemas may differ.
statements.explanation: MCP standardizes communication rather than a universal game-editor API.

questions.stem: A scene-building agent may inspect, edit and test repeatedly. Its operator sets a maximum of ten edit attempts and requires it to report unresolved failures. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reaching ten attempts establishes that the scene is correct.
statements.explanation: The limit is a stopping condition, not an acceptance condition.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The attempt limit bounds a possible repair loop.
statements.explanation: Repeated unsuccessful edits cannot continue indefinitely under that policy.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The agent should compare observed state with the requested outcome after an edit.
statements.explanation: Tool invocation is only one step in verification.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Preserving failure evidence helps a human decide the next step.
statements.explanation: Unresolved symptoms are useful diagnostic context.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Removing a failing requirement is equivalent to satisfying it.
statements.explanation: Changing the target hides failure rather than fixes it.

questions.source: Foundational: Spark versus an editor bridge
questions.stem: Unity Spark is presented as a browser-based game-creation experience. A Unity MCP integration connects an external assistant to editor capabilities. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A team should evaluate either workflow against its actual game requirements.
statements.explanation: Product labels are not acceptance evidence.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Using the same vendor's products establishes that their project workflows are interchangeable.
statements.explanation: Workflow compatibility needs evidence.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Spark is the expanded spelling of the MCP acronym.
statements.explanation: MCP means Model Context Protocol.

statements.label: D
statements.text: These descriptions identify different product roles.
statements.explanation: A creation experience and an integration interface serve different purposes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A Spark demonstration does not establish which tools an installed MCP server exposes.
statements.explanation: The server's own capabilities need inspection.

questions.stem: A vendor note says an older in-editor MCP server is deprecated and a CLI-hosted MCP server replaces it. A Unity team uses the older server. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A replacement server can be assumed to preserve every old tool name.
statements.explanation: The replacement's catalog and contracts must be checked.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The team should identify its installed integration before changing configuration.
statements.explanation: The note applies to a particular component.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Deleting the project's scenes is a necessary first migration step.
statements.explanation: Connection migration does not justify deleting game content.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Deprecating one server means that the MCP protocol itself has been retired.
statements.explanation: A component lifecycle is not a protocol lifecycle.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The team should verify the replacement in a small project before migrating production work.
statements.explanation: A bounded trial exposes compatibility problems.

questions.stem: A Unity automation package offers both direct commands and an MCP interface to its editor operations. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The same high-level task may be automated without language-model inference.
statements.explanation: Scripted automation can invoke known operations directly.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Direct commands make authorization unnecessary because no MCP message is involved.
statements.explanation: The commands can still change project state.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A tool-based interface can expose structured inputs for an operation.
statements.explanation: A schema can describe the accepted arguments.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An agent's supported interfaces affect which route is usable.
statements.explanation: Some hosts expose tools while others can run commands.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Both routes still require checking the editor operation's result.
statements.explanation: Interface choice does not prove correctness.

questions.stem: Two Unity projects are open and each contains a scene called Arena. An agent is asked to add a light to one project's Arena scene. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A successful tool connection proves that it targets the correct project.
statements.explanation: Connectivity does not identify the user's intended workspace.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The most recently opened editor is necessarily the requested target.
statements.explanation: Recency is not user intent.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The agent should verify project identity as well as scene identity.
statements.explanation: A shared scene name is ambiguous across projects.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A light appearing in either Arena satisfies the request.
statements.explanation: The destination project is part of the requirement.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Matching the scene name is sufficient to select the intended project.
statements.explanation: Both projects satisfy that name.

questions.stem: A Unity scene contains twenty instances of a lamp prefab. The request is to make just one named lamp blue while leaving the other lamps as they are. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The intended scope is the selected instance.
statements.explanation: The request identifies one placed lamp.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The agent should verify the other lamps after editing.
statements.explanation: That checks the stated preservation requirement.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Applying the selected instance's change to the prefab asset preserves a one-instance scope.
statements.explanation: Applying a change can propagate it to other instances.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Editing a shared material asset is guaranteed to affect only the selected lamp.
statements.explanation: Other objects may reference the same material.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Deleting the prefab asset is a reasonable way to isolate the selected lamp.
statements.explanation: That damages the reusable asset rather than scopes the edit.

questions.stem: An agent changes a Unity script, then tries to configure a component whose new serialized field is missing. The editor reports compilation errors. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The compilation errors should be investigated before assuming the new field is available.
statements.explanation: The revised script may not have loaded successfully.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Hiding console errors makes the new component definition usable.
statements.explanation: Display filtering does not fix compilation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The agent should inspect the component after the editor has successfully processed the script.
statements.explanation: That checks the actual loaded state.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The text file being saved is weaker evidence than successful compilation.
statements.explanation: Saving bytes does not validate code.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Repeating the field assignment repairs a compiler error in the script.
statements.explanation: The cause must be corrected in the code or dependencies.

questions.stem: A Unity tool reports a successful scene edit. After closing and reopening the project, the change is missing. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The missing change proves that the language model forgot the scene.
statements.explanation: Project persistence is an editor/storage issue, not conversational memory.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The agent should verify which scene and project were actually saved.
statements.explanation: Saving the wrong target does not persist the intended change.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Reopening the saved scene is a useful persistence check.
statements.explanation: It tests that the change survives reload.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The success result may describe a completed mutation without describing a completed save.
statements.explanation: The tool contract determines what success means.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The investigation should distinguish in-memory state from saved scene state.
statements.explanation: An edit can exist in memory without durable persistence.

questions.stem: A texture file has been copied into a Unity project. The editor is still importing it when an agent tries to assign it to a material. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The agent should wait for the import result before relying on the asset.
statements.explanation: A copied file may not yet be an available engine asset.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Import errors are relevant evidence if the asset remains unavailable.
statements.explanation: The processing step can fail independently of file copying.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A file's presence proves that the editor has finished processing it.
statements.explanation: Filesystem presence and engine readiness are different states.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Assigning a placeholder proves that the requested texture was imported.
statements.explanation: A placeholder does not verify the requested asset.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Creating more copies is the appropriate way to wait for import completion.
statements.explanation: Duplicates add ambiguity rather than resolve readiness.

questions.stem: A hypothetical Unity placement tool accepts local position. A parent object is translated ten units along an axis and has identity rotation and scale. Its child is assigned local position zero. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Renaming the child changes the coordinate space used by the tool.
statements.explanation: Names do not change transform semantics.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Local position zero puts the child at the world origin despite the parent translation.
statements.explanation: The parent's transform contributes to world position.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The child lies at the parent's world position.
statements.explanation: Zero local offset places it at the parent origin.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A world-origin requirement needs a conversion or a tool that accepts world coordinates.
statements.explanation: The tool's coordinate contract matters.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Reading the world transform verifies the intended placement.
statements.explanation: The requested outcome is expressed in world space.

questions.stem: A Unity agent changes one wall's material color. Several other walls change too. The walls reference the same material asset. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A screenshot of only the selected wall establishes that the scope was correct.
statements.explanation: It does not show unintended changes elsewhere.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The intended scope should determine whether to edit the shared asset or use an appropriate per-object solution.
statements.explanation: The desired propagation is a design choice.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The additional color changes establish an MCP transport fault.
statements.explanation: Shared asset semantics already explain them.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The shared reference explains why an asset edit can affect several walls.
statements.explanation: They consume the same material definition.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Moving the selected wall to a different position makes its material reference independent.
statements.explanation: Transform changes do not clone materials.

questions.stem: A team proposes a hypothetical tool that changes the intensity of one identified light instead of granting an agent a general script evaluator. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Reporting the previous and resulting intensity supports review and recovery.
statements.explanation: The record describes the actual change.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A narrow tool's existence proves its implementation has no bugs.
statements.explanation: Implementation quality still needs verification.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A free-text request to be careful provides the same enforcement as argument validation.
statements.explanation: Instruction following is not a technical validation boundary.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The tool still needs authorization to modify the project.
statements.explanation: A narrow operation remains a write.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Validating light identity and an allowed intensity range narrows the operation.
statements.explanation: The tool can enforce a specific contract.

questions.stem: A team receives a playable prototype from an AI-assisted game-creation workflow and wants to use it as the basis for a Unity release. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The team's target-device performance budget remains relevant.
statements.explanation: A preview does not establish release performance.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The ability to create a prototype establishes support for the team's required export workflow.
statements.explanation: Export and integration capabilities require separate verification.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The prototype should be tested against explicit controls and win/lose conditions.
statements.explanation: Being playable does not establish requirement coverage.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A convincing demonstration proves the project can be maintained by the team.
statements.explanation: Maintainability requires inspecting and working with the deliverable.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The team needs evidence about asset rights and dependencies.
statements.explanation: Generated output does not settle provenance or distribution conditions.

questions.stem: An Unreal MCP service exposes editor operations to an external assistant. A designer asks whether this makes the assistant part of the shipped game's AI. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A successful editor query demonstrates that an NPC makes correct runtime decisions.
statements.explanation: The query does not exercise the NPC's behavior.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A tool that places an Actor can help construct a level.
statements.explanation: Placement is an editor operation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The editor connection replaces the packaged game's gameplay code.
statements.explanation: The built game still needs gameplay logic.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Connecting an editor assistant installs its reasoning loop into each NPC.
statements.explanation: Runtime behavior requires its own implementation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Editor automation and runtime game AI are different roles.
statements.explanation: One changes the project; the other controls behavior during play.

questions.stem: An Unreal editor MCP endpoint responds, but the agent cannot find the expected scene-editing tools. The integration loads its tools from separately enabled toolsets. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The agent should inspect the actual catalog after configuration changes.
statements.explanation: That verifies which tools are available now.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A reachable endpoint does not establish that the needed operation is installed.
statements.explanation: Connectivity is only one prerequisite.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Changing the requested Actor's label adds a missing tool to the server.
statements.explanation: Actor metadata does not register tool implementations.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Toolset enablement is relevant to the missing catalog.
statements.explanation: The endpoint and the exposed operations are separate components.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A reachable endpoint proves that every optional toolset is active.
statements.explanation: The stem states that tools are separately enabled.

questions.source: Foundational: Actor instance versus Blueprint class
questions.stem: An Unreal level contains twelve Actors created from one Blueprint class. A designer asks for one placed Actor to start with a different health value. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Testing the selected Actor and unchanged peers helps verify scope.
statements.explanation: Both the intended change and preservation requirement matter.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Deleting the Blueprint class is required before an instance can differ.
statements.explanation: The class/instance model supports instance customization where exposed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The request identifies an instance-level customization.
statements.explanation: Only one placed object is named.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The agent should inspect existing overrides before assuming propagation.
statements.explanation: Overrides can change which value is used.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Changing a class default can have broader effects than changing that instance.
statements.explanation: Other instances may inherit the class default.

questions.stem: An Unreal Actor has a visible mesh but no configured collision response for a projectile. A hypothetical agent tool can inspect and configure its components. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A screenshot of the mesh is enough to validate projectile blocking.
statements.explanation: The interaction needs to be exercised.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The investigation should include collision components and their response settings.
statements.explanation: Rendering and collision are separate concerns.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Reconnecting MCP directly repairs the collision settings.
statements.explanation: A connection is not a gameplay configuration change.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Renaming the Actor to Wall configures its collision response.
statements.explanation: Labels do not define physical behavior.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A visible mesh establishes that projectile collision is configured correctly.
statements.explanation: Visibility does not demonstrate collision behavior.

questions.stem: An agent changes a Blueprint graph and reports that it compiles. The requirement is that a door opens only after the player has collected a key. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Compilation is useful evidence that the graph is structurally acceptable to the engine.
statements.explanation: It catches some graph errors.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Removing the key condition is a valid repair if the door previously failed to open.
statements.explanation: That violates the requirement.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Playing the no-key and has-key cases tests the stated condition.
statements.explanation: Both branches matter for the requirement.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Seeing the open-door animation proves that the no-key case is blocked.
statements.explanation: It covers only an opening outcome.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Compilation establishes that the key condition is implemented correctly.
statements.explanation: A valid graph can encode wrong logic.

questions.stem: An Unreal integration documents that tool invocations execute serially on the game thread. An agent must create an Actor and then configure it. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Adding more client threads guarantees a higher editor mutation rate.
statements.explanation: The documented execution path remains serial.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Configuration should use the identity returned or resolved after creation.
statements.explanation: The target must exist before the dependent operation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A slow operation can delay subsequent work in the same queue.
statements.explanation: Serial execution creates ordering dependencies.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Issuing both calls concurrently proves configuration runs after creation.
statements.explanation: Submission timing does not establish the required dependency.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The client should respect the integration's sequencing contract.
statements.explanation: Unsupported overlapping calls can cause failures or ambiguity.

questions.stem: An editor MCP service is configured for same-machine access without a remote authentication layer. A teammate suggests exposing its port to the internet so a remote agent can connect. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The team should inspect the integration's documented network limitations.
statements.explanation: Those limitations affect safe deployment.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The proposed network exposure changes the security boundary.
statements.explanation: Remote callers would gain a new route to editor operations.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Keeping the client near the editor can avoid exposing the editor endpoint publicly.
statements.explanation: A local connector can communicate with the editor on the same machine.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A remote workflow needs a supported design with appropriate access controls.
statements.explanation: Local assumptions are not a remote security design.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Changing the listening address supplies user authentication.
statements.explanation: Address binding controls reachability, not identity verification.

questions.stem: An agent places Actors in an Unreal level and observes them in the editor. The requested deliverable is a saved level another teammate can open. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An editor screenshot establishes that all needed packages were saved.
statements.explanation: It shows appearance, not persistence.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A successful tool invocation makes version-control review redundant.
statements.explanation: Review is still needed to see what files changed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Saving an unrelated level satisfies the request if the Actors remain visible.
statements.explanation: The requested level must contain the durable edits.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The level's saved state must be verified.
statements.explanation: Visible in-memory state is not the complete deliverable.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Required referenced assets must also be available to the teammate.
statements.explanation: A level may depend on other content.

questions.stem: A hypothetical Unreal MCP tool can launch an automation test for a pressure plate. The test should open a door when a player stands on the plate. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Writing the door's open flag directly is sufficient to test the pressure plate.
statements.explanation: That bypasses the causal path.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The test should trigger the interaction through a representative player action.
statements.explanation: This exercises the behavior under test.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The agent should retain the actual test outcome and diagnostics.
statements.explanation: The evidence supports acceptance and troubleshooting.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A test launch acknowledgment is equivalent to a passing result.
statements.explanation: Starting and completing successfully are separate events.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The test should observe the door state after an appropriate wait or condition.
statements.explanation: It must measure the result.

questions.stem: An Unreal agent edits an Actor visible during a play session, but the designer expected a persistent change to the authoring level. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The agent should determine whether it edited a runtime instance or authoring data.
statements.explanation: The two states have different persistence roles.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Extending the play session ensures the value is saved to the authoring level.
statements.explanation: Elapsed play time is not a save operation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The designer's request is satisfied by a screenshot of the temporary instance.
statements.explanation: The requirement was persistence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The intended change should be verified after ending play and reopening the saved level.
statements.explanation: That checks the deliverable the designer requested.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A value observed during play proves the level asset contains that value.
statements.explanation: Runtime state can differ from saved authoring state.

questions.stem: Two Unreal Actors reference one material instance asset. A designer wants only the first Actor's appearance to change. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Changing the Actor label breaks its material reference.
statements.explanation: Label changes do not make shared assets independent.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The second Actor is part of the verification set.
statements.explanation: It must remain unchanged.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The word instance in the asset's name proves it is private to one Actor.
statements.explanation: A material instance asset can have multiple consumers.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Editing the referenced asset may affect both Actors.
statements.explanation: They share the same material instance asset.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The agent must choose a solution whose ownership matches the requested scope.
statements.explanation: An independent asset or suitable per-object runtime approach may be appropriate.

questions.stem: A studio adds a hypothetical custom tool that replaces selected placeholder Actors with approved props. It must preserve each placeholder's transform. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The tool should validate the replacement asset and all target identities before making changes.
statements.explanation: Preflight checks reduce partial failures.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Comparing before/after transforms checks a key invariant.
statements.explanation: The task explicitly requires transform preservation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The result should identify replaced objects and any failures.
statements.explanation: A per-target record makes partial completion visible.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An aggregate success message establishes that every transform was preserved.
statements.explanation: The invariant needs per-object evidence.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Deleting the placeholders first is sufficient validation of replacement availability.
statements.explanation: Deletion does not establish that replacement can succeed.

questions.section: Agent security and local versus cloud execution
questions.source: Foundational: local server and cloud model
