statements.text: If the path does not lead to a node, get_node returns an empty node object and no error appears, so mistakes are silent.
statements.explanation: Godot's reference says that when the path does not point to a valid node, get_node generates an error and returns null.

questions.stem: A bullet node in a Godot game must be removed when it hits a wall. Check each statement about doing it.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Once queue_free() has been called, the bullet's other callbacks in the same frame can no longer run.
statements.explanation: The node is only deleted at the end of the frame, so its callbacks can still run until then.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Calling queue_free() twice on the same node is an error, because the second call finds the node already queued.
statements.explanation: The reference says it is safe to call queue_free more than once.

statements.label: C
statements.text: free() deletes the node immediately, so code that still holds a reference to it and uses it afterwards can fail.
statements.explanation: free removes the object at once, and old references to it become invalid.

statements.label: D
statements.text: queue_free() queues the node for deletion at the end of the current frame, and until then the node can still be accessed.
statements.explanation: Godot's reference says queue_free queues the node for deletion at the end of the frame and that it can still be accessed before then.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Freeing the bullet with queue_free() also frees all of its child nodes.
statements.explanation: The reference says freeing a node also frees all of its children.

questions.stem: A game developer wants the vocabulary for 2D art straight before instructing a coding agent. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A texture is image data applied to a surface or drawn; a sprite uses a texture, but the words are not synonyms.
statements.explanation: Texture names the image data, sprite names the thing drawn from it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A sprite is a 2D image, or one frame of one, drawn as an object in the game scene.
statements.explanation: A sprite is the drawn 2D object; its pixels come from a texture.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A 32 x 48 pixel image has a resolution of 32 by 48 pixels, which is 1,536 pixels in all.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The same 32 x 32 sprite appears larger when the viewport is scaled up, so file pixels and on-screen size differ.
statements.explanation: On-screen size depends on the scale applied at display time, not on the file's pixel dimensions alone.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Resolution is the shape of an image, such as 16:9, while aspect ratio is its total pixel count in millions.
statements.explanation: The two are swapped: resolution is the pixel dimensions, aspect ratio is the width-to-height proportion.

questions.stem: An image generator returns a reference picture of 1,024 x 873 pixels. The game is drawn in a 640 x 360 viewport (a 16:9 shape, ratio about 1.78). The developer wants to place the picture in the game. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Stretching it to exactly 640 x 360 distorts it: its ratio is about 1.17 and the viewport's about 1.78.
statements.explanation: 1,024 / 873 is about 1.17 and 640 / 360 is about 1.78, so non-uniform scaling changes the proportions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A 40-pixel-tall sprite takes up about a quarter of this viewport's height, so it would dominate the screen.
statements.explanation: 40 / 360 is about 11 percent, closer to one ninth than one quarter.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Enlarging a low-resolution picture by interpolation adds real detail that was missing from the original.
statements.explanation: Interpolation creates more pixels but not more information; the added detail is guessed, not recovered.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Fitting the picture inside 640 x 360 without stretching gives exactly 640 x 360 pixels, because the viewport sets the size.
statements.explanation: Keeping the ratio leaves unused space on one axis; only a stretched copy fills both dimensions exactly.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Fitting the picture inside 640 x 360 without stretching gives an image about 422 pixels wide and 360 tall.
statements.explanation: The scale factor is 360 / 873, about 0.412, so the width becomes 1,024 x 0.412, about 422.

questions.stem: A developer asks an image generator for a character sprite 'on a transparent background' and receives a file named hero.jpg. In the engine the sprite appears inside a white rectangle. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Setting the sprite node's opacity to 50 percent makes the white rectangle transparent while the character stays opaque.
statements.explanation: Node opacity fades the whole image, character and white background alike.

statements.label: B
statements.text: JPEG has no alpha channel, so a .jpg file cannot hold transparency no matter what the prompt asked.
statements.explanation: Godot's documentation notes that JPEG does not support transparency.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A white background painted into the pixels is content, not transparency; remove it and save as PNG or another format with alpha.
statements.explanation: Transparency needs an alpha value per pixel, which PNG stores and JPEG does not.

statements.label: D
statements.text: After removing a white background by colour, light fringe pixels can remain around the character's edge.
statements.explanation: Anti-aliased edge pixels are a blend of the character and the old background, so a colour key misses them.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A pixel with an alpha of 255 in an 8-bit channel is fully transparent and shows nothing of its colour.
statements.explanation: 255 is fully opaque; 0 is fully transparent.

questions.stem: A 32 x 32 pixel-art sprite is shown in a game at four times its size (128 x 128 screen pixels). At its original size it looks crisp, but in the running game its edges look blurry and smeared. The developer asks a coding agent to fix it. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Nearest filtering takes the colour of the single closest texel, so enlarged pixel art keeps hard edges.
statements.explanation: Nearest samples one texel per screen pixel, producing blocks.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The right fix is to regenerate the sprite at a higher resolution and keep the same filtering, since extra pixels resist blur.
statements.explanation: More pixels still get blended by linear filtering; the cause is the sampling mode, not the source size.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The instruction 'make it sharper' tells the agent that the texture filter should be set to nearest.
statements.explanation: The word does not name the setting; the agent may sharpen the image file or change something else.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Linear filtering blends neighbouring texels when a texture is enlarged, which softens hard pixel edges into blur.
statements.explanation: Linear filtering interpolates between neighbouring texels.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A filter mode set as the project-wide default applies to each sprite that does not set its own, while a mode set on one sprite applies only to that sprite.
statements.explanation: Scope follows where the setting is placed: a default covers everything that does not override it, and a setting on one sprite covers only that sprite (in Godot 4 this is the node's texture filter, which can inherit the project default).

questions.stem: A pixel-art game is drawn in a 640 x 360 viewport with nearest filtering, and the window shows it scaled up to fill the screen. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A non-integer scale is harmless to pixel art as long as nearest filtering is on.
statements.explanation: Nearest filtering makes the unevenness visible as pixels of different widths.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In a 1,600 x 900 window the scale is 2.5, so some source pixels cover 2 screen pixels and others 3.
statements.explanation: 1,600 / 640 = 900 / 360 = 2.5; nearest filtering rounds each pixel to a whole number of screen pixels.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In a 1,280 x 720 window the scale is exactly 2, so each source pixel becomes a 2 x 2 block of screen pixels.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Switching to linear filtering removes the uneven pixel widths at a non-integer scale with no other change to the look.
statements.explanation: Linear filtering hides the unevenness by blurring everything.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In a 1,366 x 768 window the scale is exactly 2 in both directions.
statements.explanation: 1,366 / 640 is about 2.13 and 768 / 360 is about 2.13, neither a whole number.

questions.stem: A developer is deciding which of four things to ask a coding agent to create or use: a sprite sheet, a texture atlas, a tileset and a tilemap. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A sprite sheet is one image holding the frames of an animation, typically in a regular grid of equal cells.
statements.explanation: This is the usual meaning, and the engine slices it into frames.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An atlas packs many separate images, often of different sizes, into one texture with a record of each rectangle.
statements.explanation: Its purpose is to reduce texture switching so more sprites can be drawn together.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A tilemap is the image file holding all the tile artwork, and a tileset is the painted level layout.
statements.explanation: The two terms are swapped.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A sprite sheet and a tileset can both be a single PNG laid out as a grid; they differ in how the engine uses the cells.
statements.explanation: A sheet's cells are played in order as frames, while a tileset's cells are placed individually on the map.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A tileset is a library of reusable tiles; a tilemap is the level grid whose cells each reference one of them.
statements.explanation: The tileset supplies the pieces and the tilemap places them.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: tileset or tilemap
questions.stem: A designer wants to paint cave levels quickly with 16 x 16 pixel tiles for floor, wall, ceiling and corners, so a 40 x 22 cell room can be painted with a brush. The designer tells a coding agent: 'make me a cave tilemap'. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The artwork the designer needs is a tileset; 'tilemap' names the painted grid, not the library of tile art.
statements.explanation: The reusable tile images are the tileset.

statements.label: B
statements.text: 'Make me a cave tilemap' is precise enough, because the agent can infer tile size, tile count and edge rules from the word 'cave'.
statements.explanation: Nothing in the phrase fixes tile size, which tiles exist or how edges match.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A precise request gives tile size (16 x 16), the tile types, matching edges, and one PNG with transparency in a grid.
statements.explanation: Each element removes a guess the agent would otherwise make.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The tile size can be left out of the request, because the engine works it out from the image.
statements.explanation: The engine has to be told the size of one tile to cut the image into tiles.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The wording could be met by one 640 x 352 pixel painting of a finished room that cannot be rearranged.
statements.explanation: 40 x 16 = 640 and 22 x 16 = 352; a single picture of that size matches the words but not the need.

questions.stem: An image generator is asked for a four-frame walk cycle 'in one row' and returns a single image of 800 x 200 pixels. The developer slices it as a grid of 4 columns and 1 row and plays the cells in order. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The playback speed of the walk cycle is stored in the image file as part of its pixel data.
statements.explanation: Speed is set in the engine, for example as frames per second on the animation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A frame count of 4 confirms that the four figures are four poses of one character.
statements.explanation: A count says how many cells there are, not whether the figures are the same creature.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the character's feet sit at a different height in each cell, the animation bobs even though each frame looks fine alone.
statements.explanation: Frames must share a baseline and scale to play as one motion.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Equal slicing gives correct frames whether or not the generator spaced the figures evenly, because each figure ends up centred in its cell.
statements.explanation: Slicing cuts at fixed positions; unevenly spaced figures get cut apart or shifted.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Equal slicing gives four cells of 200 x 200 pixels.
statements.explanation: 800 / 4 = 200 wide and the height stays 200.

questions.stem: An interviewer asks why a 2D game with 64 sprites, each a separate 32 x 32 image file, can run better after the images are packed into one 256 x 256 atlas. Check each statement that is true about a sound answer.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An atlas stores fewer pixels in total than the separate images it replaces, which is why it saves memory.
statements.explanation: Padding and unused space can make it larger; the gain is fewer state changes, not fewer pixels.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The 64 sprites of 32 x 32 add up to 65,536 pixels, exactly the area of a 256 x 256 atlas, so the atlas has no room left for padding.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Packing sprites into an atlas changes their on-screen size, so the sprites must be redrawn at the new scale.
statements.explanation: An atlas changes where pixels are stored, not how large the sprite is drawn.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Sprites sharing one texture can often be batched into fewer draw calls, with no texture switch between them.
statements.explanation: Fewer texture switches allow batching.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Without padding, linear filtering or scaling can pull colour from a neighbouring sprite and bleed at the edges.
statements.explanation: Sampling near a sprite's edge can read the next sprite's pixels.

questions.stem: A developer generates a 256 x 256 grass image to repeat across a large ground plane and will tell a coding agent to turn on repeat (tiling) for it. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An image that looks good as a single picture will therefore look right when repeated across a surface.
statements.explanation: Nothing about a single view guarantees the edges line up with their copies.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A seamless (tileable) texture is one whose opposite edges match, so repeated copies show no visible join.
statements.explanation: Seamlessness is a property of the image's edge content.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Making the image tileable requires making it smaller than 256 x 256, so the edges can be blended.
statements.explanation: Tileability depends on matching edges, not on image size.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A seamless texture shows no visible repetition across a large area, however large the area is.
statements.explanation: Without a visible join the pattern can still repeat noticeably when distinctive features recur.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The way to test tileability is to view a single copy at full size, since a seam can only exist at the image's edge.
statements.explanation: A seam is the join between copies, so test with copies placed side by side.

questions.stem: A pixel-art game restricts all art to a 16-colour palette. An image generator is asked for an enemy sprite 'using only these 16 colours', and the returned file is opened in a script that counts its distinct colours. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Counting distinct colours and testing each against the palette is a check a script can do.
statements.explanation: It is an exact, automatable test.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Smoothed or anti-aliased edges introduce in-between colours that are not in the palette, so a count above 16 is likely.
statements.explanation: Blended edge pixels are extra colours.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An indexed-colour image stores a palette plus an index per pixel, so editing palette entries recolours the sprite without changing the index data.
statements.explanation: That separation is what makes palette swaps cheap.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A palette is a fixed set of colours the art draws from, and using one palette across assets helps them look like they belong together.
statements.explanation: A shared palette is a main source of visual consistency in pixel art.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An image generator reliably honours 'only these 16 colours', so counting the colours in the result is unnecessary.
statements.explanation: Generators approximate such constraints; the count is a check that costs nothing.

questions.stem: In Godot, a PNG added to a project is converted by an importer, and its import settings (such as compression mode and mipmaps) are stored in a small text file next to it; that file holds the choices made for this image, which the engine cannot work out from the PNG alone. A developer asks a coding agent to 'make the sprite crisp'. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The small settings file next to the PNG is created by the engine on import, so it can be left out of version control without losing the choices made for the sprite.
statements.explanation: The file records the choices made for the image, which cannot be recovered from the PNG alone, so a clone without it falls back to default import settings; it belongs in version control with the asset.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For 2D pixel art, hardware (VRAM) texture compression is the recommended setting because it makes textures smaller with no visible cost.
statements.explanation: Godot's documentation recommends lossless for pixel art and says VRAM compression shows noticeable artifacts in 2D.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Turning on mipmaps sharpens a sprite that is drawn at its native size.
statements.explanation: Mipmaps are pre-shrunk copies for drawing something smaller; they add memory and do not sharpen.

statements.label: D
statements.text: 'Make the sprite crisp' is precise enough to tell the agent which filter, compression and mipmap settings to change.
statements.explanation: The phrase names a result, not the settings; the agent may change the wrong ones or the image itself.

statements.label: E
statements.text: At runtime the engine uses the imported copy, so changing import settings changes the result without editing the PNG.
statements.explanation: Import settings act between the source file and the game.

questions.stem: A sound effect is stored as uncompressed (PCM) audio with 16 bits per sample, 2 channels (stereo) and 44,100 samples per second. It lasts 10 seconds. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Converting to mono at the same rate and bit depth reduces the data to 441,000 bytes.
statements.explanation: One channel halves the size to 882,000 bytes, not 441,000.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A 5 kHz tone can be captured at 8,000 samples per second, since 5,000 is below 8,000.
statements.explanation: The limit at 8,000 samples per second is 4,000 Hz, so a 5 kHz tone cannot be represented correctly.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The highest frequency this sample rate can represent is half of it, 22,050 Hz.
statements.explanation: A sampled signal can represent frequencies up to half the sample rate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The data size is 44,100 x 2 bytes x 2 channels x 10 s = 1,764,000 bytes.
statements.explanation: 16 bits is 2 bytes per sample per channel.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Raising the sample rate to 88,200 samples per second makes the sound louder.
statements.explanation: Sample rate sets how finely time is sampled and the highest frequency, not the level.

questions.stem: A model generates an 8-bar music track at 120 beats per minute in 4/4 time to loop behind a level, and the developer wants it to loop with no audible gap or jump. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: At 120 BPM in 4/4, eight bars last 16 seconds, which is 705,600 samples at 44,100 Hz.
statements.explanation: 8 bars x 4 beats = 32 beats at 2 beats per second = 16 s; 16 x 44,100 = 705,600.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Cutting the loop at a bar line, not an arbitrary point, keeps the rhythm unbroken across the join.
statements.explanation: A loop that ends mid-bar shifts the beat on every repeat.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A track that sounds smooth when played once from start to end is guaranteed to loop seamlessly.
statements.explanation: A single play never exercises the join between end and start.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A fade-out baked into the end of the file does not matter, because the loop restarts at full volume.
statements.explanation: The fade makes an audible dip followed by a jump back up at each repeat.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A sharp jump between the last and first sample can cause an audible click at the loop point.
statements.explanation: An abrupt jump in value is heard as a click.

questions.source: SFX versus music; lossless versus lossy
questions.stem: A developer is choosing file formats and playback behaviour for a short coin-pickup effect and a three-minute background track. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Lossless audio (WAV, FLAC) keeps all samples; lossy audio (Ogg Vorbis, MP3) discards detail for good.
statements.explanation: Lossy encoding trades information for size.

statements.label: B
statements.text: FLAC is a lossy format, because any compressed audio file has thrown some detail away.
statements.explanation: Compressed does not mean lossy; FLAC compresses without discarding anything.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An effect is usually short, event-triggered and may overlap itself; music is long and usually loops.
statements.explanation: These differences drive format and playback choices.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Converting one lossy file to another lossy format at the same bit rate loses nothing extra, since the rate is unchanged.
statements.explanation: Each lossy encoding discards more detail, so quality degrades with every generation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Once a track is saved as a lossy file, the original uncompressed audio can be rebuilt exactly from it.
statements.explanation: The discarded detail is gone, so only an approximation can be rebuilt.

questions.stem: A game routes sound effects to a bus named SFX and music to a bus named Music. Both feed a Master bus that goes to the speakers. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A bus whose volume is set to 0 dB is silent, because zero means no signal is passed on.
statements.explanation: 0 dB means no change in level (unity gain); silence is a very large negative value.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Raising the SFX bus by 6 dB multiplies the amplitude of the effects on it by 6, which is why small steps are safe.
statements.explanation: 6 dB is a factor of about 2; adding 12 dB gives about 4.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A bus is a channel audio passes through on the way to the output; its volume and effects apply to all sources routed to it.
statements.explanation: Godot's documentation describes a bus as a place audio is channelled through before playback.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Lowering the Music bus by 6 dB cuts the amplitude of all music to roughly half and leaves the SFX bus unchanged.
statements.explanation: A 6 dB change is about a factor of 2 in amplitude, and only sources routed to that bus are affected.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If loud sounds sum past the digital maximum at the Master output, the result clips and distorts.
statements.explanation: Simultaneous sounds sum, and the sum can exceed the maximum representable level.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: polyphony
questions.stem: In a platformer, the coin pickup sound is played by one audio player node limited to a single simultaneous voice. When the player grabs three coins within 0.15 seconds, the sound is heard as one clipped blip. A developer asks a coding agent to 'make the coin sound better'. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Allowing more simultaneous voices on the player lets overlapping copies of the sound be heard together.
statements.explanation: Raising polyphony is the direct fix.

statements.label: B
statements.text: With a limit of one voice, each new play request cuts off the sound still playing, which explains the clipped blip.
statements.explanation: Exceeding the voice limit drops the oldest playing sound.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Playing the sound once when the player first touches a coin, rather than repeatedly during the overlap, makes the cut-off worse.
statements.explanation: Triggering on the transition into overlap reduces repeated play calls.

statements.label: D
statements.text: 'Make the coin sound better' tells the agent that the real problem is the limit on simultaneous voices.
statements.explanation: The phrase names no problem; the agent may re-edit or replace the sound file.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Making the audio file louder fixes the clipped blip, because the sound will survive being cut off.
statements.explanation: Loudness is unrelated to voices being cut off.

questions.stem: A studio is reviewing sprites produced by an image generator for a pixel-art game. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A smoothed, JPEG-compressed picture of pixel-art-looking creatures can be turned into clean pixel art by shrinking it with linear filtering.
statements.explanation: Shrinking blends the artifacts into the result and does not restore a clean grid.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A generated picture can look like pixel art while its 'pixels' are several source pixels wide and blurred, so it sits on no exact grid.
statements.explanation: The look of blocky pixels does not guarantee a true pixel grid.

statements.label: C
statements.text: 'Pixel art' means an image with a retro colour scheme, however it was made.
statements.explanation: The term describes how the image is built, not only how it looks.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Pixel art is authored at a low resolution on a grid, with each pixel placed deliberately.
statements.explanation: Control over individual pixels is what defines the style.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Pixel art is normally shown at a whole-number scale with nearest filtering so each art pixel stays a crisp block.
statements.explanation: Uneven scaling or blending destroys the intended pixel shapes.

questions.stem: A developer is shipping a game that uses an AI-generated sprite and an AI-generated music track. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A generating tool's terms can restrict use, for example to non-commercial work, so read them before shipping.
statements.explanation: Some models and services carry non-commercial terms.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Having written the prompt gives the developer full copyright in the output, in the countries where the game is sold.
statements.explanation: Ownership of generated output depends on the tool's terms and the jurisdiction, and prompts alone may not suffice.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An unrecorded reference image can leave its licence doubt attached to anything generated from it.
statements.explanation: A result derived from an unknown reference inherits the doubt about the reference.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Provenance is the record of an asset's origin: tool and version, prompt and settings, terms, edits and references.
statements.explanation: A provenance log is the evidence trail for an asset.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A provenance record helps regenerate or replace an asset later, since it holds the prompt and settings.
statements.explanation: Recorded settings make an asset reproducible and replaceable.

questions.stem: A modeller makes a simple box in a 3D tool: 8 corner points, 12 straight lines joining them and 6 flat four-sided surfaces. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The 8 points are vertices, the 12 lines are edges and the 6 surfaces are faces.
statements.explanation: These are the three basic parts of a polygon mesh.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A five-sided face is split into 3 triangles for drawing.
statements.explanation: An n-sided face triangulates into n - 2 triangles, and 5 - 2 = 3.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A face is the same thing as a vertex that carries a position and a colour.
statements.explanation: A vertex is a point; a face is a surface bounded by edges between vertices.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Each four-sided face is drawn as two triangles, so the box has 12 triangles.
statements.explanation: GPUs draw triangles; a quad is split into two, and 6 x 2 = 12.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The box has 6 triangles because it has 6 faces.
statements.explanation: Each quad face becomes two triangles, so the box has 12.

questions.stem: A low-poly post is an eight-sided cylinder: 8 rectangular side faces plus a single eight-sided face at each end, with no extra cuts. Triangulation splits an n-sided face into n - 2 triangles. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Removing both end caps leaves 8 triangles.
statements.explanation: The 8 side faces still give 16 triangles.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The post has 24 triangles in total.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The two eight-sided end caps give 12 triangles between them.
statements.explanation: Each cap is 8 - 2 = 6 triangles, so two caps give 12.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Triangle count has no effect on performance, because GPUs process faces rather than triangles.
statements.explanation: GPUs draw triangles, and more of them means more vertex and rasterisation work.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The 8 side faces give 16 triangles between them.
statements.explanation: Each rectangle is two triangles, and 8 x 2 = 16.

questions.source: Vertex count in the tool versus on the GPU
questions.stem: An interviewer says: 'My modelling tool reports 8 vertices for a hard-edged cube, yet the engine's profiler reports 24 vertices for the same cube.' Check each statement that is true as an explanation.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The profiler must be wrong, because a cube has 8 vertices and engines do not add more.
statements.explanation: 8 is the count of corner positions; GPU vertex data duplicates them when attributes differ.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The 24 vertices mean the cube has 24 faces, each drawn separately by the engine.
statements.explanation: The cube still has 6 faces; the extra vertices come from duplicated corners.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A vertex is also split where adjacent faces have different UV coordinates, such as along a UV seam.
statements.explanation: Different UVs at the same position require separate GPU vertices.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A smooth mesh whose faces share normals and UVs at a corner can share one vertex there.
statements.explanation: Shared attributes allow shared vertices.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Three faces meet at each corner with different normals, so the GPU keeps a vertex per face: 8 x 3 = 24.
statements.explanation: A GPU vertex bundles position, normal and UV, so a corner with three normals needs three vertices.

questions.stem: An imported crate has several faces that look black or vanish when viewed from outside. Another crate looks flat although a normal map texture is assigned to it. The developer must name each problem correctly to a coding agent. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A normal map is a texture of per-texel directions that fakes fine detail; it is not the mesh's own normals.
statements.explanation: The mesh normals are geometry data; the normal map is image data.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Recalculating normals to point outward repairs inside-out faces and adds no surface detail from any texture.
statements.explanation: It corrects direction only; detail from a texture is a separate matter.

statements.label: C
statements.text: 'Fix the normals' and 'fix the normal map' are the same instruction, because a normal map is the mesh's own normals saved as an image.
statements.explanation: One recalculates face directions on the mesh, the other repairs or replaces a texture.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A normal is a direction perpendicular to a surface, used for lighting; inward-pointing normals can make faces dark or culled.
statements.explanation: Lighting and culling depend on which way the face points.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Applying a normal map adds real triangles and vertices to the mesh, which is why the surface looks bumpy.
statements.explanation: A normal map changes lighting per pixel and leaves the geometry unchanged.

questions.stem: A coding agent builds a crate mesh and a wood texture. In the engine the texture is missing on one object that was created without unwrapping, and the wood grain looks stretched on another. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A mesh with no UV map still shows an image texture correctly, because the engine computes coordinates from the vertex positions.
statements.explanation: Without UVs the renderer has no mapping from surface to image.

statements.label: B
statements.text: UV coordinates are stored inside the texture image file, next to the pixels they refer to.
statements.explanation: They are stored on the mesh, as a per-vertex attribute.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Stretched wood grain proves the texture image itself has too low a resolution, so a larger file is needed.
statements.explanation: Stretching comes from a mismatch between UV layout and surface shape, not from the image's pixel count.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Unwrapping paints the texture image onto the model; the 2D layout it produces is a by-product that can be ignored.
statements.explanation: Unwrapping produces the 2D layout (the UV map) itself; painting or choosing the image is a separate step.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A UV map gives each vertex a 2D (u, v) coordinate in the texture, saying which part of the image lands where on the surface.
statements.explanation: UVs are the link between a 3D surface and a 2D image.

questions.stem: A modeller creates a post with a metal pole and a red cloth pennant. The object has two material slots, one holding a metal material and one holding a cloth material, and every face is assigned to one of the slots. The model is exported to glTF and imported into an engine. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Renaming a slot changes nothing about how its faces look; the material it holds decides that.
statements.explanation: A slot name is a label.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A material slot is a numbered position on an object that holds a material; each face uses one slot.
statements.explanation: Faces point at slots, and slots point at materials.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Each extra material typically adds at least one draw call, so ten cost more to draw than one.
statements.explanation: Surfaces with different materials generally cannot be drawn in a single call.

statements.label: D
statements.text: After import, the metal and cloth faces typically become separate surfaces with their own materials.
statements.explanation: glTF keeps one primitive per material, and engines import them as separate surfaces.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A texture and a material are the same thing, since a material is an image applied to faces.
statements.explanation: A material defines how a surface is shaded and may use textures as inputs.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: origin and pivot
questions.stem: A developer asks a coding agent for 'a door' model. When the door is placed in a level and rotated by script, it swings about its middle instead of its edge. A crate model, 1 m tall, that the agent also built sinks halfway into the floor when placed at floor height, y = 0. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The crate sinks because its origin is at its centre: at y = 0, half of its 1 m height is below the floor.
statements.explanation: A 1 m crate centred on the origin extends 0.5 m below it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: 'Make a door' already specifies where the origin goes, so the agent will place it at the hinge.
statements.explanation: The phrase names the object, not its pivot, so the agent can choose any origin.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The origin (pivot) is the point an object's position and rotation refer to; a swinging door needs it on the hinge edge.
statements.explanation: Rotation happens about the origin.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Moving an object's origin to a new point moves its visible geometry along with it, since the two are one thing.
statements.explanation: Tools can reposition the origin while the geometry stays where it is.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A door whose origin is at its centre will swing about its hinge once the script rotates the node by 90 degrees.
statements.explanation: Rotation about the centre keeps the centre fixed; it cannot make a door swing about its edge, whatever the angle.

questions.stem: An engine treats 1 unit as 1 metre, and its player character is 1.8 units tall. A modeller who was thinking in centimetres builds a tree 540 units tall, and the file is exported and imported with no conversion. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The quickest correct fix is to make the player character 300 times taller so the proportions match.
statements.explanation: That would break every other object sized in metres.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Scaling the tree node to 0.01 in the engine is as good as fixing the mesh, because collision and physics ignore node scale.
statements.explanation: Scaled nodes carry their scale into collision and anything built from them, which engines advise avoiding.

statements.label: C
statements.text: glTF stores distances in centimetres, so the engine converts the tree down on import.
statements.explanation: glTF specifies metres for all linear distances, so nothing is converted.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Units are only labels, so physics settings such as gravity behave the same for large and small models alike.
statements.explanation: Physics is tuned for metre-scale objects, so wrongly sized objects behave wrongly.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The tree appears 540 m tall in the engine, which is 300 times the player's height of 1.8 m.
statements.explanation: 540 / 1.8 = 300, and 1 unit is 1 m.

questions.stem: In a modelling tool, a modeller adds a cube whose mesh is 2 m on each side and scales the object to (0.1, 0.1, 0.9) to make a pole that looks 0.2 x 0.2 x 1.8 m. The object is exported without applying transforms. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Applying transforms can only be done on the engine side, because exporters cannot bake them.
statements.explanation: The step belongs in the modelling tool before export.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The mesh data still describes a 2 m cube; only the object's scale makes it look like a pole.
statements.explanation: Scale lives on the object and the vertices are unchanged.

statements.label: C
statements.text: After applying the scale, the object's scale is (1, 1, 1) and the vertices themselves are 0.2 x 0.2 x 1.8 m apart.
statements.explanation: Apply bakes the object's scale into the vertex positions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In the engine the node carries a non-unit scale, which anything built from it, such as a collider, inherits.
statements.explanation: The exporter writes the object scale onto the node.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Applying the scale changes how the pole looks in the viewport, since the vertices move.
statements.explanation: Apply keeps the appearance identical and changes only where the numbers are stored.

questions.stem: A modelling tool treats +Z as up, while glTF and Godot treat +Y as up. A person 1.8 m tall is modelled standing along Z. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: With the exporter's up-axis conversion on, the 1.8 m height arrives along Y.
statements.explanation: The conversion maps the tool's Z extent onto Y.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Unreal Engine's editor is also Y-up, so no conversion is needed for it.
statements.explanation: Epic's documentation says the Unreal Editor uses a Z-up axis.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Rotating each imported node by 90 degrees in the level scripts fixes the orientation at the source, so any other tool that opens the asset will also see it upright.
statements.explanation: The node rotation only hides the problem on that instance: it must be repeated wherever the model is used, and the asset's own axes, pivot and child nodes stay in the wrong frame.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Up axis and handedness are the same property, so fixing one fixes the other.
statements.explanation: Handedness describes how the axes are arranged (right- or left-handed); the up axis is a separate choice.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the exporter does no axis conversion, the person arrives lying on their side in Godot, with the 1.8 m extent along Z.
statements.explanation: The height stays on the Z axis, which is not up in Godot.

questions.stem: A developer asks a coding agent to 'export the model for the engine'. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: glTF 2.0 is an open interchange format: .glb is one binary file, while .gltf is a text description plus separate data files.
statements.explanation: GLB is the single-file form and glTF the text-plus-files form.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A single glTF 2.0 asset can describe meshes, materials, textures, a skeleton and animations together, which is why it suits rigged and textured props.
statements.explanation: glTF's scene description covers geometry, materials, textures, skins and animations, so one export can carry a whole prop.

statements.label: C
statements.text: 'Export the model for the engine' already fixes format, up axis, scale and what to include.
statements.explanation: The phrase names none of them, so each is left to the agent's defaults.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The OBJ format carries skeletal skinning and animation as well as geometry, which is why studios favour it.
statements.explanation: Godot's documentation says OBJ does not support skinning, animation, UV2 or PBR materials.

statements.label: E
statements.text: glTF carries a modelling tool's custom shader node graphs into the engine unchanged, so the looks match.
statements.explanation: glTF carries a metallic-roughness material model; tool-specific node graphs do not cross.

questions.stem: A level contains a stone archway the player must walk through and a loose boulder the player can push. The developer asks a coding agent to give both 'accurate mesh collision'. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Concave shapes are the most accurate and also the cheapest for the physics engine to process.
statements.explanation: Godot's documentation calls them the slowest option.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In Godot, concave shapes are only usable on static bodies, so a pushable boulder needs a convex or primitive shape.
statements.explanation: Godot's documentation says concave shapes work within static bodies only.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A concave (trimesh) shape can follow the arch's opening, so the player can walk through it.
statements.explanation: Concave shapes follow the mesh's triangles exactly.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A convex hull of the archway is the smallest convex shape around it, so it fills the opening and blocks the player.
statements.explanation: A convex shape cannot have a hole or dent, so the opening disappears.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A roughly round boulder is usually well served by a primitive sphere or a convex hull, which cost less than a trimesh.
statements.explanation: Simple shapes are cheaper and adequate for a nearly convex object.

questions.source: Collider is not the visual mesh
questions.stem: A character model has 30,000 triangles, including a cape, a sword and a hat plume. A developer tells a coding agent: 'use the model's mesh as its collider'. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In Godot, a trimesh collider is a poor fit for a moving character: concave shapes are slow and work only on static bodies.
statements.explanation: Godot's documentation restricts concave shapes to static bodies and calls them the slowest.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A collider should match the visible silhouette, so the cape and sword block the player as they look.
statements.explanation: Matching every protrusion makes the character catch on scenery and costs more.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A collider is sized from what should feel solid, such as a capsule around the body, even if the cape extends outside it.
statements.explanation: Collision is about gameplay fairness, not the visible outline.

statements.label: D
statements.text: 'A capsule collider 0.4 m in radius and 1.8 m tall' is more precise because it states shape and size.
statements.explanation: It names the shape and its dimensions, removing the guess.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The collision shape is a separate thing from the visible mesh and may be far simpler than it.
statements.explanation: Collision geometry is authored or chosen separately from the visual mesh, and simple shapes are the norm.

questions.stem: A scene shows 50 identical trees of 12,000 triangles each (600,000 triangles in all). Up close the detail matters; far away the trees are small on the screen. A developer asks a coding agent to add levels of detail (LOD), with a 1,500-triangle version for distant trees. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If 40 trees are far enough to use the 1,500-triangle version, they cost 60,000 triangles instead of 480,000.

statements.label: B
statements.text: LOD keeps several versions of a mesh with decreasing triangle counts; the engine picks one by distance or screen size.
statements.explanation: That is the definition of level of detail.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The lower-detail meshes are free: they add nothing to the project's storage or load time.
statements.explanation: Each extra version is more data that has to be stored and loaded.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Switching between LOD versions is not noticeable to the player, because the versions are built to match.
statements.explanation: A visible pop can occur when the engine switches versions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: LOD cuts the triangles processed per tree but does not by itself reduce the number of trees drawn.
statements.explanation: Each visible tree is still drawn once, just with a smaller mesh.

questions.stem: A developer wants a coding agent to produce a crate model reproducibly. The agent writes a Python file that uses Blender's built-in Python API, bpy, and runs Blender with no window (background mode) to execute it as one step of an automated build. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An automated build step can judge whether the script step succeeded from the error text in the log; the process's exit status adds nothing to that.
statements.explanation: The log text and the process's exit status are two separate signals; an automated step reads the exit status as its machine-checkable verdict, and a program can print an error and still exit with status 0, so the status has to be checked as well.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the script finishes without an error, the exported model is correct, since the script produced it.
statements.explanation: A script can run cleanly and still encode a wrong assumption about size, axes or scale.

statements.label: C
statements.text: bpy is Blender's Python interface, so a script can build, modify and export scenes without anyone clicking.
statements.explanation: Scripts call the same operations the interface does.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A script can be reviewed, diffed and rerun to regenerate the asset; live clicks leave no such record.
statements.explanation: A script is a reproducible, reviewable recipe.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Background mode means the script cannot read the mesh or write files, because there is no window.
statements.explanation: Background mode runs the same data operations and exports without an interface.

questions.source: What an MCP server lets an agent do
questions.stem: A developer connects a coding agent to Blender through an MCP server and a Blender add-on, so the agent can act on a Blender window that is open. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A conversation of MCP tool calls is as easy to regenerate and review as a script file, since each call is logged.
statements.explanation: Live tool calls leave a transcript, while a script is a single artifact that can be diffed and rerun.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The server relays tool calls to Blender, which carries them out and returns results; the model does not run inside Blender.
statements.explanation: The model stays in the agent; Blender executes the requested actions.

statements.label: C
statements.text: MCP gives the agent modelling skill that the underlying model did not already have, by teaching it Blender.
statements.explanation: MCP supplies access to actions and results, not new capability in the model.

statements.label: D
statements.text: MCP is a standard way for an agent to discover and call tools that a separate program exposes.
statements.explanation: MCP defines how tools are listed and invoked.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An unguarded run-code tool lets anything that reaches the connection run code as the user, so keep it local and trusted.
statements.explanation: Executing generated code without checks is a real exposure.

questions.stem: An agent reports that an exported prop 'looks right'. The developer wants numbers a headless test can check after the model is imported into the engine. The prop should be 0.2 x 1.8 x 0.2 m (width, height, depth, with Y up), sit on the floor when placed at y = 0, be at unit scale, and have two materials named PostMetal and PennantRed. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The lowest point of the mesh should sit at y = 0 relative to the node when the origin was set at the base.
statements.explanation: That is what makes the prop stand on the floor when placed at y = 0.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The node's scale should be (1, 1, 1); a 2 m cube wearing scale (0.1, 0.9, 0.1) would look right yet fail.
statements.explanation: Looking right and carrying the right numbers are different things.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The mesh's bounding box should measure (0.2, 1.8, 0.2) m; (0.2, 0.2, 1.8) would mean it lies on its side.
statements.explanation: The extents reveal which axis the height ended up on.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Passing all of these checks shows the prop looks good under the game's lighting and reads as a post.
statements.explanation: These checks measure geometry and names; appearance needs a person looking at a render.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The names of the imported surfaces' materials can be listed and compared with the two expected names.
statements.explanation: Material names cross in glTF and can be asserted.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: a precise asset request
questions.stem: A developer needs a crate and compares several requests to a coding agent. Check each statement that is true about how clearly the request specifies the asset.

statements.label: A
statements.text: 'Make the crate about the right size' is as precise as the full request, because the engine works in metres.
statements.explanation: The phrase gives no number, so the engine's units do not settle the size.

statements.label: B
statements.text: 'Low-poly crate, 1 x 1 x 1 m, origin at base centre, under 200 triangles, scale applied, one material, .glb, +Y up' settles what the agent would guess.
statements.explanation: Each phrase removes a decision the agent would otherwise make.

statements.label: C
statements.text: 'Export it with the usual settings' is precise, since exporters share the same defaults for axes, scale and included data.
statements.explanation: Defaults differ between tools and versions, so the phrase leaves them open.

statements.label: D
statements.text: 'Keep the triangle count under 200' is checkable by reading the exported mesh's triangle count.
statements.explanation: It names a number that a test can read.

statements.label: E
statements.text: 'Add a collision shape' is enough, because the agent will pick a cheap convex or primitive shape.
statements.explanation: It could just as well add an expensive trimesh or none that suits.

questions.stem: A developer moves between engines and wants the collision vocabulary straight. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In Unreal, simple collision uses primitives and convex hulls, while complex collision is the object's per-triangle trimesh.
statements.explanation: This is how Epic's documentation divides the two.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An Unreal object that must be physically simulated should use complex collision so that it matches its visible shape exactly.
statements.explanation: Simulated bodies rely on simple collision shapes (primitives or convex hulls), not on the exact triangle mesh.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Unreal's simple collision corresponds roughly to primitive or convex shapes, and complex to concave (trimesh).
statements.explanation: The mapping holds: shapes without dents versus the exact triangle mesh.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In Unreal, the simple and complex collision of an object are the same shape, because both are taken from the visible mesh.
statements.explanation: Simple collision is made of primitives or convex hulls, while complex collision is the per-triangle mesh; they usually differ.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Unreal and in Godot alike, exact per-triangle collision is the costly kind and primitives or convex hulls are the cheap kind.
statements.explanation: Testing against every triangle costs more than testing against a primitive or hull; Godot's documentation calls concave shapes the slowest option, and Unreal pairs cheap simple shapes with the exact complex mesh.

questions.source: Collider versus trigger, say it to the agent
questions.stem: A designer wants a coin that disappears and adds to the score when the player touches it, while the player keeps walking straight through the coin's space without being stopped. The developer asks a coding agent for "a coin collider". Assume a 2D Godot game in which the player is a CharacterBody2D and every collision layer and mask is left at its default. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An Area2D pushes the player back slightly on contact, so designers usually keep its shape small to avoid shoving the player around.
statements.explanation: An Area2D never pushes or blocks; it only reports overlaps (and can influence gravity or damping inside it).

statements.label: B
statements.text: An Area2D with a collision shape on the coin, connected to its body_entered signal, gives the behaviour the designer described.
statements.explanation: An Area2D reports the player's entry without blocking, and the handler can add the score and remove the coin.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Collider" does not say whether the coin blocks the player, so the agent might build a solid body that stops the player.
statements.explanation: "Collider" is used for solid shapes and for detection regions alike, and the request never says which one the coin is.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A clearer instruction is "a trigger area on the coin that removes it when the player enters, without blocking".
statements.explanation: It names the role (detection region), the event (entry), the result, and the explicit non-requirement (no blocking).

statements.label: E
statements.text: A detection region needs no shape of its own, because it reports any body whose sprite overlaps the coin's sprite.
statements.explanation: Detection uses the collision shape; the sprite is only a drawing and the physics engine never reads it.

questions.stem: Engines use the single word "collision" for two different jobs. A solid collider stops or deflects other objects. A trigger (a Godot Area, a Unity collider with Is Trigger enabled, an Unreal overlap response) only reports that something is inside its region. Assume that any sensing of nearby objects is done with trigger regions, not with code queries such as a sphere overlap test. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A solid collider produces a collision response such as blocking; a trigger produces none and only reports the overlap.
statements.explanation: Response is the difference: a collider acts on the objects it meets, a trigger leaves them alone and notifies code.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In Unity one collider is either solid or a trigger, so a crate that blocks and also senses a nearby player with a trigger region needs two colliders.
statements.explanation: One collider has one Is Trigger value, so blocking and sensing need separate collider components.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A trigger can report only that an object entered its region; it cannot report that an object is still inside or has left.
statements.explanation: Triggers also report leaving (Godot body_exited, Unity OnTriggerExit, Unreal end overlap) and can be asked who is inside right now.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Layers and masks affect solid colliders but not triggers, so a trigger reports bodies inside its region without checking their layer.
statements.explanation: Layers and masks still decide what a trigger can detect; in Godot an area detects a body only if the body's layer is in the area's mask.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Switching a solid collider to a trigger keeps it blocking the player and adds enter events on top of the existing collision response.
statements.explanation: A trigger lets other colliders pass through it, so switching to a trigger removes the blocking.

questions.source: Collider versus trigger, say it to the agent
questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: "Add a wall on the right edge of the room that detects when the player touches it." The agent adds an Area2D with a rectangle collision shape and a body_entered handler that plays a bump sound. In testing the bump sound plays, but the player walks straight through the wall and out of the room. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The wall needs a solid body, in Godot a StaticBody2D with a collision shape; the Area2D can stay as a child for the sound.
statements.explanation: A static body supplies the blocking and the child area still supplies the touch event.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The Area2D does what an area does: it reports overlap and does not block, so passing through is expected.
statements.explanation: Detection regions do not stop bodies; blocking needs a solid body.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In Unity the same mistake is a wall whose collider has Is Trigger enabled where a solid collider was needed.
statements.explanation: A Unity trigger collider lets other colliders pass through it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Adding more layers to the area's collision mask will make the area block the player, because it will then scan the player's layer.
statements.explanation: The mask only chooses what the area scans for; blocking comes from being a solid body, not from any mask value.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The instruction never says in words that the player must be stopped, so the agent had to infer it from the word "wall"; a precise instruction would state it.
statements.explanation: "Detects when the player touches it" states the touch event only; stopping the player is at best implied by the word "wall", so the agent built what was literally written and a precise instruction names the blocking.

questions.stem: Godot's 2D physics offers several node types, and the choice decides who is responsible for movement and for the response to contact. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A RigidBody2D is moved by the engine's simulation, so it is normally driven with forces or impulses, not by writing its position each frame.
statements.explanation: The class reference warns that changing its transform or velocity very often can give unpredictable behaviour.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An Area2D detects bodies and areas that overlap its shape, can locally override gravity or damping, and does not block anything.
statements.explanation: Detection and influence are its jobs; it is not a solid object.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A CharacterBody2D is pulled down by the engine's gravity, like a RigidBody2D, so a platformer player built on it needs no gravity code.
statements.explanation: A CharacterBody2D has collision detection but no physics simulation; gravity must be added to its velocity in code.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A StaticBody2D takes part in collision but is not moved by collisions or forces, which suits walls and floors.
statements.explanation: Static bodies are fixed obstacles that other bodies collide with.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A CharacterBody2D detects collisions but leaves the response to your code, usually through move_and_slide or move_and_collide.
statements.explanation: It is the code-driven body type: you decide the movement and, with move_and_collide, the response.

questions.stem: Unity sorts colliders by how they are driven. A static collider has a collider and no Rigidbody. A dynamic body has a Rigidbody with Is Kinematic off. A kinematic body has a Rigidbody with Is Kinematic on. A designer plans an elevator platform whose position is set by code each physics step. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A kinematic body is not moved by forces or collisions; code moves it, and it can push dynamic bodies in its path.
statements.explanation: Kinematic bodies are driven from outside the simulation but still act on dynamic bodies they run into.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The elevator should be dynamic (Is Kinematic off), because dynamic is the setting for bodies that are moved by code rather than by physics.
statements.explanation: Dynamic bodies are the ones the simulation moves; code-driven motion is the kinematic case.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A kinematic Rigidbody still satisfies Unity's Rigidbody requirement for trigger events.
statements.explanation: Unity's trigger rule asks for a Rigidbody on at least one object, and kinematic ones qualify.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An elevator whose motion is scripted from outside the simulation is a kinematic body in this scheme.
statements.explanation: Code- or animation-driven motion is the kinematic case.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A dynamic body is moved by the physics engine in response to gravity, forces and collisions.
statements.explanation: Dynamic means the simulation owns the body's motion.

questions.stem: A developer asks a coding agent for a 2D platformer player in Godot. The agent builds the player as a CharacterBody2D. In _physics_process it adds gravity * delta to velocity.y, sets velocity.x from input, calls move_and_slide(), and allows a jump only while is_on_floor() is true. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Multiplying velocity by delta before calling move_and_slide() is also required, because movement must be scaled by the frame time.
statements.explanation: move_and_slide() applies the time step itself, so scaling velocity by delta again would make movement far too slow.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The agent should have put this code in _process, because the movement has to be updated once per rendered frame.
statements.explanation: Collision movement belongs in the fixed-rate physics callback; the per-frame callback runs at a variable rate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The agent could have used a RigidBody2D and overwritten its position each frame to get the same result, since the engine handles that case well.
statements.explanation: The documentation warns that changing a rigid body's transform very often leads to unpredictable behaviour.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The gravity line is needed because a CharacterBody2D is not simulated by the engine; nothing pulls it down unless the code changes its velocity.
statements.explanation: Character bodies have collision detection but no physics, so gravity is the developer's job.

statements.label: E
statements.text: After a landing, move_and_slide() updates the body's velocity itself, for example removing the downward part when the body rests on a floor.
statements.explanation: The class documentation says it adjusts velocity on collision, such as resetting vertical speed after landing.

questions.stem: In Godot every collision object has a collision layer (the layers it is in) and a collision mask (the layers it scans). Use the rule: object A can detect object B only if B is in a layer that A scans. A game puts walls on layer 1, the player on layer 2, enemies on layer 3 and coins on layer 4. Each coin is an Area2D on layer 4 whose mask scans layer 2 only. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The coin's own layer, 4, is what lets other objects find the coin: only objects whose masks include layer 4 can detect it.
statements.explanation: Layer says where an object appears; a scanner must include that layer in its mask.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A coin detects the player, because the player is in layer 2, which the coin's mask scans.
statements.explanation: The coin scans layer 2 and the player is in it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Layer and mask are two views of one setting, so moving the coin from layer 4 to layer 5 also changes which layers it scans.
statements.explanation: They are independent fields: layer is where the object appears, mask is what it scans.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the coin's mask were set to 0, the coin would stop detecting anything.
statements.explanation: A mask of 0 scans no layers.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A coin also detects enemies that touch it, because an area reports the bodies that overlap it.
statements.explanation: Enemies are in layer 3, which the coin does not scan, so they are not reported.

questions.stem: In the Godot editor collision layers are numbered 1 to 32. In scripts, collision_layer and collision_mask hold a bitmask integer in which layer n has the value 2^(n-1): layer 1 is 1, layer 2 is 2, layer 3 is 4, layer 4 is 8, and values add up when several layers are set. A project names layer 1 World, layer 2 Player, layer 3 Pickups and layer 4 Hazards. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A mask of 0 means the object scans the full layer range, because no layer is excluded.
statements.explanation: A mask of 0 scans no layers at all.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Writing collision_layer = 4 in a script puts the object on layer 3 (Pickups), not on layer 4 (Hazards).
statements.explanation: The integer 4 is the bit value of layer 3.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A player mask that scans World and Hazards (layers 1 and 4) is the integer 9.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A mask that scans only Hazards (layer 4) is the integer 4 in a script, the same number the editor shows for that layer.
statements.explanation: The editor shows layer numbers but a script stores bit values; layer 4 has the value 8, and the integer 4 is layer 3 (Pickups).

statements.label: E
statements.text: A mask of 6 scans layers 1 and 5, because 1 + 5 = 6.
statements.explanation: Values add, not layer numbers: 6 = 2 + 4, which is layers 2 and 3 (Player and Pickups).

questions.source: Layers and masks, say it to the agent
questions.stem: A top-down game has walls on layer 1, the player (a CharacterBody2D) on layer 2 and enemies (RigidBody2D) on layer 3. All masks, the player's and the enemies', are still at the Godot default, which scans layer 1 only. The designer wants enemies to bounce off walls and off the player but to pass through one another. The developer writes to the agent only: "make the enemies not collide with each other". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A precise instruction names the layers: enemies in layer 3 with a mask that scans layers 1 and 2 but not 3.
statements.explanation: Enemies that scan walls and the player but not their own layer meet both but not each other.

statements.label: B
statements.text: With the enemies on layer 3 and all masks left at that default, enemies and player would not collide with each other either.
statements.explanation: Neither the enemies' mask nor the player's mask includes the other's layer, so nothing links them.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Disabling the enemies' collision shapes meets the request, since a body with no shape cannot collide with other enemies.
statements.explanation: It also removes collisions with walls and the player, which the designer still wants.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In Unity the equivalent is to untick the World/Enemy pair in the Layer Collision Matrix, which stops enemies colliding with each other.
statements.explanation: The matching change is unticking the Enemy/Enemy pair; unticking World/Enemy lets enemies pass through walls.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Making the enemies much heavier meets the request, because a heavy enemy cannot be pushed by another enemy.
statements.explanation: Mass changes the response to a collision, not whether a collision is detected.

questions.stem: A level has an icy floor on which the player should slide and a rubber ball that should bounce back up almost to the height it was dropped from. A designer asks a coding agent to "make the floor slippery and the ball bouncy". A physics material holds surface properties such as friction and bounce; in Godot's PhysicsMaterial, friction runs from 0 (frictionless) to 1 and bounce runs from 0 (no bounce) to 1 (full bounciness). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Slippery" maps to low friction and "bouncy" maps to high bounce, both set on physics materials.
statements.explanation: Friction near 0 lets bodies slide and bounce near 1 returns almost all the impact energy.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The floor looks like polished ice because it has a glossy render material, and that glossy material is what makes the player slide.
statements.explanation: Contact behaviour comes from a physics material; a glossy render material changes only how the surface is drawn.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The ball bounces because its collider is round; a box-shaped collider given the same bounce value would not rebound.
statements.explanation: The rebound comes from the bounce value of the contact, not from the collider's outline; a box with the same value rebounds as well.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Bounciness comes from how light the body is, so to get a bouncier ball the designer should lower its mass rather than raise its bounce value.
statements.explanation: Bounce is a contact property set on a physics material; mass only sets how hard the body is to accelerate and is a separate property.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The icy floor should also get a high bounce value, because a surface that lets a body keep its speed while sliding must give back its energy on impact too.
statements.explanation: Sliding is governed by friction and rebound by bounce; the two are set independently, so a slippery floor can have no bounce at all.

questions.stem: A raycast asks the physics world: starting from an origin and going in a direction for a given length, what is the first thing the ray hits? In Godot a ray query returns a dictionary describing one hit, or an empty dictionary when nothing is hit, and by default it does not report Area nodes. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A basic ray query reports only the first hit along its path, so a wall between two points hides anything behind it from the ray.
statements.explanation: The result describes a single nearest hit.

statements.label: B
statements.text: With default settings a ray passing through a coin's Area2D reports the coin, the same way it reports a wall.
statements.explanation: Areas are not hit unless the query is told to collide with areas.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A ray has width, so it reports the objects inside a narrow cone around the line as well as those on it.
statements.explanation: A ray is an infinitely thin line; checking an area needs a shape query.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A hitscan weapon, whose shot lands instantly with no travelling bullet, is usually built on a raycast.
statements.explanation: The shot is an instant line test from the muzzle along the aim direction.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A raycast from an enemy's eyes to the player tests line of sight, because it finds the first solid thing along the line.
statements.explanation: If the first hit is the player, nothing solid is in between.

questions.stem: A bomb must damage every enemy within 3 metres of it, in any direction. A developer tells a coding agent: "cast rays from the bomb to find enemies near it". An overlap query (a shape query) asks which objects overlap a given shape, such as a sphere, at this moment. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A sphere query of radius 3 m around the bomb returns the objects inside that region.
statements.explanation: A shape query returns all matching overlaps, not just the first.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An area's list of overlapping bodies is refreshed at the moment a body is moved in code, so it is up to date within the same frame.
statements.explanation: The list is updated once during the physics step, not when objects are moved.

statements.label: C
statements.text: After the region query, a ray from the bomb to one enemy can check whether a wall stands between them.
statements.explanation: Region query for who is near, ray for what is in between.

statements.label: D
statements.text: One ray from the bomb is enough, because a ray finds the nearest object in the whole area around it.
statements.explanation: A ray covers one line; a region of 3 metres needs a shape query or many rays.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A shape query can find only trigger regions, because solid bodies are handled by the ray query instead.
statements.explanation: Shape queries test against colliders in general, filtered by layer, and return solid bodies as well.

questions.stem: A bullet with a circular collider of radius 2 px is a RigidBody2D travelling at 1,200 px/s in a game whose physics runs at 60 steps per second. Continuous collision detection is off, so overlaps are tested only at the position the body has after each step. A thin wall is 6 px thick. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Doubling the wall to 12 px guarantees the bullet is stopped, since the wall is then thicker than the bullet is wide.
statements.explanation: The bullet still moves 20 px per step, more than 12 + 4 = 16 px, so it can still skip over the wall.

statements.label: B
statements.text: This failure is called tunnelling, and it comes from testing discrete positions instead of the path travelled between them.
statements.explanation: Nothing checks the space between two steps.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Tunnelling happens because a fast body's collision layer stops being recognised by the wall's mask.
statements.explanation: Layers do not depend on speed; the wall is simply never tested against the bullet between steps.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Continuous collision detection tests the path swept during a step, at extra cost per body.
statements.explanation: It is slower but more precise, and thin-wall misses affect fast, small bodies.

statements.label: E
statements.text: At 20 px per step, the bullet can jump from one side of a 6 px wall to the other without overlapping it at a tested position.
statements.explanation: 1,200 / 60 = 20 px per step against 6 + 4 = 10 px of overlap window.

questions.stem: A developer asks a coding agent for three behaviours: a crate that is knocked away when a bomb explodes next to it, a rocket that speeds up for as long as its engine burns, and a paddle that must move at exactly 300 px/s while a key is held. In physics terms a force acts over time and produces acceleration, an impulse is an instantaneous change of momentum applied once, and velocity is a body's current speed with direction. In Godot's RigidBody2D, apply_force is meant to be applied every physics update and apply_impulse is time-independent. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Setting a body's velocity to 300 px/s and applying an impulse are the same operation.
statements.explanation: Setting velocity replaces the current motion with an exact value; an impulse adds to it.

statements.label: B
