statements.text: A force is a faster impulse: both change the body's position directly and leave its velocity alone.
statements.explanation: Both change velocity (momentum), not position directly.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The crate's knock-back is best modelled by one impulse applied at the moment of the explosion.
statements.explanation: A one-time impact is the use case for an impulse.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A constant force applied over several steps makes the rocket's velocity grow steadily, until drag or a collision changes that.
statements.explanation: Constant force means constant acceleration.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The rocket's engine is best modelled by one impulse applied at launch, because an impulse keeps accelerating a body for as long as it exists.
statements.explanation: One impulse changes velocity once; sustained thrust needs a force applied over time.

questions.stem: A designer asks a coding agent to "move the platform right at 100 pixels per second" and, separately, to "teleport the player to the checkpoint". The player is a CharacterBody2D. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Velocity exists only on RigidBody2D; a CharacterBody2D has no velocity property.
statements.explanation: CharacterBody2D has a velocity property that move_and_slide() reads and updates.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A velocity of (100, 0) and a velocity of (-100, 0) are the same velocity because they have the same speed.
statements.explanation: They have equal speed but opposite directions, so they are different velocities.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Writing the player's position directly moves it without the engine checking the path in between, so a destination that overlaps a wall can leave the player embedded in it.
statements.explanation: A direct position write is a teleport with no sweep and no response.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Adding a small amount to position in the physics callback and setting velocity before move_and_slide() are equivalent, because both make the body slide along walls.
statements.explanation: Writing position does not run collision handling; move_and_slide() does.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Velocity is a vector with a speed and a direction, measured as distance per unit time, whereas position says where the body is.
statements.explanation: Velocity is a rate of change of position, with direction.

questions.stem: Collision handling has two stages: detection (are two shapes overlapping, and where) and response (what the engine or your code then does about it). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For a RigidBody2D the engine only detects contact; the developer writes the code that stops the body at a wall.
statements.explanation: The simulation supplies the response for rigid bodies.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Detection and response are one inseparable step in a physics engine, so an overlap cannot be detected without a response being applied.
statements.explanation: Triggers and overlap queries detect without any response.

statements.label: C
statements.text: move_and_collide() stops at the first contact and returns the details for your code to handle; move_and_slide() applies a sliding response.
statements.explanation: One leaves the response to you, the other supplies the common slide response.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A bouncing ball's bounciness belongs to detection, because detection decides how fast the ball leaves.
statements.explanation: Bounce affects the response, the speed returned after contact; detection only finds the contact.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A trigger performs detection and then stops the body once it overlaps, the way a wall would.
statements.explanation: A trigger only reports; it applies no blocking response.

questions.stem: A game runs on three machines that render 30, 60 and 144 frames per second. Its physics runs on a fixed time step of 1/60 s. A studio asks candidates why movement that collides belongs in the fixed-step callback (Godot's _physics_process, Unity's FixedUpdate) and not in the per-frame callback. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Putting the movement in the per-frame callback is fine as long as it is multiplied by delta, so the choice of callback is only a matter of style.
statements.explanation: Scaling by delta fixes speed but not collision tests, jump arcs or contact timing, which still vary with the step size.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Each physics step covers the same amount of game time, so jump arcs and collision results are essentially the same on all three machines, apart from how smooth the picture looks.
statements.explanation: A constant step removes frame rate from the simulation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A variable step is preferred for physics, because larger steps on slow machines make the simulation more precise.
statements.explanation: Larger steps make the simulation less accurate and more likely to miss contacts.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The engine can run zero, one or several physics steps for one rendered frame, so the two callbacks are not called equally often.
statements.explanation: Physics catches up or waits to keep its own clock steady.

statements.label: E
statements.text: With a variable step, a long frame becomes a long step in which a fast body can travel farther than a thin wall is thick, and tunnel through it.
statements.explanation: Long steps skip over thin obstacles.

questions.stem: In a melee action game a developer tells a coding agent: "when the sword hits the enemy, damage it". The designer wants the team to use three terms in the melee convention: a hitbox is a region that deals damage during an attack, a hurtbox is a region on a character that receives damage, and a body collider is the solid shape that blocks movement. In this game one swing is meant to damage a given enemy once. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The sword's hitbox should be active only during the frames of the swing in which the blade can hurt.
statements.explanation: An always-on hitbox would damage things the blade is not near.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Each enemy normally has a solid body collider that blocks movement and a separate hurtbox region that receives hits.
statements.explanation: Blocking and receiving damage are different jobs, so they use different shapes.

statements.label: C
statements.text: On the enemy, the region that registers an incoming sword hit is its hitbox, and the sword carries the hurtbox.
statements.explanation: The roles are the other way round: the sword carries the hitbox that deals damage, and the enemy carries the hurtbox that receives it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A hit is registered when a hitbox overlaps a hurtbox, which is detection, so neither region needs to block movement.
statements.explanation: Both are usually detection regions (areas or triggers).

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Hits the enemy" leaves repeats open; because one swing is meant to damage an enemy once, a precise instruction states that limit.
statements.explanation: Overlap lasts several ticks, so without a rule one swing could hit many times.

questions.stem: A platformer has ledges the player can jump up through from below, then stand on, and drop through when pressing down. In Godot 2D this is a collision shape with one-way collision enabled, which makes the shape collide on one side only. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Enabling one-way collision on a shape that belongs to an Area2D has no effect, because areas do not block anything.
statements.explanation: The documentation says one-way collision has no effect on a child of an Area2D.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Dropping through can be done by letting the player briefly stop colliding with the ledge, for example by turning off that shape for a moment.
statements.explanation: A short collision pause lets the player fall past it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The ledge is still a solid collider; it blocks from one side only, normally the top.
statements.explanation: One-way platforms are solid from one direction and open from the other.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A one-way platform is a trigger that detects the player from below and lifts the player onto it.
statements.explanation: It is a solid collider; triggers do not lift or block anything.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A ledge on a layer that the player's mask does not scan gives the same result, since the player can pass through from below.
statements.explanation: The player would pass through from above as well and would never stand on it.

questions.stem: Lava should hurt the player once every 0.5 s for as long as the player stands in it. The developer wrote "the lava hurts the player when they touch it", and the agent built the lava as an Area2D whose body_entered handler subtracts 1 health. In testing, the player jumps in, loses 1 health once, and then stands in the lava taking no more damage. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The build is correct as written, because "hurts the player when they touch it" means a single hit on contact.
statements.explanation: The designer wants damage every 0.5 s while inside; the instruction left once-versus-repeatedly unsaid, which is how a single-hit build arose.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A fix is a 0.5 s timer that asks which bodies currently overlap the lava and damages each of them.
statements.explanation: Polling the current overlap list repeats the check while the overlap lasts.

statements.label: C
statements.text: body_entered runs once when an overlap begins, so standing still inside the lava produces no further enter events.
statements.explanation: The signal reports the start of the overlap only.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Making the lava's shape bigger would produce repeated enter events while the player stands inside.
statements.explanation: Size does not change that entry is a single event.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Connecting the same handler to body_exited fixes it, because exit events fire repeatedly while the player stays inside.
statements.explanation: Exit fires once when the player leaves.

questions.stem: Three engines name the same idea differently: a region that reports which objects are inside it without blocking them. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In Unreal both objects' responses count: if one is set to Ignore the other's type, no overlap is reported even though the other is set to Overlap.
statements.explanation: Whether two objects block, overlap or ignore each other depends on both of them; with one side set to Ignore, no overlap events fire.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In all three engines the region must have a visible mesh or sprite, because detection is done on the drawn pixels.
statements.explanation: Detection uses collision shapes; the drawing is irrelevant.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In Godot an area detects a body only if the body's collision layer is among the layers in the area's collision mask.
statements.explanation: Layer says where an object appears; the area's mask says what it scans.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A detection region finds objects through its collision shape, so a region whose shape has been switched off reports nothing even when objects are inside it.
statements.explanation: Detection is computed from collision shapes, so a shape that is switched off takes no part and the region has nothing to report.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Godot this is an Area2D or Area3D, in Unity a collider with Is Trigger enabled, and in Unreal a collision component whose response to the other object's type is Overlap.
statements.explanation: Each engine has a non-blocking detection region under its own name.

questions.source: Ground check, say it to the agent
questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: "only let the player jump when touching the ground". The player is a CharacterBody2D in Godot. Candidate approaches are is_on_floor(), a short raycast pointing down from the feet, and a small Area2D sensor at the feet. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A feet sensor made from an Area2D detects solid ground only if the area's mask scans the layer the ground is on.
statements.explanation: Areas report only bodies whose layer is in their mask.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A ray cast from the feet that returns an empty result means the player is standing on the ground.
statements.explanation: An empty result means the ray hit nothing, so there is no ground within its length.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Touching" is ambiguous: contact with a wall or a ceiling is also touching, so the instruction should say that the contact surface must count as floor.
statements.explanation: Floor, wall and ceiling are different contact surfaces.

statements.label: D
statements.text: is_on_floor() is true whenever the body's shape is anywhere inside a floor shape, since it tests plain overlap.
statements.explanation: It reports contact found by the last move, classified by the surface direction, not an overlap test.

statements.label: E
statements.text: is_on_floor() describes the result of the most recent move_and_slide() call, so it reflects the last physics step's movement.
statements.explanation: It is updated by move_and_slide() and is not a live overlap test.

questions.stem: A developer replaces a character's sprite with a larger, more detailed drawing and asks a coding agent to "update the character art". Afterwards the character's arms poke into walls, and enemy attacks seem to hit empty air beside the drawing. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The physics engine reads the sprite's transparent pixels, so the empty areas of the drawing do not collide.
statements.explanation: Transparency is a rendering property; collision comes from shapes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Characters are usually given simple shapes such as capsules because they are cheaper to test and move more steadily.
statements.explanation: Primitive shapes are fast to test and avoid snagging on small details.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Scaling the sprite node also scales a sibling collision shape, because they belong to the same character.
statements.explanation: A sibling shape is unaffected by the sprite's own scale; only a shared parent's scale reaches both.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The collision shape is separate from the sprite, so replacing the art does not resize it.
statements.explanation: Physics reads shapes, not pictures.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A debug view (in Godot, Visible Collision Shapes) draws the shapes at runtime and exposes such a mismatch.
statements.explanation: Seeing the shape over the art shows where they disagree.

questions.stem: A team is deciding what to write down before building a 2D platformer. Check each statement about a game design document (GDD) that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A GDD should contain the source code of each mechanic, so the document and the game cannot disagree.
statements.explanation: A GDD describes intended behaviour in words, tables and numbers; code is the implementation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A GDD is written once before production and then frozen, so design disagreements are settled for the whole project.
statements.explanation: Designs change after prototypes and playtests, and a GDD that is never revised becomes a stale artifact.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If a newer GDD exists, it shows that the build in the repository already behaves as the document says.
statements.explanation: A document is a promise; only running the build against the stated criteria shows it is kept.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A GDD records what the game is and how it should behave, in enough detail for builders and testers to work from.
statements.explanation: That is its purpose: a shared description that engineers and testers can act on.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A short pitch or brief states the core idea and scope; a GDD develops those decisions in detail.
statements.explanation: The brief is the compact form, and the GDD is the detailed one.

questions.stem: A team's design pillars are "fast restarts", "readable danger" and "one-button depth". Late in development someone proposes a 30-second unskippable cutscene after every death. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Make the game fun" is a strong pillar, because nobody on the team can disagree with it and it fits the whole feature list.
statements.explanation: A pillar that excludes nothing cannot settle any decision.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Enemies flash 0.4 s before an attack lands" is closer to a requirement than a pillar, because a test can check it.
statements.explanation: Pillars guide judgement; requirements give numbers that a test can check.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Design pillars are a few short statements of the experience the game must deliver, used to judge proposed features.
statements.explanation: Pillars are a decision tool for keeping features consistent with the intended experience.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Pillars should list the planned features in the game so that nothing is forgotten when decisions are made.
statements.explanation: A feature list is separate; pillars are few and about the experience.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The cutscene conflicts with "fast restarts", so the pillars give the team a reason to reject or change it.
statements.explanation: A proposal that works against a pillar needs a very good reason.

questions.stem: In a roguelike the player enters a room, fights the enemies, picks up a reward and enters the next room. When a run ends, the player spends earned currency on permanent upgrades and starts a new run. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The core loop is the engine's update loop, the code that runs once per frame to read input and draw.
statements.explanation: That is the programming game loop; the design term is about what the player repeats.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In a core loop, a verb is anything the game does to the player, such as spawning an enemy or starting a timer.
statements.explanation: A verb is an action the player chooses to perform.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The core loop is the short cycle of actions the player repeats most often, here entering, fighting and collecting.
statements.explanation: It is the moment-to-moment cycle that the rest of the game is built around.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Spending currency between runs belongs to a longer meta or progression loop wrapped around the core loop.
statements.explanation: Loops nest: short ones inside, longer ones around them.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The core loop is the list of all the game's features, grouped by importance and by the team that builds each.
statements.explanation: A feature list is not a loop; a loop is a repeated cycle of player actions and feedback.

questions.stem: The MDA framework separates mechanics (the rules and systems the designer builds), dynamics (behaviour that emerges when players use those rules) and aesthetics (the emotional responses players have). A designer adds a rule to a shooter: the player carries at most 12 rounds and cannot pick up more than one magazine per room. Players start avoiding fights and hoarding rounds, and report feeling tense. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Avoiding fights and hoarding rounds is a dynamic: it emerges from play and is not a line in the rules.
statements.explanation: Dynamics arise from rules meeting player choices.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The designer can set the aesthetic directly by writing "tense" into the rules, as the designer sets the magazine limit.
statements.explanation: Aesthetics are responses of players; the designer can only shape the rules that tend to produce them.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A playtest is how the designer finds out which dynamics and feelings a rule actually produces, because they cannot be read off the rule text.
statements.explanation: Dynamics and aesthetics emerge only when players meet the rules, so they have to be observed in play.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The 12-round limit is a mechanic.
statements.explanation: It is a rule the designer wrote.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Tension is an aesthetic, the emotional response that the rules and the play produce.
statements.explanation: Aesthetics are the felt experience.

questions.stem: Two requirements arrive for the same game. One says: "The player can interact with the world." The other says: "The player can jump, dash and grapple." A player verb is an action the player can choose to perform. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Health regeneration is a player verb because it happens often during play and affects the outcome.
statements.explanation: The player does not choose it; it is a system rule.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Interact with the world" is too vague to build from, since it names no input, no target and no change of state.
statements.explanation: An agent cannot tell what to implement from it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Each listed verb still needs an input, a rule for what changes, and feedback the player can perceive.
statements.explanation: A verb becomes buildable when input, effect and feedback are stated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Jump, dash and grapple are player verbs because the player chooses when to do each.
statements.explanation: Verbs are chosen actions.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A game's verbs are fixed by its genre, so choosing them is not a design decision for the team.
statements.explanation: Choosing and limiting verbs is a central design choice.

questions.stem: A team plans three builds: a weekend prototype of the core mechanic with placeholder boxes, a vertical slice, and a minimum viable product (MVP). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A prototype exists to answer a design question, such as whether the mechanic is fun, and may be thrown away.
statements.explanation: Prototypes are tools for learning, not products.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A vertical slice is a rough, whole-game version in which the full set of levels exists but none is polished.
statements.explanation: That describes a horizontal pass; a vertical slice is a thin portion built to near-final quality across art, audio, UI and rules.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A prototype is only valid if it uses final art and audio, since otherwise players cannot judge it.
statements.explanation: Placeholder art is normal for a prototype; the question is about the mechanic.

statements.label: D
statements.text: An MVP contains the whole feature roadmap, built at its first usable quality, so nothing planned is left out.
statements.explanation: Minimum means only what the game needs to be releasable and to teach the team from players.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An MVP is the prototype with a nicer menu and some sound added to it.
statements.explanation: An MVP is a complete, releasable game with the minimum feature set, not a polished prototype.

questions.stem: Four weeks before a deadline, a team has one working level. A teammate proposes online co-op, a crafting system and ten new enemy types. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Scope is what a team commits to deliver by a date, and cutting a feature is a legitimate way to protect the date.
statements.explanation: Scope, schedule and quality trade against each other, and cutting is one of the levers.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An out-of-scope list records decided non-goals, which makes such proposals easier to decline.
statements.explanation: A written non-goal turns a repeated argument into a settled decision.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Scope creep means any change to the design made after a prototype exists, whether or not it affects the deadline.
statements.explanation: Scope creep is uncontrolled growth of the commitment without matching changes to time or resources.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A feature should be accepted whenever it would improve the game; cost and schedule do not enter the decision.
statements.explanation: Scope decisions weigh the benefit against cost and the date.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Scope creep is harmless when each added feature is small, because small features cost no schedule time.
statements.explanation: Many small additions add up, and each needs design, building and testing.

questions.stem: A game studio has a level designer and a worldbuilder. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A level can be well designed with almost no worldbuilding, as in an abstract puzzle room.
statements.explanation: Level quality depends on verbs, pacing and teaching, not on lore.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Worldbuilding is the same as level design done at a larger scale, so a map of the world is a level.
statements.explanation: A world map describes the setting; a level is a playable arrangement.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Worldbuilding establishes the setting (places, history, rules, cultures) and can inform levels without being a layout.
statements.explanation: Setting and layout are different jobs that influence each other.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Worldbuilding is finished when the tile layout of the first level is drawn and the map is approved.
statements.explanation: A tile layout is level work; the setting can still be undefined.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Level design arranges space, obstacles, enemies and pacing so that the player's verbs are tested in sequence.
statements.explanation: It is the design of playable spaces.

questions.stem: A designer gives a coding agent this requirement for a 2D platformer with 32 px tiles: "The jump should feel snappy and reach a good height." The intent is that a jump from the floor rises 96 px (3 tiles) at its highest point. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The criterion should state the starting situation, such as the player standing on the floor, because the same jump input gives a different result from the air.
statements.explanation: A test needs a defined starting state; without it, two testers can set up different situations and disagree about pass or fail.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A testable version names a quantity and unit: the highest point is 96 px above the starting height.
statements.explanation: Quantity and unit remove guessing.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Adding "and the jump should be fun" makes the criterion more testable, because it states the designer's goal and gives the agent something to aim for.
statements.explanation: It adds a judgement that no automated test can decide.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A tolerance such as 4 px is needed, since physics steps are discrete and the apex seldom lands on exactly 96 px.
statements.explanation: A tolerance defines what counts as a pass.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Snappy" and "a good height" cannot be checked by a stranger, so they are not acceptance criteria.
statements.explanation: A stranger cannot write a pass or fail test from them.

questions.stem: A team writes acceptance criteria in the form "given a starting situation, when an action happens, then an observable result follows". Check each statement that is true, where a statement counts as true when it is a criterion that a stranger could turn into a pass or fail test without asking the designer anything.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Enemies should be hard but fair, so that players feel challenged without feeling cheated, with each attack telegraphed clearly enough to dodge.
statements.explanation: Hard and fair are opinions that need playtesting.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Given 3 health, when the player first touches a spike, then health becomes 2 and spike contact is ignored for 1.0 s.
statements.explanation: It names the starting state, the trigger, exact results and a duration.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The game should handle damage well, giving the player a fair and satisfying response when they are hit.
statements.explanation: "Well" is a judgement with no observable result.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Given the player is on the floor, when the player presses jump, then within 0.1 s the player is moving upward.
statements.explanation: It states the situation, the action, an observable result and a time limit.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The menu opens quickly and looks good on the screen sizes the game supports, including very small ones.
statements.explanation: "Quickly" and "good" are not measurable as written.

questions.stem: Two instructions are written for the same shield pickup. Instruction X: "Add a Timer node named ShieldTimer set to 3.0 s, store the state in a boolean called shielded, and connect area_entered in code." Instruction Y: "After the player touches a shield pickup, enemy contact deals no damage for 3.0 s; touching a second pickup restarts the 3.0 s; once 3.0 s have passed, enemy contact deals damage again." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Because Y states behaviour, a test can check it without knowing which node or variable the agent used.
statements.explanation: Behaviour is observable regardless of the internals.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Y is a behavioural specification (what must be true) and X is implementation detail (how it is built).
statements.explanation: A spec states observable behaviour; implementation names the mechanism.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Reading the code is enough to recover what the designer intended, because the code is the final design.
statements.explanation: Code shows what the game does, not what it was meant to do.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A specification should name node types and variable names so that the agent has no freedom.
statements.explanation: Naming the mechanism ties the work to one design and hides the behaviour that matters.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the implementation is later rewritten, a behavioural test written from Y should still apply.
statements.explanation: Tests tied to behaviour survive refactoring.

questions.stem: A coding agent reports: "Shield pickup finished; all tests pass." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An automated test checks specific conditions, such as the shield lasting 180 physics ticks, and can be rerun.
statements.explanation: Repeatable, exact checks are what automation offers.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A playtest can replace automated tests, because people notice the errors a test would find, even rare ones.
statements.explanation: People miss rare, exact-timing cases that scripted tests catch.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Shortening the shield to 0.5 s on purpose and watching the test fail checks that the test measures what it claims.
statements.explanation: A test that still passes on a broken build is not measuring the feature.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A passing automated test shows the feature is fun, since the test was written from the design and covers the whole feature.
statements.explanation: A test checks stated conditions, not enjoyment.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A playtest can reveal whether players notice the shield, understand it and enjoy it; a test cannot.
statements.explanation: Comprehension and enjoyment need people.

questions.source: Vague requirement, say it to the agent
questions.stem: A designer writes to a coding agent: "Make the boss hard." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Hard" is a judgement, not a build instruction; it must become parameters and be confirmed by playtesting.
statements.explanation: Parameters can be built and tested; the judgement is confirmed with players.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Multiplying the boss's health by ten is the obvious reading of "hard", so the agent can proceed without asking.
statements.explanation: Hard could mean fast, accurate, numerous or punishing; health alone may only make the fight longer.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Once the numbers are written down, an automated threshold test can show whether the boss is hard enough for players.
statements.explanation: A test can confirm the numbers; only players can say whether the result is hard enough.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Attack interval 1.2 s, damage 2 of 5 hearts, 0.4 s wind-up" is a requirement that a test can check.
statements.explanation: It gives quantities and times a test can read.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Adjectives like "hard" belong in the acceptance criteria because the team will understand them.
statements.explanation: Shared understanding is not a stranger-testable criterion.

questions.stem: A designer's requirement for a checkpoint reads: "When the player reaches the checkpoint flag, dying should send them back there." The developer wants an agent to build it and a test to check it, so the precise instruction given to the agent covers the behaviour, the test and the limits on the change. Check each statement that is true about details that instruction should add.

statements.label: A
statements.text: What happens if the player re-enters the flag after it has activated can be left out, because the sentence already defines the behaviour.
statements.explanation: Repeat entry is a common edge case that an unstated rule leaves to chance.

statements.label: B
statements.text: How the test puts the game into each state it checks, such as playing through with real input or setting the state directly, because a shortcut skips part of the path a player would take.
statements.explanation: Playing through proves the whole path works; setting state directly proves only the step being checked, so the route should be stated.

statements.label: C
statements.text: What must not change, such as existing movement behaviour and the existing tests, which must still pass.
statements.explanation: Invariants protect behaviour the change should not touch.

statements.label: D
statements.text: What counts as reaching the flag: for example, the player's body entering a trigger region of a stated size, activating once.
statements.explanation: "Reaches" has to become an observable event.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Where "back there" is, with a unit and a tolerance, such as within 8 px of a named respawn marker.
statements.explanation: A location without a tolerance cannot be tested.

questions.source: Invariants and scope of an instruction
questions.stem: A developer instructs a coding agent: "Add a double jump. Do not change run speed, gravity or the camera. Edit only player.gd and a new test file. If a criterion cannot be met, stop and report which one instead of loosening it." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Stop and report instead of loosening" guards against the agent making a criterion or a test weaker so that it passes.
statements.explanation: It closes the easy route to a false pass.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Naming the files the agent may edit limits the change to a surface that a reviewer can read in full.
statements.explanation: A small change surface is easier to review.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Do not change run speed, gravity or the camera" states invariants: things that must stay true after the change.
statements.explanation: Invariants fence off existing behaviour.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Invariants make a requirement untestable, because they add conditions beyond the feature itself, which a test cannot cover.
statements.explanation: They make it more testable, since existing behaviour can be re-checked.

statements.label: E
statements.text: These constraints are implementation detail and belong in code comments, not in the instruction, because the agent reads the code anyway.
statements.explanation: They are requirements on the work and must be in the instruction to bind the agent.

questions.stem: A team on a desktop computer scopes a touch version and a networked version of its game. It has no phone and no second machine. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A feature that cannot be verified on the available hardware should be deleted from the design document.
statements.explanation: It should stay, marked as unverified, so the gap is visible.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Mouse-emulated touch can show that the game responds to touch events, but not that the game feels right on a phone's screen.
statements.explanation: An emulation tests event handling, not real hands and screen.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A desktop simulator of a headset is enough to prove that the movement is comfortable in virtual reality.
statements.explanation: Comfort depends on the real device and the person wearing it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Two copies of the game on one computer, talking over the loopback address, show that the game works over the internet with packet loss.
statements.explanation: Loopback has no real network distance, loss or latency.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The scoping note should describe both versions as working, since the code for them exists.
statements.explanation: Code existing is not evidence of working on the target.

questions.stem: A renderer draws two opaque triangles. Triangle 1 covers 300 screen pixels. Triangle 2, drawn later and nearer to the camera, covers 100 pixels, all of which are also covered by triangle 1. Rasterization is the step that turns each triangle into fragments. Assume every fragment runs the fragment shader (no early rejection). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Rasterizing triangle 1 produces 300 fragments, each carrying interpolated values such as texture coordinates and depth.
statements.explanation: Rasterization generates one fragment per covered screen position and fills in its values by interpolating the vertex outputs.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A fragment is a vertex that the vertex shader has already moved to its final screen position, ready to be coloured.
statements.explanation: A vertex is a corner point of a triangle; a fragment is produced for every covered screen position inside it, and there are usually far more fragments than vertices.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The 100 pixels covered by both triangles each receive two fragments, but only the nearer one decides the pixel's colour.
statements.explanation: Both triangles produce a fragment for the overlapped pixels, and with opaque surfaces the depth test lets the nearer one win; the other is wasted work (overdraw).

statements.label: D
statements.text: A fragment is a finished pixel colour that has already passed the depth test and will appear in the final image.
statements.explanation: A fragment is only a candidate: depth test, discard or blending can reject or combine it before it becomes the pixel's final colour.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The fragment shader runs 400 times in total for these two triangles, 300 for the first and 100 for the second.
statements.explanation: The shader runs once per fragment, and triangle 1 yields 300 fragments while triangle 2 yields 100, so 400 runs under the stated assumption.

questions.stem: A 2D sprite is drawn on a quad made of two triangles with four corner vertices. The quad covers exactly 64 × 64 = 4096 screen pixels. Three quarters of the sprite's texels have alpha 0 (fully transparent). Assume no multisampling and that every covered fragment runs the fragment shader. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The fragment shader runs only for the 1024 pixels whose alpha is above zero, because the others are invisible.
statements.explanation: Transparency does not stop a fragment from being generated; the quad covers 4096 pixels, and all 4096 run the shader, with 3072 of them simply producing alpha 0.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The vertex shader runs for the four corners of the quad, not for each of the 4096 covered pixels.
statements.explanation: The vertex stage runs per vertex, and a quad has four.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The GPU skips fully transparent fragments, so the cost of drawing the sprite equals the cost of its visible part only.
statements.explanation: A transparent texel still costs a shader run and, if blending is on, a blend operation; the quad's whole area is paid for.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Tinting only the visible artwork, and not the empty texels, is a vertex-shader job because it sees the whole sprite.
statements.explanation: The vertex shader sees four corner points and can only hand interpolated values to the fragment stage; telling artwork from empty texels needs the texture, which is sampled per fragment.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the sprite is drawn three times larger (192 × 192 pixels), it still has four vertices but 36,864 fragments.
statements.explanation: 192 × 192 = 36,864 covered pixels, while the vertex count is a property of the mesh and stays at four.

questions.stem: Two programmable stages of the graphics pipeline are the vertex shader and the fragment shader. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The fragment shader runs once per vertex of the mesh and outputs each vertex's final position on the screen.
statements.explanation: The fragment shader runs per fragment and outputs a colour; positions are the vertex shader's output.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The vertex shader runs once per vertex and normally outputs where that vertex lands, plus data for the fragment stage.
statements.explanation: The vertex stage processes each vertex once and typically outputs a clip-space position together with values such as UV or colour that are passed on.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A fragment shader can move one corner of a triangle, which is how a flat mesh is made to bend.
statements.explanation: By the time fragments exist, the triangle's corners have already been placed; bending geometry is done by changing vertices in the vertex stage.

statements.label: D
statements.text: For a mesh that covers much of the screen, the fragment shader runs far more often than the vertex shader, because it runs per covered pixel position and not per corner point.
statements.explanation: The vertex stage runs once per vertex of the mesh, while the fragment stage runs once per rasterized fragment, and a large on-screen mesh covers many more pixel positions than it has vertices.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Sampling a texture to choose each covered pixel's colour belongs in the fragment shader.
statements.explanation: Per-pixel decisions, such as reading a texture at an interpolated UV, are made in the fragment stage.

questions.stem: In shader vocabulary, a uniform is a value supplied from outside the shader that is identical for every invocation in one draw, and a varying (also called an interpolant) is a value the vertex stage outputs and the fragment stage receives interpolated across the triangle. A developer needs (1) one enemy's health ratio, set by game code, to control a health-bar fill, and (2) a gradient that goes smoothly from 0 at the left edge of a quad to 1 at the right edge. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The health ratio is a natural uniform: it comes from game code and is the same for all fragments of that draw.
statements.explanation: A uniform is the channel through which game code hands a per-draw value to the shader, and every fragment sees the same value.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The left-to-right gradient is a natural varying: corner values 0 and 1 are interpolated for each fragment.
statements.explanation: Interpolating the corner values across the triangle gives each fragment its own position along the gradient.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A fragment shader can assign a new value to a uniform so that later fragments of the same draw see it.
statements.explanation: Uniforms are read-only inside the shader; invocations run independently and cannot pass results to each other that way.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A varying has a single value per triangle, copied unchanged across the triangle's fragments, so it cannot produce a gradient.
statements.explanation: The defining property of a varying is the opposite: it is interpolated, so it differs from fragment to fragment.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Changing a uniform's value from game code forces the shader to be recompiled before the next frame.
statements.explanation: Uniform values are simply uploaded as data; the compiled program does not change when a value does.

questions.stem: A game scrolls the camera across a 4000 × 1080 pixel background sprite on a 1920 × 1080 screen. A developer asks a coding agent for a vignette, meaning darkening toward the edges of what the player sees, applied by a fragment shader on the background sprite. The agent can compute the darkness from the sprite's UV coordinates or from the pixel's screen coordinates. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A vignette computed from the background sprite's UV stays locked to the edges of the display as the camera scrolls.
statements.explanation: UV is attached to the image, so a UV-based vignette darkens the image's own far edges and slides along with the scroll.

statements.label: B
statements.text: UV coordinates describe a position on the sprite's own surface, running from 0 to 1 across the 4000-pixel-wide image.
statements.explanation: UV is a coordinate on the textured surface, normalised to the range 0 to 1 over that surface.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because the background scrolls, screen coordinates scroll with it: the display pixel in the top-left corner has a different screen coordinate each frame.
statements.explanation: A screen coordinate names a fixed place in the output image, so the top-left display pixel is always at the same coordinate; what changes is which part of the background is drawn there.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A vignette meant to hug the edges of what the player sees should use the pixel's screen position (SCREEN_UV in Godot).
statements.explanation: Screen-space coordinates are tied to the display, so the darkening stays at the display edges however the camera moves.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Screen space is the 3D coordinate system of the whole scene, with the camera at the origin and units in metres.
statements.explanation: That describes view space; screen space is the 2D coordinate system of the output image.

questions.stem: Blending combines a new fragment's colour with the colour already in the framebuffer using result = new × α + old × (1 − α). The background pixel is blue, (0, 0, 1). Two translucent layers cover it, each with α = 0.5: a red layer, (1, 0, 0), and a green layer, (0, 1, 0). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If red is drawn first and green second, the pixel ends at (0.25, 0.5, 0.25).
statements.explanation: Red over blue gives (0.5, 0, 0.5); green over that gives (0.25, 0.5, 0.25).

statements.label: B
statements.text: If green is drawn first and red second, the pixel ends at the same (0.25, 0.5, 0.25).
statements.explanation: Green over blue gives (0, 0.5, 0.5); red over that gives (0.5, 0.25, 0.25), so blending depends on draw order.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Alpha testing produces smooth, partially transparent fades along the edge of a cut-out.
statements.explanation: A tested fragment is either kept at full strength or dropped, so edges are hard and may look jagged.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Alpha testing (keep or discard each fragment by a threshold) avoids the order dependence but has only all-or-nothing transparency.
statements.explanation: Because each fragment is kept or discarded outright, nothing is blended, and the result does not depend on the order of drawing, but there are no in-between opacities.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A window pane that should show the scene dimly through it is better made with alpha testing than with blending.
statements.explanation: Dim see-through glass needs partial opacity, which only blending provides.

questions.stem: Godot has a 2D shader type (shader_type canvas_item) and a 3D shader type (shader_type spatial). Check each statement that is true about Godot.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In a canvas_item fragment function, the shader writes the pixel's final colour directly, starting from the sprite's own texture colour.
statements.explanation: A 2D fragment function decides the drawn colour itself; its colour variable begins as the texture colour (times the vertex colour) and whatever it holds at the end is what is drawn.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Setting ROUGHNESS in a canvas_item fragment function gives the sprite a glossy PBR look that responds to 2D lights.
statements.explanation: There is no ROUGHNESS in a canvas_item shader, and 2D drawing has no PBR lighting model for it to feed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A spatial fragment function sets material properties (ALBEDO, ROUGHNESS, METALLIC), and the engine's lighting makes the final colour.
statements.explanation: A spatial shader describes the surface and lets the built-in renderer do the shading.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Both shader types can define a vertex() function that runs once per vertex.
statements.explanation: vertex(), fragment() and light() exist for both spatial and canvas_item shaders.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The shader type is chosen for the look wanted rather than for what is being drawn, so a spatial shader can be assigned to a 2D sprite to give it 3D-style shading.
statements.explanation: The shader type follows the kind of object drawn: Godot's documentation describes canvas_item shaders as drawing 2D elements and spatial shaders as shading 3D objects.

questions.stem: In a shader a colour is four floats (red, green, blue, alpha), normally written in the range 0.0 to 1.0, where alpha 0.0 is fully transparent. A pixel has the colour (0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 1.0). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Multiplying the red, green and blue channels by white, (1, 1, 1), turns the pixel white because white is the brightest colour.
statements.explanation: Multiplying by 1 leaves each channel unchanged, so multiplying by white changes nothing; a flash toward white needs mixing or adding.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Mixing 25 percent of the way toward white, mix(colour, white, 0.25), gives (0.4, 0.55, 0.7) in red, green and blue.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Multiplying red, green and blue by (1.0, 0.5, 0.5) gives (0.2, 0.2, 0.3): red unchanged, green and blue halved.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In an 8-bit image 255 corresponds to 1.0, so the 8-bit colour (255, 128, 0) corresponds to roughly (1.0, 0.50, 0.0).
statements.explanation: 128 / 255 is about 0.50, so the 8-bit triple maps to the float triple above.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Writing the 8-bit numbers (255, 128, 0) into float channels would clamp to yellow (1, 1, 0) on an ordinary 8-bit target, not orange.
statements.explanation: 255 and 128 are both far above 1.0 and clamp to full intensity, giving yellow instead of orange.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: hit flash
questions.stem: A developer wants an enemy sprite to flash entirely white for a few frames when it is hit. The sprite is a multi-coloured texture on a quad. The developer is deciding how to word the request to a coding agent. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Setting the sprite's colour multiplier (modulate in Godot) to white pushes the colours of the artwork up to white for the flash.
statements.explanation: A multiplier of white is 1 in every channel, which leaves the colours unchanged.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In the fragment shader, mix the output colour toward white by a 0-to-1 uniform called flash_amount, keeping alpha unchanged; the script drives it.
statements.explanation: It names the stage (fragment), the operation (mix toward white), the control (a uniform from 0 to 1), the constraint (alpha untouched) and who drives it (the script).

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Change the vertex positions" would send the agent to the vertex stage, which moves corners and cannot recolour the artwork.
statements.explanation: The vertex stage positions geometry; recolouring every pixel is a fragment-stage job.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the instruction omits alpha, an agent may output opaque white for each fragment, turning transparent surroundings into a white rectangle.
statements.explanation: The quad covers many fully transparent texels; overwriting their alpha makes the box visible.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A shader cannot do this, so the agent has to swap in an all-white copy of the texture for a few frames, then swap back.
statements.explanation: A fragment shader can mix any output colour toward white with no extra texture.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: vertex versus fragment for a ripple
questions.stem: A flag is drawn as a flat quad with only 4 vertices (two triangles). A developer asks a coding agent: "Make the flag ripple in the wind with a shader." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A vertex-shader displacement with a sine of time can only move the four corners, so it needs a subdivided mesh to look like a ripple.
statements.explanation: Vertex displacement can only be as detailed as the vertex count; four corner points give a tilt or shear, not a wave.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A fragment-shader approach can ripple the picture on the same quad by offsetting the sampling coordinate by a sine of position and time.
statements.explanation: Distorting the sampling coordinate per fragment shifts which texel each pixel shows, giving a ripple without extra geometry.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The vertex approach changes the flag's outline; the UV-offset approach keeps the rectangle and shifts only the picture inside it.
statements.explanation: Moved vertices change the shape that gets rasterized; sampling changes leave the covered area unchanged.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In the UV-offset approach the fragment shader moves the quad's vertices to their new places, which is what makes the picture ripple.
statements.explanation: Fragment shaders never move vertices; they decide the colour of fragments the quad already produces.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A continuous ripple can use the engine's global time (TIME in Godot), because it does not have to start at a particular event.
statements.explanation: A looping effect with no start moment can read global time directly; only event-triggered effects need a value from game code.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: time as a uniform
questions.stem: A developer asks a coding agent: "When the player is hit, run a 0.4 second flash starting at the moment of the hit." The agent writes, in a Godot shader, flash = 1.0 - clamp(TIME / 0.4, 0.0, 1.0), where TIME is the engine's global time in seconds since the engine started. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: TIME restarts from zero at each hit, so the flash plays correctly on repeated hits without any extra code.
statements.explanation: TIME counts from engine start and is not reset by game events.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The flash plays once right after the engine starts, then the expression stays at 0, so later hits show nothing.
statements.explanation: After 0.4 seconds of engine time the clamp saturates at 1.0, so flash stays at 0 forever.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A fix is a uniform set by game code, such as the time of the last hit or a progress value animated from 0 to 1.
statements.explanation: Game code knows when the hit occurred, and a uniform is how it passes that to the shader.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The shader can detect by itself that a hit happened in game logic, because it runs each time a frame is drawn.
statements.explanation: A shader only sees its inputs; game events reach it only through uniforms, textures or vertex data.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Saying "driven by a uniform that game code sets at the hit" tells the agent where the event knowledge lives.
statements.explanation: Naming the uniform and who sets it prevents the agent from guessing that the shader can know about events.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: neighbour sampling
questions.stem: A developer asks a coding agent for a one-pixel white outline around the opaque shapes of a sprite. The sprite texture is 64 × 64 texels and is drawn on a quad. Each fragment-shader invocation runs independently. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A fragment cannot read the final colour that a neighbouring fragment computed in the same draw.
statements.explanation: Invocations are independent, so effects that need neighbours sample an already-available texture, not another fragment's output.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The outline can be made by a vertex shader that moves each pixel of the sprite one step outward and recolours it.
statements.explanation: The vertex stage handles vertices, not pixels; it cannot move individual pixels.

statements.label: C
statements.text: One texel is 1/64 in UV units here, so the outline can sample the sprite's alpha at offsets of ±1/64 in u and v.
statements.explanation: UV runs 0 to 1 over 64 texels, so one texel is 1/64.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A fragment that is transparent but has an opaque neighbouring sample can be coloured white to form the outline.
statements.explanation: Checking the sprite's own alpha at neighbouring offsets is the standard way to find pixels just outside a shape.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the artwork touches the quad's edge, outline pixels outside the quad cannot be drawn, because no fragments exist there.
statements.explanation: Fragments exist only where the geometry covers the screen, so the quad needs padding around the artwork.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: dissolve with discard
questions.stem: A developer asks a coding agent for a dissolve effect: an enemy sprite breaks into holes that follow a noise pattern as a uniform called dissolve goes from 0 to 1, until the sprite is gone. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Discarding fragments gives smooth, partially transparent hole edges, because discarded pixels fade out gradually.
statements.explanation: A discarded fragment is dropped entirely, so edges are hard; smooth edges need partial alpha and blending.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Discarding a fragment has no performance cost, since the fragment is thrown away before it is drawn.
statements.explanation: Godot's documentation warns that discard has a performance cost because it prevents the depth prepass from being effective.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Comparing a noise sample with the dissolve uniform and discarding fragments below it gives sharp-edged holes that follow the noise.
statements.explanation: This is the usual noise-threshold dissolve: the decision is per fragment.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A smooth alpha fade near the threshold is independent of draw order, because the fade is computed in the shader.
statements.explanation: Partial alpha is blended with what is behind it, and blending depends on the order of drawing.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A discarded fragment writes nothing, so the pixel keeps what was already drawn at that position.
statements.explanation: Discard means nothing is written for that fragment.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: choosing the stage
questions.stem: A developer wants requests to a coding agent to land in the right shader stage. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Turn the whole level black-and-white when the player dies" is a fragment-stage job, since it recolours each pixel.
statements.explanation: Desaturating means changing the final colour of every pixel, which is what the fragment stage decides.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Squash and stretch the character's mesh when it lands" is a fragment-stage job, since it changes how the character looks.
statements.explanation: Squash and stretch changes the shape of the geometry, which is done by moving vertices (or transforming the object).

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Draw horizontal scanlines over the screen" is a vertex-stage job, because lines are geometry.
statements.explanation: Scanlines are a pattern in screen position computed per pixel, not extra geometry.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Swap the character's palette" is a vertex-stage job, because the palette belongs to the whole object.
statements.explanation: A palette swap changes the colour looked up per pixel, so it belongs to the fragment stage.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Make the grass blades sway at their tips" is a vertex-stage job when each blade is a mesh with vertices that can be displaced.
statements.explanation: Swaying tips are a displacement of vertex positions, weighted toward the tips.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: shaders do not change gameplay
questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: "Use a shader to shrink the boss to half size so the player can slip under its attacks." The boss has a collision shape that is separate from its sprite. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Physics queries read the pixels the shader outputs to decide what overlaps, so a shrunken image shrinks the hit area.
statements.explanation: Collision is computed from shapes, not from rendered pixels.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Vertex positions changed in a shader are written back to the node's transform, so the physics body moves too.
statements.explanation: Shader output stays on the GPU as image data and never updates game-side transforms.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the shader discards the lower half of the sprite's fragments, the collision shape shrinks to match what remains.
statements.explanation: Discarding fragments only changes what is displayed; the collision shape is untouched.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A shader changes how the boss is drawn, but not the size or position of its collision shape.
statements.explanation: Rendering and physics are separate systems, and a shader belongs only to the first.

statements.label: E
statements.text: For the player to slip under, the instruction must say to change the collision shape (or body scale) in game code.
statements.explanation: Gameplay consequences live in game code, so the instruction must name the collision change explicitly.

questions.stem: An interviewer asks a candidate to explain why shaders run on the GPU and what they cannot do. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A GPU runs the same small program over many vertices or fragments at once, which suits colouring millions of pixels.
statements.explanation: Parallel execution of one small program over many independent items is what GPUs are built for.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Data a shader needs, such as the player's position, arrives through uniforms or textures set from the CPU side.
statements.explanation: Shaders have no access to game objects; the CPU passes values in.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A shader can print a debug line and read a variable of a game script directly, as long as the variable is a number.
statements.explanation: A shader has no print function and no access to script variables; the only output is the colour or position it writes.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A frame can be CPU-bound or GPU-bound: limited by game logic and draw preparation, or by shading work, whichever is slower.
statements.explanation: Both processors work on each frame, and the slower one sets the frame time.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Moving a calculation from a script into a fragment shader makes the game faster, because the GPU is faster than the CPU.
statements.explanation: A fragment shader runs per covered pixel, so a calculation that was cheap once per object can become expensive millions of times per frame.

questions.stem: A simplified view of how a 3D mesh becomes pixels is this chain: vertex data, vertex shader, mapping to the screen, rasterization, fragment shader, depth and stencil tests plus blending, framebuffer. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Rasterization is a programmable stage that developers write in the shader language, like the vertex and fragment stages.
statements.explanation: In the standard pipeline, rasterization is fixed-function hardware that developers configure but do not program.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The fragment shader runs before rasterization to decide which pixels a triangle covers, and rasterization then fills them in.
statements.explanation: The fragment shader only runs on fragments that rasterization has already produced.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Blending happens before the fragment shader, because it must know which colours are already in the framebuffer.
statements.explanation: Blending uses the fragment shader's output colour, so it comes after the shader, using what is already stored.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Rasterization turns each triangle into fragments for the covered pixel positions, with the vertex outputs interpolated.
statements.explanation: Producing covered positions and interpolating the vertex outputs for them is exactly what rasterization does.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The vertex shader's output is already in screen pixels, so no conversion is needed before rasterization.
statements.explanation: The vertex shader typically outputs clip-space positions, which the pipeline converts to screen positions before rasterization.

questions.stem: A mobile game draws a 1920 × 1080 screen (2,073,600 pixels). A full-screen translucent fog sprite is drawn, then a second full-screen translucent glow sprite on top, then the UI. Each full-screen layer runs the fragment shader for every pixel it covers. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The two full-screen layers together cost 4,147,200 fragment-shader runs per frame, before the UI.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Making the fog layer's shader simpler reduces its cost even though the number of covered pixels stays the same.
statements.explanation: Per-fragment cost is the shader's work times the fragment count, so either factor can be reduced.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because the glow sprite is mostly transparent, the GPU skips low-alpha fragments, so its cost follows the visible glow.
statements.explanation: Low alpha does not stop the shader from running; the full area is shaded and blended.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Rendering the fog layer at half the width and half the height cuts its fragment count to a quarter, 518,400.
statements.explanation: Halving both dimensions leaves 960 × 540 = 518,400 pixels, a quarter of 2,073,600.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Overdraw means the same screen pixel is shaded by more than one fragment in a frame; here each pixel has at least two.
statements.explanation: Each pixel receives a fog fragment and a glow fragment, which is overdraw.

questions.stem: A fragment shader reads a texture with texture(tex, uv). The texture is a 16 × 16 pixel-art icon drawn on a quad that covers 128 × 128 screen pixels. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Enlarging the icon eight times with linear filtering still leaves the texels as crisp blocks, because filtering matters when a texture is shrunk, not when it is enlarged.
statements.explanation: Linear filtering blends neighbouring texels whenever a lookup falls between texel centres, which is what happens when a small texture is enlarged, so the blocks blur; nearest filtering keeps them crisp.

statements.label: B
statements.text: UV coordinates count texels, so the centre of the 16 × 16 icon is at uv (8, 8).
statements.explanation: UV is normalised to 0 to 1 across the whole texture, so the centre is (0.5, 0.5) regardless of the texture's size in texels.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A uv of (1.25, 0.5) lies outside the texture, so the lookup has no colour to return and the pixel is left undrawn.
statements.explanation: Sampling outside 0 to 1 is legal: the sampler's wrap mode (such as repeat or clamp) decides which texel comes back, so a colour is still returned.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Nearest filtering is the better choice for a smooth water texture, because it returns the single most accurate texel instead of a blur.
statements.explanation: Nearest filtering gives blocky results that suit pixel art; a smooth texture such as water looks better with linear filtering, which blends neighbouring texels.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the icon fills the quad and is sampled with nearest filtering, each texel (one pixel of the texture image) appears as a flat 8 × 8 block of screen pixels, since 128 / 16 = 8.
statements.explanation: 128 / 16 = 8 screen pixels per texel along each axis, and nearest filtering returns a single texel's colour for all of them.

questions.stem: A hit flash fades from 1.0 to 0.0. Version A, driven by game code, lowers it by 1/12 on every rendered frame. Version B sets it to 1.0 − elapsed_seconds / 0.4, where elapsed_seconds is accumulated from the time each frame took. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Version A lasts 0.4 seconds at 30 frames per second and 0.2 seconds at 60 frames per second.
statements.explanation: Twelve frames last 12/30 = 0.4 s at 30 fps and 12/60 = 0.2 s at 60 fps.

statements.label: B
statements.text: At 144 frames per second Version A lasts about 0.083 seconds.
statements.explanation: 12/144 is about 0.083 s.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Version A lasts the same wall-clock time at 30 and 144 frames per second, because the shader runs once per frame.
statements.explanation: A frame-counted fade lasts a number of frames, so its duration changes with the frame rate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Version B lasts noticeably longer at 30 frames per second than at 144.
statements.explanation: Version B ends when 0.4 s have elapsed, which does not depend on how many frames are drawn.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Version B is frame-rate independent because it measures elapsed seconds instead of counting frames.
statements.explanation: Using accumulated time makes the duration a fixed number of seconds.

questions.stem: In physically based rendering, a surface is described by a few separate properties. One of them is albedo (also called base colour). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Albedo is the colour a surface reflects diffusely, independent of the scene's lights; the renderer combines it with lighting.
statements.explanation: Albedo is the intrinsic colour of the surface; lights, shadows and reflections are applied on top of it by the renderer.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The colour a pixel shows on screen equals its albedo, because albedo is the finished colour of the surface.
statements.explanation: The final pixel colour also depends on light colour, light direction, shadows and reflections, so it is not the albedo alone.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An albedo texture with shadows and highlights painted in will look double-shaded once the engine's lighting is applied.
statements.explanation: Baked lighting in the texture stacks with the engine's lighting, giving shadows twice and shading that does not move with the lights.

statements.label: D
statements.text: For a bare metal, the base colour tints the reflections, since a metal has little diffuse colour of its own.
statements.explanation: In the metallic-roughness model, a metal's reflectance colour comes from the base colour.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Albedo controls how blurry the surface's reflections are, with darker albedo giving sharper reflections.
statements.explanation: Blur of reflections is controlled by roughness.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: shinier means roughness, metallic or specular
questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: "Make the ship's hull shinier." The hull's material currently has an albedo texture of weathered wood, metallic 0, roughness 0.8 and the default specular value. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Lowering roughness (for example from 0.8 to 0.3) makes reflections sharper and highlights tighter, which reads as shinier.
statements.explanation: Roughness controls how blurred reflections are; lower values concentrate them into sharper highlights.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Brightening the albedo texture makes the hull shinier, since lighter surfaces reflect more of the light that hits them.
statements.explanation: Albedo changes the base colour, not how glossy the surface is.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Shinier" is ambiguous: glossy paint (non-metal, low roughness) and polished metal (metallic near 1, low roughness) are different looks.
statements.explanation: The word covers different material setups, and the agent needs to know whether metallic changes too.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Raising the emission colour is the right change, because emission adds the highlights to a surface and so reads as shine.
statements.explanation: Emission adds light of its own regardless of the scene, so it makes the hull glow rather than reflect.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In an engine that uses smoothness instead of roughness, such as Unity's standard lit materials, shinier means lowering smoothness.
statements.explanation: Smoothness is roughly the opposite of roughness, so a shinier surface has a higher smoothness value.

questions.stem: In the metallic-roughness material model, a surface has a metallic value between 0 and 1. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Metallic controls how blurry the reflections are, so metallic 1 gives the blurriest reflections.
statements.explanation: Reflection blur is roughness.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Metallic 0 is a non-metal (dielectric) such as plastic, wood or skin; metallic 1 is a bare metal such as steel or gold.
statements.explanation: Metallic is the switch between the non-metal and metal behaviours of the model.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A fully metallic surface with a pure black albedo still shows bright, naturally coloured reflections of its surroundings.
statements.explanation: For a metal the base colour supplies the reflection tint, so a black albedo gives almost no reflection.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Intermediate metallic values mostly mark transitions, such as rust, dirt or chipped paint at the edge of a metal.
statements.explanation: A real surface is metal or not at each point, so in-between values stand for mixed or partly covered areas.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Metallic and specular are two names for the same control, and raising either has the same effect.
statements.explanation: Specular scales the strength of reflection on non-metals, while metallic changes the kind of material.

questions.stem: A technical artist sets up three surfaces in the metallic-roughness model. Rubber ball: metallic 0, roughness 0.9. Chrome sphere: metallic 1, roughness 0.05. Glossy plastic toy: metallic 0, roughness 0.2, default specular. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The chrome sphere shows a sharp, mirror-like reflection of its surroundings.
statements.explanation: Metallic 1 with roughness near 0 gives a near-mirror finish.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The rubber ball shows sharp reflections, since roughness 0.9 means a very smooth surface.
statements.explanation: A roughness of 0.9 blurs reflections almost completely; it is a rough surface.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The plastic toy's highlights are tinted by its albedo, as a metal's reflections are.
statements.explanation: Highlights on a non-metal are mostly untinted (whitish), while the diffuse body takes the albedo colour.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Setting the rubber ball's metallic to 1 while leaving roughness at 0.9 would turn it into a mirror.
statements.explanation: It would become a dull, blurred metal, because roughness 0.9 still smears the reflections.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Raising the chrome sphere's roughness to 0.9 would make its reflection sharper.
statements.explanation: Higher roughness spreads and blurs the reflection, the opposite of sharpening it.

questions.source: Normal map versus height or bump map
questions.stem: A brick wall has two supporting images: a height map (greyscale, white = high, black = low) and a tangent-space normal map (a mostly purple-blue colour image). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Both can make a flat surface shade as if it had bumps without adding any triangles.
statements.explanation: Both alter the normal used in lighting, so the surface reacts to light as if it were uneven.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A normal map stores a surface direction in each texel, with red, green and blue encoding the x, y and z of a vector.
statements.explanation: A normal map is a vector image: each texel's three channels encode a direction.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A normal map changes the silhouette of the wall seen at a grazing angle, so the bricks stick out of its outline as real geometry would.
statements.explanation: The geometry's outline is unchanged, so at a grazing angle the edge of the wall still looks straight.

statements.label: D
