statements.text: A height map used for bump mapping gives the slope between neighbouring texels, from which a shading normal can be derived.
statements.explanation: Bump mapping derives a normal from how the height changes between texels.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Real displacement, which changes the silhouette, needs enough vertices (a dense mesh or tessellation); normal and bump maps only change shading.
statements.explanation: Actually moving the surface requires geometry to move; parallax tricks only fake depth.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: which image goes in which slot
questions.stem: A developer downloads a wood-floor texture pack with the files floor_albedo.png, floor_normal.png, floor_roughness.png and floor_ao.png, and tells a coding agent: "Put the wood floor texture on the floor mesh." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The instruction is complete, since the word "texture" already tells a coding agent which of the four images goes in which slot.
statements.explanation: "Texture" names four different kinds of image here, each belonging to a different quantity.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If floor_normal.png is put in the albedo slot, the floor is tinted blue-purple but also keeps the bumps, since the image still carries the surface directions.
statements.explanation: In the albedo slot the image is read only as colour, so the floor turns blue-purple and gets no bumps from it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The instruction is too vague: it does not say which file belongs in which slot, so the agent may put an image in the wrong slot.
statements.explanation: Naming the slot for each file, or at least saying which file is which kind of map, removes the guesswork.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If floor_albedo.png is put in the normal slot, the floor still shows the wood colouring, because the picture's colours are drawn from whichever slot it is in.
statements.explanation: A colour picture in the normal slot is read as directions, so the wood colours do not appear and the shading is noisy and wrong.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A greyscale roughness image placed in the albedo slot still acts as roughness, because the engine looks at what an image contains to decide how to use it.
statements.explanation: Engines read an image according to the slot it is assigned to, not according to what it looks like.

questions.stem: A tangent-space normal map stores a direction in each texel. Each 8-bit channel value c (0 to 255) is converted to a vector component by n = 2 × (c / 255) − 1, with red as x, green as y and blue as z. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The texel (128, 128, 255) decodes to about (0.5, 0.5, 1.0), a direction tilted well away from the surface normal.
statements.explanation: 2 × (128/255) − 1 is about 0.004, not 0.5, so the first two components are near zero.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The texel (128, 128, 255) decodes to about (0, 0, 1), straight out of the surface, so that texel shades as flat.
statements.explanation: The decoded vector is (0.004, 0.004, 1.0), essentially the unperturbed surface normal.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because the vectors are in tangent space, the map must be re-baked each time the object rotates in the scene.
statements.explanation: The vectors are stored relative to the surface, so rotating the object does not invalidate the map.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Tangent space means the vectors are relative to the surface (x along U, y along V, z along its normal), so the map survives rotation.
statements.explanation: Expressing directions in the surface's own frame is what makes a tangent-space map reusable on any orientation or deformation.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A normal map looks mostly purple-blue because most texels are near (128, 128, 255): most of the surface points almost straight out.
statements.explanation: Blue is z, which is near full for slight slopes, and red and green sit near the middle value 128.

questions.stem: A wooden crate has an ambient occlusion (AO) texture that is white where light reaches freely and dark in the creases between planks. The crate sits in a scene lit by one strong directional light plus a dim ambient light. Assume the engine applies the AO texture to ambient light only, which is the default behaviour in Godot and matches the glTF 2.0 specification. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The AO texture is a shadow cast by the directional light, so it moves when the light rotates.
statements.explanation: AO is baked into the material and does not depend on the position of a light.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The AO texture and screen-space ambient occlusion (SSAO) are the same effect, so enabling both changes nothing.
statements.explanation: The texture is authored in advance, while SSAO is a post-process computed from the depth buffer each frame; using both can darken creases twice.

statements.label: C
statements.text: AO approximates how much ambient light reaches each point, so creases receive less of it, as in a real crevice.
statements.explanation: Ambient occlusion models how enclosed a point is, and so how much indirect light can reach it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because the AO texture does not dim the directional light, the creases look only slightly different from a version without AO.
statements.explanation: With AO limited to ambient light, the strong direct light still lights the creases fully.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The AO texture holds colour, so it should be imported as sRGB colour data like the albedo texture.
statements.explanation: AO is a single-channel data image whose values are used as numbers, so it is read as linear.

questions.stem: A designer gives a lamp mesh an emission colour so that it appears to glow. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Emission adds colour to the surface's final appearance independent of scene lighting, so the lamp still glows in a dark room.
statements.explanation: Emission is added to the lit result, so it is not dimmed by darkness.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In a basic real-time renderer with no global illumination, an emissive mesh also lights the nearby walls the way a point light does.
statements.explanation: Emission only affects the pixels of the emissive surface itself, unless a global-illumination feature reads it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Emission values above 1.0 are meaningless, because colours cannot exceed 1.0 on a modern display pipeline.
statements.explanation: High-dynamic-range rendering allows values above 1.0, which are what bloom or glow effects pick up.

statements.label: D
statements.text: To light nearby surfaces, the developer needs a light source or a global-illumination feature that treats emissive surfaces as lights.
statements.explanation: Lighting neighbours needs a real light or a feature that treats emissive surfaces as light sources.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Emission is another name for albedo at a higher brightness, so a brighter albedo would glow the same way.
statements.explanation: Albedo is reflected colour that depends on lighting; emission is light the surface gives off.

questions.stem: PBR (physically based rendering) is the standard way modern engines describe materials. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: PBR requires a photorealistic art style, so stylised or cartoon games cannot use it and have to use a different material system.
statements.explanation: PBR is a way to organise material parameters, and stylised games commonly use it with non-realistic textures.

statements.label: B
statements.text: PBR does not require ray tracing; it is a way of describing surfaces and light that works in ordinary rasterizing renderers.
statements.explanation: PBR materials are used in rasterizers; ray tracing is a separate rendering technique.

statements.label: C
statements.text: PBR describes a surface by properties such as base colour, roughness and metallic that stay meaningful under different lighting.
statements.explanation: Separating the surface description from the lighting is the main benefit of PBR.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Energy conservation is a PBR principle: a surface cannot reflect more light than it receives, so rougher highlights are wider and dimmer.
statements.explanation: When a highlight is spread over a wider area, it is also dimmer, because the same light energy is distributed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Physically based" refers to the model of light and surface; artists still tune values by eye rather than measuring real objects.
statements.explanation: The values are authored or tuned; the model only constrains how they combine.

questions.stem: A material pack contains five images: albedo, normal map, roughness, ambient occlusion and emission colour. Colour images are normally stored in the sRGB encoding, and the renderer decodes them to linear values before lighting math. Data images hold numbers that must be used as stored. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Albedo is colour and should be flagged or imported as sRGB, so it is decoded to linear for lighting.
statements.explanation: Albedo is a picture of a colour as seen by people, so it is stored in sRGB.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The normal map, roughness and ambient occlusion images are all colour images and should be flagged as sRGB, like albedo.
statements.explanation: These three are data maps and must be read linearly; they are images only because that is how the data is stored.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Emission colour is colour, authored like albedo, and should be treated as sRGB.
statements.explanation: Emission is a colour and is authored like albedo.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A roughness image is data: its stored value is the number the shading uses, so an sRGB decode would change the number.
statements.explanation: A data value of 0.5 should stay 0.5; decoding it as sRGB turns it into about 0.22.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A wrong colour-space flag raises no error, so the developer should tell the agent which maps are colour and which are data.
statements.explanation: Because nothing fails visibly, the instruction to the agent needs to say which map is which.

questions.stem: A roughness map has a uniform mid-grey value of 128 out of 255 (about 0.50), meant to read as roughness 0.50. The texture is wrongly imported as an sRGB colour texture, so the renderer applies the sRGB-to-linear decode to it. For an input of 0.502 that decode gives about 0.216. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The error is invisible, because the decoded number is the same mid-grey.
statements.explanation: The decode changes the number from about 0.50 to about 0.22, which changes the look.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The surface is shaded with a roughness of about 0.22 instead of 0.50, so it looks glossier than intended.
statements.explanation: Lower roughness means sharper, stronger reflections, so the surface looks glossier.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If a mid-grey albedo (128/255) were wrongly treated as linear data instead of sRGB colour, the surface would come out darker than intended.
statements.explanation: Treating sRGB as linear skips the decode, so 0.502 is used instead of 0.216 and the surface looks brighter and washed out.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The correct fix is to multiply the roughness in the shader by about 2.3.
statements.explanation: The sRGB curve is not a constant factor, and a multiplier would be a hack; the correct fix is the import flag.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Importing the roughness map as linear data would use 0.502 unchanged, as authored.
statements.explanation: A linear import uses the stored value as the number, which is what a data map needs.

questions.stem: A long tiled floor uses a high-contrast checker texture of 2048 × 2048 texels stored as RGBA8 (4 bytes per texel, 16 MiB for the base level). Far from the camera the floor shimmers and crawls as the camera moves. A coding agent is asked to fix the shimmering and turns on mipmaps, a chain of precomputed half-size copies (1024 × 1024, 512 × 512, and so on down to 1 × 1). The full chain, including the base level, occupies about 21.3 MiB. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Mipmaps make the texture look sharper when the camera is very close to the floor, because extra levels add detail.
statements.explanation: Close up, the full-size level is used, so mipmaps change nothing about magnification.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For distant floor where many texels fall in one screen pixel, the GPU reads a smaller pre-averaged level, which removes much of the shimmer.
statements.explanation: Averaging in advance avoids the aliasing that comes from sampling a few texels out of many.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The mip chain adds about one third to the texture's memory (16 MiB becomes about 21.3 MiB).
statements.explanation: 1 + 1/4 + 1/16 + ... approaches 4/3 of the base size; 16 MiB × 4/3 is about 21.3 MiB.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Enabling mipmaps replaces the full-size level, so the texture no longer has its 2048 × 2048 detail up close.
statements.explanation: The base level stays in the chain and is still used where the surface is large on screen.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A 2D sprite drawn at its native size is not shrunk, so it gets little benefit from mipmaps.
statements.explanation: Mipmaps help only when a texture is minified, and a native-size sprite is not.

questions.stem: A 2048 × 2048 albedo texture is a 3 MB PNG file on disk. Kept as plain RGBA8 in video memory (32 bits per texel) its base level takes 16 MiB. A GPU block-compressed format that stores 8 bits per texel would take 4 MiB for the same base level. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A 3 MB PNG tells you little about video memory use: kept uncompressed on the GPU, it still occupies 16 MiB.
statements.explanation: Lossless file formats such as PNG shrink the file on disk, but the GPU needs the decoded texels unless a GPU format is used.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Block-compressed GPU formats are lossless, so image quality is identical to the PNG and nothing is traded away.
statements.explanation: Block compression is lossy and can show banding or blocky artefacts, especially on smooth gradients.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Block-compressed textures can stay compressed in video memory, because the GPU decodes them on the fly when sampling.
statements.explanation: This is why block compression reduces video memory and bandwidth, not just disk size.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A normal map can be compressed with the same format and settings as an albedo texture with no concern for artefacts.
statements.explanation: Small errors in normal vectors show up as lighting artefacts, so engines offer dedicated normal-map compression.

statements.label: E
statements.text: At 8 bits per texel, the base level takes 4 MiB, a quarter of the 32-bits-per-texel size.
statements.explanation: 2048 × 2048 × 8 bits is 4 MiB, one quarter of the 16 MiB at 32 bits.

questions.stem: A texture is sampled when a screen pixel maps to a spot that lies between texel centres or covers many texels. Engines offer these filtering modes: nearest (point), bilinear, trilinear and anisotropic. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Nearest takes the single closest texel, so a magnified texture looks blocky but keeps hard edges, which suits pixel art.
statements.explanation: Nearest filtering keeps each texel as a hard block.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Bilinear filtering blends the four closest texels of one mip level to give smooth magnification.
statements.explanation: Bilinear interpolation uses the four texels around the sample point.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Trilinear filtering also blends between two adjacent mip levels, which hides the seam where the level in use changes.
statements.explanation: Blending two mip levels removes the visible banding between them.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Anisotropic filtering adds no extra texture reads, so it costs nothing compared with bilinear filtering.
statements.explanation: Anisotropic filtering takes extra samples along the stretched direction, so it costs more than the simpler modes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Anisotropic filtering mainly improves surfaces seen at shallow angles, such as a floor stretching away from the camera.
statements.explanation: Surfaces at a shallow angle cover a stretched patch of texture, which plain mipmapping blurs and anisotropic filtering keeps sharper.

questions.stem: A floor is 8 m wide and uses a seamless 512 × 512 texel brick texture. With UV scale 1 the texture is stretched once across the 8 m. A developer asks a coding agent: "make the bricks smaller." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A UV scale of 4 leaves the floor's texel density, the number of texels per metre of surface, at 64, because the image is still 512 × 512 texels.
statements.explanation: Density counts texels per metre of surface: 512 texels over 8 m is 64 per metre at scale 1, and at scale 4 there are 2048 texels over 8 m, which is 256 per metre.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A UV scale of 4 makes the texture four times larger in memory, because four copies of it are now drawn on the floor.
statements.explanation: UV scale changes how coordinates are mapped, not the texture's size in memory.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A UV scale of 4 repeats the texture four times across the width: each repeat covers 2 m, so bricks look four times smaller.
statements.explanation: Multiplying the UVs by 4 fits four copies across the same surface, each 8 / 4 = 2 m wide.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A UV scale of 4 makes the floor mesh four times as large, because scaling the mapping scales the geometry too.
statements.explanation: UV scale changes the mapping on the mesh and leaves the mesh itself alone.

statements.label: E
statements.text: For the repeats to look right the texture must be seamless and the wrap mode must be repeat; with clamp, edge texels smear.
statements.explanation: Repeating requires a seamless image so no joins show, and a repeat wrap mode so coordinates beyond 1 wrap around.

questions.stem: A forest scene has three tree meshes. All three use the same bark shader program, but each tree's material has a different bark texture and a different tint value. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A shader is the program that computes how a surface is drawn; a material bundles a shader with its values and textures.
statements.explanation: The shader is the code; the material holds the shader plus its parameter values and texture bindings.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A texture is a kind of material, so the scene contains three shaders, one per texture.
statements.explanation: A texture is image data that a material uses, not a kind of material, and the scene has only one shader.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because they share one shader, the three trees share one material, so changing the tint on one changes all three.
statements.explanation: Each tree has its own material with its own parameter values, so changing one material does not affect the others.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The scene has three materials that all point at the same shader program.
statements.explanation: Three different parameter and texture sets means three materials, all pointing at the same program.

statements.label: E
statements.text: One bark texture could also be used by several different materials at once.
statements.explanation: Textures are shared resources that any number of materials can reference.

questions.stem: Twenty enemy nodes share a single material resource. A developer asks a coding agent: "make the enemy that was just hit turn red." The agent changes the colour parameter on the shared material, and all twenty enemies turn red. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The agent edited the shared material, so all objects that use it change; the change is not per object.
statements.explanation: A material is a shared resource; objects reference it, and editing it affects all references.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A fix is to give the hit enemy its own material copy or instance, or a per-object parameter (in Godot, a per-instance shader uniform).
statements.explanation: Per-object materials or per-instance parameters make the change local to one enemy.

statements.label: C
statements.text: When several nodes reference one material resource, editing the material through one node's reference changes only that node, because each node keeps a private copy.
statements.explanation: A reference points at the one shared resource, so an edit made through any node's reference changes what all of them draw; only a real copy isolates one node.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Making a per-object copy of a material compiles a brand-new shader program for each enemy, which is why copies are costly.
statements.explanation: A copy shares the same shader program and differs only in its parameter values.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A material instance, a child that inherits a parent material and overrides only parameter values, reuses the parent's shader program, so changing its parameters does not require compiling a new shader.
statements.explanation: An instance differs from its parent only in parameter values, so it shares the parent's compiled shader and changing the values needs no recompile.

questions.stem: An artist packs sixteen 256 × 256 prop textures into one 1024 × 1024 texture atlas (4 × 4 cells). Each prop's UV coordinates are changed to address its own cell. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Props that share the atlas can share one material, which can reduce material and texture switches and draw calls.
statements.explanation: One material and one texture can serve many meshes, so fewer state changes are needed when drawing them.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Hardware texture repeat can still tile one prop's cell, because the sampler wraps at the cell edge.
statements.explanation: Wrapping happens at the edge of the whole texture, not of a cell, so a cell cannot be tiled by hardware repeat.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The atlas makes each prop's texture sharper, since it is part of a larger, higher-resolution image.
statements.explanation: Each prop keeps its own resolution of 256 × 256; packing does not add detail.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A texture atlas is the same thing as a mipmap chain, since both hold several images in one texture.
statements.explanation: An atlas holds different images side by side; a mip chain holds the same image at decreasing sizes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: With filtering and mipmaps, colours from neighbouring cells can bleed across a border unless each cell is padded.
statements.explanation: Filtering reads texels near a border, which may belong to the next cell, so padding is needed.

questions.stem: To save memory and texture reads, some pipelines pack three greyscale maps into the red, green and blue channels of one image. One common arrangement, called ORM (or ARM), is red = ambient occlusion, green = roughness, blue = metallic. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A packed ORM image can be dropped into any engine's mask-map slot unchanged, since the channel order is standardised.
statements.explanation: Channel layouts differ between pipelines, so a packed texture usually has to be repacked for a different engine's slot.

statements.label: B
statements.text: In an engine that uses smoothness instead of roughness, the green channel can be used as it is, with no inversion.
statements.explanation: Smoothness is roughly 1 minus roughness, so the channel would have to be inverted.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A packed image holds data, not colour, so it should be read as linear rather than sRGB, or the values are altered.
statements.explanation: Its channels are numbers used by the shading model, which a colour decode would corrupt.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Packing replaces three separate texture reads with one read that returns all three values.
statements.explanation: One texture sample returns all three values at once, which saves memory bandwidth and texture slots.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the roughness lookup reads the blue channel by mistake, glossiness follows the metallic map instead of the roughness map.
statements.explanation: A wrong channel binding gives plausible-looking but wrong values, with roughness taking the metallic map's pattern.

questions.stem: A developer asks a coding agent to change a shader that tints a character. The agent replies: "Done. The shader compiles with no errors and the existing automated tests pass." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A clean compile shows that the shader's output matches the intended look, because the compiler checks the formulas against the design document.
statements.explanation: The compiler checks syntax and types; it has no knowledge of the intended look.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A compile error means the shader source was rejected by the compiler, whereas a visual bug means it built and ran but drew a wrong result.
statements.explanation: Rejection by the compiler is a compile error; a shader that builds but draws wrongly is a visual bug.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A shader that multiplies a colour by the wrong factor still compiles, so a compile check cannot tell it from a correct one.
statements.explanation: A wrong factor is still valid code, so the compiler accepts it and nothing in the compile output differs.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the existing tests passed both before and after the change, the change cannot have altered how anything is drawn, since a test suite covers the whole game.
statements.explanation: Tests that never inspect rendered pixels cannot see a change in drawing, so they pass whether or not the picture changed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The agent's reply is a claim; the compile log and passing tests are evidence only for narrow things such as valid syntax and unchanged game logic.
statements.explanation: A compile log and a test suite each cover a narrow property, so the reply asserts more than the evidence shows.

questions.source: What headless and software rendering can show
questions.stem: A continuous-integration machine has no graphics card. It runs the game engine in headless mode, where (as with Godot's `--headless` option) the display driver is a dummy and no pixels are drawn. A second option on the same machine is a software renderer, which executes the rasterization on the CPU and does produce an image. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A headless run that reports no errors proves that the shader's output colours are correct, since a shader with wrong colours would raise an error.
statements.explanation: A dummy driver draws nothing, so "no errors" says nothing about what the shader outputs, and wrong colours raise no error.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A headless run can check game logic that feeds a shader, such as which value a script writes to a shader parameter each frame.
statements.explanation: Script-to-parameter logic runs on the CPU and does not need a display, so a headless test can observe it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A frame time measured on the software renderer predicts the frame time on players' graphics cards, since both execute the same shader code.
statements.explanation: The software renderer runs on a CPU with a different execution model, so its speed does not transfer to a GPU.

statements.label: D
statements.text: With a dummy display driver the shader still executes, on the CPU, so a headless timing of a heavy fragment shader reflects its GPU cost.
statements.explanation: With a dummy driver no fragments are shaded at all, so fragment work is absent from the measurement.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An image from a software renderer can check colours, but it may differ from a real GPU's image in precision, filtering or driver behaviour.
statements.explanation: A software renderer is a different implementation of the same pipeline, so small output differences from real hardware are expected.

questions.stem: A team verifies a shader change with a golden-image test. A fixed test scene is rendered at 1280 × 720 (921,600 pixels), captured, and compared with an approved reference image. A pixel counts as different when any channel differs by more than 2 (out of 255). The test fails if more than 0.5 percent of the pixels are different, which is 4,608 pixels. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A wrong-coloured block of 60 × 60 pixels (3,600 pixels) on an otherwise identical capture passes this test, even though it is a real defect.
statements.explanation: 3,600 pixels is below the 4,608-pixel limit, so a visible defect can hide under a percentage threshold.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Tightening the rule to 0.25 percent (2,304 pixels) would make the same 60 × 60 block fail.
statements.explanation: 0.25 percent of 921,600 is 2,304, and 3,600 exceeds it, so the block would now fail.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the reference image was captured from a buggy build and approved without anyone looking at it, the test will still report that bug when it runs.
statements.explanation: A reference that contains the bug makes the buggy output match it, so the test passes and the bug is baked in.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A pass on a scene that does not draw the part of the shader that changed shows that the change is correct, because nothing differed from the reference.
statements.explanation: A scene that does not exercise the changed code gives identical output before and after, which proves nothing about that code.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The per-channel tolerance of 2 keeps tiny rounding or driver differences from failing the test, and it also makes the test blind to very small real colour shifts.
statements.explanation: A tolerance trades false failures against sensitivity; a shift smaller than the tolerance cannot be seen.

questions.source: Evidence versus a claim of success
questions.stem: An agent has rewritten a shader that tints a sprite when the character is damaged and reports: "Verified, it works." The developer wants evidence, not a claim. Check each request that is a sound way to get it.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Confirm once more that you are sure it works, and explain in detail why you believe the tint is correct."
statements.explanation: Repeating and explaining a belief is still a claim, and an explanation from reading code is not an observation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Say which of your statements you observed in a run and which you inferred from reading the code."
statements.explanation: Separating observed from inferred shows which statements rest on evidence and which only on reasoning.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Add a comment at the top of the shader recording that it was verified, with today's date and your name."
statements.explanation: A comment records an assertion and cannot confirm anything about the output.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Render a fixed test scene at tint amounts 0, 0.5 and 1, capture it, and report pixel values at known points beside the values the specification predicts."
statements.explanation: Controlled inputs with measured outputs placed beside predicted values are an observation that can contradict the claim.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Run the compile check again and paste the output line that reports no errors, so that we have it in the log."
statements.explanation: Rerunning the same compile check can only repeat the same result, so it adds no new information.

questions.source: Coordinate spaces: local, world, view, screen
questions.stem: Shader code works with positions and directions in several coordinate spaces. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Local (object or model) space measures positions from the object's own origin and axes, so a vertex keeps the same local position when the object moves or rotates.
statements.explanation: Local coordinates are stored with the mesh and do not change when the object's transform changes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: World space is shared by all objects in the scene; moving a position from local to world space applies the object's transform.
statements.explanation: The model transform is exactly the step that carries local positions into the shared world.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Screen space is the same thing as texture coordinates (UV): both run from 0 to 1 across the mesh, so a screen position can be read directly as a UV.
statements.explanation: UV coordinates are per-vertex texture coordinates, whereas screen space says where a fragment lands on the display, usually in pixels.

statements.label: D
statements.text: View (camera or eye) space measures positions relative to the camera, which sits at the origin.
statements.explanation: View space is defined relative to the camera, which is why it changes whenever the camera moves.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the camera has only been moved and not rotated, a point's view-space position still differs from its world-space position.
statements.explanation: Moving the camera shifts every point's view-space position by the camera's offset, so the two spaces do not coincide.

questions.stem: A coding agent writes a fragment shader for a flood line: everything below a height of 0.5 in the world should be drawn darker, as if water stood at that level. The agent takes each fragment's height from the vertex position exactly as the mesh stores it and compares it with 0.5, with no transformation. The prop is a crate 2 units tall whose origin is at its centre, so its stored heights run from −1 to +1. The crate stands on a platform so that its centre is at world height 10. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The crate is not darkened at all, because it stands at world height 10, far above the flood line of 0.5, and the shader is meant to affect only low objects.
statements.explanation: The shader never leaves local space, so the lower three quarters of the crate (stored heights −1 to 0.5) are darkened wherever it stands.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The stored vertex position is in local space, so the shader compares height measured from the crate's own centre with 0.5, not height in the level.
statements.explanation: Mesh-supplied positions are local, and comparing them with a world-space value mixes two spaces.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Moving this one crate to world height 0 would make the effect correct for the props across the level, because the flood line is then at the right height.
statements.explanation: That would hide the bug for one crate only; props at other heights, rotated or scaled, would still be wrong.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Converting the position to view space instead would give a fixed flood line, because view space does not depend on where the camera is.
statements.explanation: View space is measured from the camera, so the flood line would move every time the camera moved.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If the crate is turned upside down, the darkened band ends up at its top in the world, because the stored heights turn with the object.
statements.explanation: Stored heights rotate with the object, so the region where they are below 0.5 turns upside down with it.

questions.stem: A surface runs along the direction t = (1, 1, 0) and has the normal n = (1, −1, 0), so t · n = 0 and the two are perpendicular. The object is then scaled non-uniformly by (1, 4, 1), making it four times taller. A vertex shader carries the surface direction through the model matrix and gets t′ = (1, 4, 0). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Carrying n through the same model matrix gives n′ = (1, −4, 0), which is not perpendicular to t′, because t′ · n′ = 1 − 16 = −15.
statements.explanation: The model matrix stretches the normal's y component the same way it stretches the surface, which tilts it out of perpendicular.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Carrying n through the inverse transpose of the matrix gives (1, −0.25, 0), which is perpendicular to t′, because t′ · n′ = 1 − 1 = 0.
statements.explanation: The inverse transpose scales the normal's y component by 1/4 and keeps it perpendicular to the transformed surface.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The model matrix gives correct normals under a non-uniform scale, so the inverse transpose is a mathematical convenience that can be skipped.
statements.explanation: Under non-uniform scale the model matrix does not preserve perpendicularity, which is exactly why normals need the inverse transpose.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If an object is only rotated or scaled equally on all axes, the model matrix followed by normalizing gives a normal with the right direction.
statements.explanation: A rotation or a uniform scale keeps angles, so only the length changes and normalizing fixes it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Normalizing a normal after the model matrix has been applied repairs its direction under non-uniform scale, because normalizing removes the distortion.
statements.explanation: Normalizing changes length only; the direction (1, −4, 0) is still not perpendicular to t′.

questions.stem: Shading languages let a variable be declared in full precision (32-bit float) or half precision (16-bit float). Half-precision values are spaced 1/1024 apart between 1 and 2, exactly 1 apart between 1024 and 2048, and exactly 2 apart between 2048 and 4096; the largest half-precision value is 65,504. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Half precision is fine for world positions in the thousands of units, because its range reaches 65,504 and range is what matters for a position.
statements.explanation: The range is enough but the spacing at 3,000 is 2 units, so positions can only land on every second unit.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Half precision is usually adequate for colours in the range 0 to 1, where an error of about 0.001 is not visible.
statements.explanation: Between 0.5 and 1 the spacing is about 0.0005, far below what an eye can see in a colour.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A half-precision variable can hold the value 3001 exactly, since 3001 is well inside the format's range.
statements.explanation: Between 2048 and 4096 only even integers are representable, so 3001 rounds to 3000 or 3002.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A half-precision variable holding 1500 stays at 1500 when 0.4 is added, because values there are 1 apart and 1500.4 rounds back.
statements.explanation: A change smaller than half the spacing is lost when the sum is rounded.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Half precision can be applied to a shader's variables as a routine speed-up, with no need to compare the picture afterwards, because the digits it loses are small.
statements.explanation: The lost digits are small for colours but not for large values (at 3,000 the spacing is 2 units), so the picture can change; any speed-up also depends on the hardware, so the change has to be checked against the picture.

questions.stem: A scrolling-water effect looks smooth on the developer's desktop. On a mid-range phone, after the game has run for a while, the texture starts to move in visible jumps. The shader computes the texture offset as elapsed time × 0.1 and keeps it in a half-precision variable. By the time the jumps appear the offset has reached 10.0, where half-precision values are spaced 1/128 (0.0078125) apart. The water texture is 512 texels wide. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The smooth result on the desktop shows the shader is correct, because the same source ran there and produced the right motion.
statements.explanation: A desktop GPU may compute everything at full precision whatever the declaration says, so the bug can be invisible there.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Near an offset of 10.0 the smallest representable change is 0.0078125, which is 4 texels of a 512-texel texture, so the motion advances in jumps.
statements.explanation: 0.0078125 × 512 = 4 texels, so the offset can only move in steps of 4 texels.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Switching to a larger texture, such as 1024 texels wide, would remove the jumps, because the jumps are measured in texels.
statements.explanation: The step in texture-coordinate units is unchanged, so on a 1024-texel texture the jump would grow to 8 texels.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Raising the frame rate would remove the jumps, because they come from how often the frame is drawn.
statements.explanation: The jumps come from the spacing of representable values at that magnitude, not from how often the frame is drawn.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A sound fix is to compute the offset in full precision, or to reduce it to its fractional part before storing it in half precision.
statements.explanation: Keeping the value small, or computing it at full precision, removes the coarse spacing.

questions.stem: A GPU runs the fragment shader for neighbouring pixels together in lockstep groups (called warps, wavefronts or SIMD groups, depending on the vendor). A fragment shader contains an `if` whose two sides are each expensive, for example one side samples several textures and does long arithmetic. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: When the condition differs from pixel to pixel within a group, an `if` still saves time compared with computing both results and blending them, because each pixel runs the side it takes and skips the other.
statements.explanation: Where pixels in a group disagree, the group runs both sides, so there is no saving, and computing both results and blending can be no slower.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If all pixels in a group take the same side of the `if`, the group can run only that side and skip the other.
statements.explanation: With a coherent condition the group follows a single path and the other side costs nothing.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If pixels in the same group disagree about the condition, the hardware runs both sides for that group with the non-participating pixels switched off.
statements.explanation: Divergence within a group forces both paths to execute in lockstep, with results masked.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A condition computed from a value that differs from pixel to pixel, such as noise, is as cheap as a condition taken from a uniform.
statements.explanation: Per-pixel conditions can diverge within a group, so they can cost far more than a uniform-based one.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A condition taken from a uniform, which is constant across the whole draw, cannot make pixels in a group disagree.
statements.explanation: Every pixel reads the same uniform value, so all of them take the same side.

questions.source: Default uniform values and shared materials
questions.stem: A shader declares a uniform named `flash_amount` with a default of 0.0. A script sets it to 1.0 on one enemy when that enemy is hit. In play, all 12 enemies, which share a single material, flash at once. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The declared default is the value each object using the material has until something overrides it.
statements.explanation: A uniform's declared default applies to every user of the material until a parameter value replaces it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The problem is a shader compile error, which would have been reported when the shader loaded, so the shader source must be fixed.
statements.explanation: The shader compiled and ran; the symptom comes from where the parameter value is stored, not from invalid code.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A material is a shared asset: all objects that reference the same material see a change made to that material's parameter.
statements.explanation: One material instance means one set of parameter values, so a write through any user is seen by all of them.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Giving each enemy its own copy of the material, or using a per-instance parameter feature (such as Godot's instance uniforms on 3D nodes or Unity's material property blocks), limits the flash to the enemy hit.
statements.explanation: Per-object materials or per-instance parameters give each enemy its own value of `flash_amount`.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A reviewer should ask what the shader draws when no script has touched the parameter, because that default is what each object starts with.
statements.explanation: The unset state is the case most objects are in most of the time, so the default must itself be a correct look.

questions.stem: A damage flash fades out over 33 frames, counted by adding 1 to an integer once per rendered frame. The design says the fade should last 0.55 seconds. The developer checks it only at 60 frames per second. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Passing the check at 60 frames per second shows that the fade is independent of the frame rate, since 60 is the usual rate.
statements.explanation: At 60 frames per second a 33-frame counter and a 0.55 s clock are the same function, so that rate cannot tell them apart.

statements.label: B
statements.text: At 30 frames per second the fade lasts 1.1 seconds.
statements.explanation: 33 / 30 = 1.1 seconds.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Driving the fade from elapsed game time (the sum of each frame's delta time) makes its length independent of the frame rate, apart from one-frame granularity.
statements.explanation: Accumulated delta time measures real game time, so the fade ends at the same moment at any frame rate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: At 144 frames per second the fade lasts about 1.3 seconds, because more frames per second means more time passes.
statements.explanation: 33 / 144 is about 0.23 seconds, so the fade is shorter, not longer.

statements.label: E
statements.text: At exactly 60 frames per second, 33 frames last 0.55 seconds, so there a frame counter and the design agree.
statements.explanation: 33 / 60 = 0.55 seconds, which is why a check at that single rate passes.

questions.stem: An agent writes a new automated check for a shader's behaviour and runs it against the changed code. It passes, and the agent reports that the change is verified. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The agent wrote the change and the check as two separate pieces of code, so a pass confirms the change independently of the agent's own assumptions.
statements.explanation: Separate files do not make separate assumptions: both came from the same author, so they can share the same mistake.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Running the same check ten more times against the same changed code adds confidence that the check can detect the bug.
statements.explanation: Repeating a run against one version cannot show whether the check would notice a bug if there were one.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The check becomes evidence about the change once it has been shown to fail on a known-bad version and to pass on a known-good one.
statements.explanation: A check that separates known-bad from known-good output carries information about the change; one that has not been shown to do so carries none.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A check that passes on the known-bad version as well as on the known-good one still supports the change under review, because it passed on that change too.
statements.explanation: A check that cannot tell good from bad passes whatever the change does, so its pass on the change means nothing.

statements.label: E
statements.text: When a check fails on a version known to be good, the fault lies in that version, because the check encodes what the design requires.
statements.explanation: A failure on known-good code often means the check is wrong, for example a tolerance that is too tight, so the check must be examined as well as the code.

questions.stem: A shader should move its colour from a base colour toward a flash colour by an amount between 0 and 1: output = base + (flash − base) × amount, with alpha unchanged. A test oracle is whatever a test compares a result against. An agent's shader contains a mistake in that formula, yet the agent's test passes, because the test computes its expected values by copying the formula from the shader. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An oracle copied from the code under test is preferable, since it follows changes to the code without extra maintenance.
statements.explanation: A copied formula repeats the code's mistakes, so it can never disagree with the code.

statements.label: B
statements.text: An oracle written from the specification (amount 0 gives the base, amount 1 gives the flash colour, a straight line between) would have caught the mistake.
statements.explanation: An independent statement of the rule disagrees with a wrong formula and exposes it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: For base (0.8, 0.4, 0.3), flash (0.1, 0.2, 0.3) and amount 0.5, the specification gives (0.45, 0.30, 0.30), computable on the CPU without running the shader.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A CPU calculation of the specification replaces the need to look at what the GPU actually drew, because both follow the same arithmetic.
statements.explanation: The model says what the screen should show, not what the GPU produced, so only observation closes that gap.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An oracle written from the specification stays valid when the shader is rewritten; one copied from the implementation is valid only while that implementation lasts.
statements.explanation: A specification does not depend on how the shader is written, whereas a copy of the code does.

questions.stem: A game renders at 1920 × 1080, which is 2,073,600 pixels. After the scene is drawn, three full-screen translucent layers are drawn on top of it: fog, a damage vignette and a colour grade. Each layer runs a fragment shader once for every pixel it covers. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Together the three layers run the fragment shader 6,220,800 times per frame (3 × 2,073,600).
statements.explanation: 3 × 2,073,600 = 6,220,800 invocations per frame.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Rendering the same frame at 3840 × 2160 multiplies each layer's invocations by 4, to 8,294,400.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A layer's cost depends mainly on how many triangles its mesh has, so a full-screen layer drawn as two triangles is almost free.
statements.explanation: Fragment cost follows the number of pixels covered, and two triangles can cover the whole screen.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Combining the three effects into one full-screen pass shades each pixel once instead of three times, although that one shader does more work per pixel.
statements.explanation: One pass means one invocation per pixel instead of three, at the price of a heavier shader.

statements.label: E
statements.text: For a 20,000-vertex mesh covering a 1080p screen, the fragment stage runs about 104 times as often as the vertex stage, so a linearly varying value is cheaper computed per vertex.
statements.explanation: 2,073,600 / 20,000 is about 104, and interpolation of a linear value gives the same result at that lower frequency.

questions.stem: While reviewing an agent's shader change, a developer prepares controlled inputs: test values chosen so that the correct output and the wrong output are far apart and easy to compute. Two suspected mistakes are alpha being applied twice and a flipped vertical texture coordinate. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A test texture that is red along the top and blue along the bottom exposes a vertical flip; a texture identical top to bottom could not.
statements.explanation: A flip swaps top and bottom, which is only visible if top and bottom differ.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A fully opaque test pixel (alpha 1.0) is the best input for exposing alpha applied twice, because it gives the cleanest colour reading.
statements.explanation: Multiplying by an alpha of 1.0 changes nothing, so doubling it is invisible.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A texture that is symmetric from top to bottom is as good as an asymmetric one for exposing a flipped coordinate, since the arithmetic is the same either way.
statements.explanation: A texture that looks the same upside down looks the same flipped, so it hides the bug.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A vertical flip turns the picture through 180 degrees, so left and right are swapped as well as top and bottom.
statements.explanation: A vertical flip is a mirror in the vertical direction only; left and right keep their places.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A shader that multiplies colour by alpha and is then drawn with ordinary alpha blending applies alpha twice: white at alpha 0.5 over black gives 0.25, not 0.5.
statements.explanation: 1.0 × 0.5 = 0.5 is already premultiplied, and the blend then multiplies by 0.5 again to give 0.25.

questions.source: A precise specification to hand an agent
questions.stem: A developer must give a coding agent a specification for a character's hit flash, precise enough that the result can be checked against it on any device, whatever its frame rate. Check each instruction that meets that bar.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Add a flash amount from 0 to 1 (0 leaves the incoming colour as it is, 1 gives (0.15, 0.21, 0.29), values in between are a linear mix, alpha unchanged), and after a hit let it fall from 1 to 0 over 33 rendered frames."
statements.explanation: A duration counted in rendered frames lasts a different time at each frame rate, so it cannot be checked against one fixed duration on every device.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Add a flash amount from 0 to 1 that pushes the player's colour toward (0.15, 0.21, 0.29), and after a hit let it fall from 1 to 0 over 0.55 seconds of game time."
statements.explanation: It names a colour and a duration but never says what the output is at any amount, so there is no expected pixel value to compare with.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Add a flash amount from 0 to 1: at 0 the output equals the incoming colour, at 1 it equals (0.15, 0.21, 0.29), in between a linear mix, alpha unchanged. After a hit the amount jumps to 1 and then returns to 0, so the player looks normal again."
statements.explanation: With no duration the fade could take any time and still count as correct, so the timing cannot be checked.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Add a flash amount from 0 to 1: at 0 the output equals the incoming colour exactly, at 1 it equals (0.15, 0.21, 0.29), in between a linear mix, alpha unchanged. After a hit it falls from 1 to 0 over 0.55 seconds of game time."
statements.explanation: It fixes the endpoints, the in-between rule, alpha and the timing in game time, so each can be tested with chosen inputs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Add a flash amount from 0 to 1: at 0 the output equals the incoming colour, at 1 it equals a strong red, in between a linear mix, alpha unchanged. After a hit it falls from 1 to 0 over 0.55 seconds of game time."
statements.explanation: "A strong red" is not a value, so no captured pixel can be compared with the flash colour.

questions.stem: A technical artist describes a campfire effect to a coding agent and uses the vocabulary of particle effects. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A particle is one small element of the effect that the system creates, updates and removes over time; it carries its own state, such as age, position and velocity, and is usually drawn as a textured quad or a small mesh.
statements.explanation: A particle is a lightweight record with a life cycle (it is born, updated each step and removed), and it is drawn as a quad or a small mesh.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Particles are separate game objects with their own scripts, which is why particle effects are expensive for the engine to run.
statements.explanation: Particles are data processed in bulk by one system; they are not individual objects with scripts.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An emitter is the source that creates particles, either steadily at some rate or in bursts.
statements.explanation: The emitter is where particles are born, and its rate or burst settings control when.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A particle system is the whole effect (spawning, simulation, drawing), and one effect can combine several emitters.
statements.explanation: The system covers emission, simulation and rendering, and a larger effect may use more than one emitter.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Emission shape (a point, sphere, box or cone) decides where particles start, while initial velocity decides how they move; the two are separate settings.
statements.explanation: Placement of births and motion after birth are independent controls.

questions.source: Emission rate versus burst, and one-shot
questions.stem: A coding agent is asked to set up how particles are emitted. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A burst spawns a stated count at one instant, whereas a continuous emission rate, such as 40 per second, spawns particles steadily.
statements.explanation: Rate is particles per unit time; a burst is a count delivered at a moment.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A burst is the same thing as a looping effect with a high emission rate, since both produce a large number of particles in a short time.
statements.explanation: A high rate spreads births over time, whereas a burst puts them all at one instant.

statements.label: C
statements.text: One-shot (non-looping) means the system plays one emission cycle and then stops until triggered again; it says nothing about the count.
statements.explanation: One-shot controls how many cycles play, not how many particles each cycle spawns.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A burst is a one-time event at the start of playback: on a looping system it fires in the first cycle, and later cycles emit only at the continuous rate.
statements.explanation: A looping system starts its cycle again when its duration ends, and a burst is scheduled at a time within the cycle, so the burst fires again in every cycle.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A one-shot system that also has a continuous rate keeps emitting until it is stopped by hand, because the rate stays above zero.
statements.explanation: One-shot means the cycle runs once and then emission stops.

questions.source: Rate, lifetime and particle count; prewarm
questions.stem: A smoke emitter spawns 40 particles per second, and each particle lives exactly 1.5 seconds. The effect starts with no particles at time 0 and runs continuously. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Doubling the rate to 80 particles per second leaves the steady-state count at 60, because lifetime alone fixes how many particles are alive.
statements.explanation: The steady-state count is rate × lifetime, so doubling the rate doubles it to 120.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Once the effect has run for more than 1.5 seconds, about 60 particles are alive at any moment (40 × 1.5).
statements.explanation: Births per second times seconds of life gives 40 × 1.5 = 60 alive.

statements.label: C
statements.text: At 0.75 seconds about 60 particles are already alive, because the emitter fills its steady-state population immediately at the start.
statements.explanation: Nothing has died yet at 0.75 s, so only 40 × 0.75 = 30 particles have been born.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the lifetime were cut to 0.5 seconds at the same rate, about 20 particles would be alive in the steady state.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A prewarm option, which simulates the system for at least 1.5 seconds before the first visible frame, starts the effect with about 60 particles alive instead of ramping up.
statements.explanation: Prewarm skips the ramp-up by starting from a population that has already reached steady state.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: "an explosion" versus a precise burst
questions.stem: A developer wants a grenade explosion in a 2D game. The first prompt to a coding agent is "add an explosion effect". A second prompt reads: "add a one-shot burst of 40 particles at the grenade's position, each living 0.6 seconds, launched outward in all directions at 150 to 300 pixels per second, no gravity, shrinking to zero size and fading to transparent over its life". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The first prompt is acceptable, because "explosion" is a standard term with a settled meaning across engines, so the agent will build what is expected.
statements.explanation: "Explosion" names no count, lifetime, speed, direction or loop behaviour, so the agent has to guess each one.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The second prompt fixes burst versus continuous, count, lifetime, speed range, direction spread, gravity and over-life changes, so two agents would build a burst with nearly the same timing and motion.
statements.explanation: Each property that defines when particles appear and how they move is given a value or a rule; texture, colour and blend mode are still open, but they do not change the timing or the motion.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The second prompt is still ambiguous about whether the 40 particles appear at once or are spread over the 0.6 seconds.
statements.explanation: "Burst" means all particles are born at one instant.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The first prompt leaves the agent free to build a looping emitter that keeps spraying after the grenade has gone off.
statements.explanation: Without "one-shot", looping versus playing once is the agent's choice.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Adding "and make it look cool" to the second prompt would improve the agent's accuracy, because it tells the agent the intended result.
statements.explanation: An adjective that cannot be measured adds no constraint and no check.

questions.stem: In a 2D game, gravity acts on particles at 98 pixels per second squared, downward. A particle is launched straight up at 150 pixels per second and lives 0.6 seconds. Measured upward, its velocity is 150 − 98t pixels per second and its height above the start is 150t − ½ · 98 · t² pixels. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A larger spread, meaning a wider cone of launch directions, makes each particle leave the emitter faster.
statements.explanation: Spread widens the range of launch directions; the launch speed is set by the initial velocity, not by the spread.

statements.label: B
statements.text: At 0.6 seconds the particle is about 72 pixels above its start.

statements.label: C
statements.text: At 0.6 seconds its vertical velocity is still upward, about 91 pixels per second.
statements.explanation: 150 − 98 × 0.6 = 91.2 pixels per second, still positive.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It would reach its highest point at about 1.5 seconds, so it does not start to fall during its 0.6-second life.
statements.explanation: The peak comes when 150 − 98t = 0, at t of about 1.53 seconds.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Initial velocity sets the starting speed and direction, while gravity is a constant acceleration that keeps changing velocity; a particle launched at zero velocity still ends up moving.
statements.explanation: Velocity changes by the acceleration each second, so zero starting velocity does not mean zero motion.

questions.stem: A particle has a lifetime of 0.6 seconds. Its scale curve falls linearly from 1.0 at birth to 0.0 at death, and its colour ramp fades alpha linearly from 1.0 to 0.0. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A curve or ramp over lifetime is indexed by seconds, so the same curve would reach 0 at 1.0 second for lifetimes of 0.6 and 1.2 seconds.
statements.explanation: The curve is read by fraction of life, so its end always falls at the particle's death.

statements.label: B
statements.text: At an age of 0.15 seconds, the scale and the alpha are both 0.75.
statements.explanation: 0.15 / 0.6 = 0.25 of the life, and 1 − 0.25 = 0.75 for a linear fall.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the lifetime were changed to 1.2 seconds, then at an age of 0.3 seconds the scale would again be 0.75, because the curve stretches over the longer life.
statements.explanation: 0.3 / 1.2 = 0.25 of the life, which gives the same 0.75.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A colour ramp sets the colour a particle has at birth; fading during its life needs a script that updates it as the particle ages.
statements.explanation: A colour ramp is sampled across the whole life, which is how fades are made without code.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Curves and ramps are read by normalised age (age divided by lifetime, 0 to 1), so they work unchanged for particles with different lifetimes.
statements.explanation: Using age divided by lifetime lets one curve serve particles of any length of life.

questions.stem: Engines offer particle systems that simulate on the CPU and others that simulate on the GPU. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The CPU or GPU setting decides who draws the particles: CPU particles are drawn by the CPU and GPU particles by the GPU.
statements.explanation: Both kinds are drawn by the GPU; the setting decides where the simulation (the per-particle update) runs.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A GPU particle system updates its particles in shaders on the graphics card, so very large counts are practical, but scripts cannot cheaply read each particle's state.
statements.explanation: On the GPU the update is data-parallel and fast, but the particle data stays on the graphics card.

statements.label: C
statements.text: GPU particles cannot use textures or blending modes, because those features belong to the CPU side of the engine.
statements.explanation: Textures and blending belong to drawing, which both kinds share.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A CPU particle system updates all particles on the CPU each frame, so its simulation cost rises roughly in proportion to the particle count.
statements.explanation: CPU simulation is per-particle work on the CPU, so more particles take more CPU time.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A CPU particle system does not depend on the graphics card for its simulation, so it is the usual fallback on hardware with weak GPU compute support.
statements.explanation: GPU simulation needs the graphics hardware to run the update, whereas CPU simulation needs nothing special, so it runs on a wider range of devices.

questions.stem: A game must run on an older phone. Effect 1 is 80 sparks per hit, and each spark must apply a gameplay rule (it damages any enemy it touches). Effect 2 is ambient snowfall with 20,000 flakes that never affect gameplay. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Effect 2 suits GPU particles: the count is large and no script needs the flakes' state.
statements.explanation: A large cosmetic effect is the case GPU simulation is built for.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Because 80 sparks cost almost nothing on the CPU, 20,000 CPU-simulated flakes would cost almost nothing too, since particles are cheap.
statements.explanation: 20,000 / 80 = 250 times as many particles, and CPU cost grows with count.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Effect 1 suits CPU particles, or ordinary gameplay objects with particles used only for the look, because per-particle gameplay logic needs state on the CPU.
statements.explanation: Gameplay rules run in scripts on the CPU, which wants the particle state there or a separate gameplay object.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Hardware support can tip the choice: CPU particle systems run on a wider range of devices, which matters on old phones.
statements.explanation: Older devices may lack good GPU compute, so a CPU system can be the safe choice.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Both effects must use the same kind of particle node so that they can be drawn in one draw call and share one material.
statements.explanation: Different node types do not have to share a draw call, and nothing about the effects requires it.

questions.stem: A spaceship flies across the screen at 300 pixels per second. Two particle effects are attached to it: an engine exhaust, whose particles should trail behind the ship as it moves, and a shield shimmer, whose particles should stay around the ship and move with it. Each particle lives 1 second. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In world coordinates, a particle born 1 second ago has been left about 300 pixels behind the ship's current position, ignoring the particle's own velocity.
statements.explanation: The ship has moved 300 pixels per second × 1 second, while the particle has stayed where it was born.

statements.label: B
statements.text: If the exhaust were set to local coordinates, particles born at the tail would be carried along with the ship, so no trail would form.
statements.explanation: In local space a particle's position is relative to the emitter, so it travels with the ship.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The local-versus-world setting makes a visible difference even when the emitter stays still, because it changes how the particles' positions are stored.
statements.explanation: With a stationary emitter both settings give the same positions; the difference shows only when the emitter moves.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Local coordinates suit the shield shimmer, because its particles move with the emitter's transform.
statements.explanation: Particles in local space stay attached to the ship, which is what a shield needs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: With world coordinates a particle keeps the position where it was born while the emitter moves, so the exhaust leaves a trail.
statements.explanation: World-space particles are no longer tied to the emitter after birth.

questions.stem: Particles can be combined with the background in different ways. In alpha blending the result is particle colour × alpha + background × (1 − alpha). In additive blending the result is background + particle colour × alpha. Colours run from 0 (black) to 1 (full intensity), and results above 1 are clamped to 1. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Over black, pure red then pure blue at alpha 0.5 each give (0.25, 0, 0.5) with alpha blending, and blue then red give (0.5, 0, 0.25), so order matters.
statements.explanation: Red first gives (0.5, 0, 0) and then blue gives (0.25, 0, 0.5); the reverse order gives (0.5, 0, 0.25).

statements.label: B
statements.text: A black particle drawn additively darkens the background by covering it, so black smoke can be made with additive blending.
statements.explanation: Adding a black colour adds 0, so the background is unchanged; additive blending can only brighten.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Two additive particles give the same result in either drawing order, because addition does not depend on order.
statements.explanation: The sum background + a + b is the same in both orders.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Additive blending suits fire, sparks and glows, because overlap brightens toward white; it is a poor fit for dark smoke, which would add nothing.
statements.explanation: Overlapping additive particles accumulate light, which fits emissive effects but not dark, opaque-looking smoke.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Three additive particles that each contribute 0.25 over a background of 0.30 give 1.05 on screen, because additive results are not limited.
statements.explanation: 0.30 + 3 × 0.25 = 1.05, which is clamped to 1.0.

questions.stem: A 3D game draws each smoke particle as a flat textured quad. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In a 2D game with a flat orthographic camera, billboarding is what keeps the quads facing the screen, so it must be switched on.
statements.explanation: With a flat orthographic 2D camera the quads already face the screen, so nothing needs to be turned.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Without billboarding, a flat quad seen exactly edge-on shrinks to a thin line or disappears, which breaks the illusion of a puff.
statements.explanation: A flat quad has no thickness, so from the side it has almost no area to draw.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A particle drawn as a mesh is also a billboard, because particles are drawn facing the camera, as quads or meshes.
statements.explanation: A mesh particle keeps its 3D shape and orientation; it is the alternative to a billboard.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A billboard is a quad that is turned each frame to face the camera, so the particle shows the same flat shape from any angle.
statements.explanation: Turning toward the camera each frame is what billboarding means.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A billboarded particle cannot spin about the view direction, because the camera fixes its orientation.
statements.explanation: A billboard can still spin about the view direction, which is how rotation over lifetime works for flat particles.

questions.stem: A 1080p frame has 1920 × 1080 = 2,073,600 pixels. A smoke effect uses 150 particles, each drawn as a 200 × 200 pixel quad, and all the quads lie inside a 400 × 400 pixel region of the screen. The smoke texture is a round puff that fills the largest circle inside its square quad, and the rest of the quad is fully transparent. Every pixel of a quad is shaded, including the transparent ones. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Making each quad 100 × 100 pixels would halve the total fragment count, to 3,000,000, because each side is halved.
statements.explanation: Area scales with the square of the side, so 100 × 100 gives 150 × 10,000 = 1,500,000, a quarter.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Averaged over the 160,000-pixel region, each pixel is shaded 37.5 times (6,000,000 / 160,000), assuming all quads lie inside the region.
statements.explanation: 6,000,000 shaded fragments spread over 160,000 pixels is 37.5 layers on average.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because 6,000,000 is more than the 2,073,600 pixels of the screen, the effect must cover the whole screen.
statements.explanation: The fragments pile up in a 160,000-pixel region, not across the whole screen.

statements.label: D
statements.text: About 21 percent of each quad's area is transparent corner outside the round puff, yet those pixels are still shaded.
statements.explanation: The circle fills π/4 (about 78.5 percent) of the square, so about 21.5 percent is empty corner.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The effect runs the fragment shader 6,000,000 times per frame (150 × 40,000).
statements.explanation: Each quad covers 200 × 200 = 40,000 pixels, and 150 quads give 6,000,000 invocations.

questions.stem: Many large transparent particles cost more than the same number of small or opaque ones. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Halving the lifetime at the same emission rate doubles the number of live particles, because particles are replaced twice as often.
statements.explanation: Live particles equal rate × lifetime, so halving the lifetime halves the count.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Doubling each particle's width and height doubles its fragment cost, because the size has doubled.
statements.explanation: Doubling both sides quadruples the area, and so the fragment count.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Opaque surfaces can be rejected by the depth test when something nearer is already drawn, whereas stacked transparent particles must each be blended in turn.
statements.explanation: The depth test can skip hidden opaque fragments, but transparent layers cannot be skipped because each contributes to the result.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Making the texture more transparent everywhere (lower alpha) reduces the number of fragments shaded, because transparent pixels are skipped.
statements.explanation: Transparent fragments are still shaded and blended; lower alpha only changes the result, not the number of fragments.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Overdraw is cheap on mobile GPUs, because tile-based rendering hides the cost of blending.
statements.explanation: Fill rate is a main constraint on mobile, and transparent overdraw is one of its most common costs.

questions.stem: A burst effect gives each particle a random speed and direction. Assume the effect takes one simulation step per rendered frame, so the length of a step follows the frame rate. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Fixing the seed makes the burst identical at 30 and 144 frames per second, because the random numbers no longer depend on time.
statements.explanation: The seed fixes the random numbers, but positions also depend on the time step, so different frame rates can give different results.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A random seed is the starting value of a pseudo-random generator; the same seed and draw order give the same numbers, so tests fix it to repeat a burst.
statements.explanation: Seeding makes the generator's output a repeatable sequence, which is what a test needs.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In shipped games a fixed seed is normally left on, so that explosions look identical, because variation counts as a flaw in a finished effect.
statements.explanation: Production effects usually use a varying seed so that repeated bursts do not look copied.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Determinism needs only a fixed seed; the size of each time step and the order in which random numbers are drawn do not affect the outcome.
