statements.explanation: Different time steps or a different order of draws change the outcome even with the same seed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: An effect that is given a fixed random seed will look different each time it is played, because the random numbers are drawn fresh from the clock.
statements.explanation: The same seed gives the same sequence of random numbers, so each play looks the same; variation between plays needs a different seed each time.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: a precise looping effect
questions.stem: A developer needs a campfire in a 3D game and gives a coding agent one of two prompts. Prompt 1: "make the fire look good". Prompt 2: "a looping emitter, 80 particles per second, lifetime 0.8 seconds, world-space coordinates, additive blending, billboarded quads, initial upward velocity 1.5 to 2.5 metres per second with a small spread, a colour ramp from yellow to transparent red, and scale shrinking to zero over life". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Prompt 2 implies about 64 live particles in the steady state (80 × 0.8).
statements.explanation: Steady-state count is rate × lifetime, 80 × 0.8 = 64.

statements.label: B
statements.text: On a torch the player carries, world-space coordinates would let the flames trail behind as the player moves.
statements.explanation: World-space particles are left behind when the emitter moves, which gives flames weight and motion.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Looping" in Prompt 2 means the emitter keeps emitting until it is stopped, as a campfire should.
statements.explanation: A looping emitter restarts its cycle again and again, so the fire does not stop on its own.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Prompt 1 specifies the same effect as Prompt 2, because the agent already knows what a campfire looks like.
statements.explanation: Prompt 1 fixes no rate, lifetime, blending, space or colour, so different agents would build different fires.

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Billboarded quads" tells the agent to turn each particle toward the camera, so a flame seen from any side does not become an edge-on line.
statements.explanation: Billboarding keeps flat particles facing the camera.

questions.stem: In a game, an enemy is destroyed the instant it is hit. A one-shot burst effect is a child of the enemy object in the scene hierarchy. During testing, a log line confirms "burst started", yet players never see the burst. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The log line "burst started" proves that the burst was drawn on screen, because the effect cannot start without being drawn.
statements.explanation: A log line records that the effect started, not that anything was visible.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A one-shot burst plays again on the next hit without any further action, because the effect resets itself after finishing.
statements.explanation: A one-shot effect plays one cycle and stays finished until it is restarted or spawned again.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A common fix is to spawn the effect as its own object in the world, at the enemy's position, so that it outlives the enemy.
statements.explanation: A separate effect object has its own lifetime, independent of the enemy.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Switching from CPU particles to GPU particles would make the burst visible, because GPU particles are not tied to a parent.
statements.explanation: The cause is the parent-child relationship, not where the simulation runs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A burst parented to the enemy can be cut off or hidden the instant the enemy is destroyed or hidden, because children go with their parent.
statements.explanation: Destroying, hiding or deactivating a parent removes or hides its children too.

questions.stem: An agent measures particle cost in a headless run (no window and no graphics card; the renderer is a dummy that draws nothing) with 50,000 particles of each kind. GPU-simulated particles cost 0.002 ms per frame and CPU-simulated particles cost 1.6 ms per frame. The frame budget at 60 frames per second is 16.67 ms. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The 1.6 ms for CPU particles is about 9.6 percent of a 60-frames-per-second frame budget (1.6 / 16.67).

statements.label: B
statements.text: The 0.002 ms figure shows that GPU particles are nearly free on a real graphics card, because the same code ran in the test.
statements.explanation: The dummy renderer does no GPU work, so the number is a property of the instrument, not of GPU particles.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The CPU figure is meaningless because nothing about a headless run resembles real play, so it cannot be used even as an estimate.
statements.explanation: CPU simulation really ran on the CPU, so its figure is a usable estimate, to be re-measured on target hardware.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The GPU figure is a valid prediction for a phone because the code being run is identical to what the phone will run.
statements.explanation: Identical code does not mean identical cost, because the GPU work was never done in the headless run.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The headless run drew nothing, so it cannot see the cost of drawing the particles, including overdraw.
statements.explanation: Drawing, fill rate and overdraw exist only when a real renderer runs, so this measurement does not include them.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: details a 2D particle node needs
questions.stem: In Godot, a developer working on a 2D game asks a coding agent for a death burst using a GPU particle node and its process material (the object that holds speed, direction, spread, gravity and over-life settings). The agent sets the count, the lifetime and a wide spread, and leaves everything else at its defaults. In a test the node reports that it is emitting, yet players see almost nothing. Godot's documentation says that a particle node with no texture draws each particle as a square of 1 × 1 pixels, and that the process material is shared by 2D and 3D particle nodes and has a flag, Disable Z, that stops particles from moving on the z axis. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The node reporting that it is emitting shows the effect was drawn at a visible size, since emitting means particles are on screen.
statements.explanation: "Emitting" is a state flag and says nothing about particle size or visibility.

statements.label: B
statements.text: With no texture assigned, each particle is a single pixel, which is almost invisible on a typical screen.
statements.explanation: By the documentation, a null texture gives 1 × 1 pixel squares.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A wide spread in a 2D game keeps the particles' motion inside the visible screen plane, because the game itself is 2D.
statements.explanation: The material is also built for 3D, so part of each velocity can point along the z axis, where a 2D view cannot show it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Giving the particles a texture is possible only by switching to the CPU particle node, since GPU nodes draw plain squares.
statements.explanation: GPU particle nodes also take a texture; the texture is an ordinary property of the node.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Because the material is shared with 3D, the developer should tell the agent to enable Disable Z, so no velocity goes into the axis a 2D view does not show.
statements.explanation: The flag removes the z component of motion, which a 2D game needs.

questions.source: Sprite sheet versus atlas versus tilemap
questions.stem: A 2D developer receives character art as one PNG file containing a regular grid of equally sized drawings of the same character in successive poses. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The engine must be told the grid layout (columns and rows, or cell size), because the pixels do not mark frame boundaries.
statements.explanation: The file carries no grid metadata, so the developer or the import settings must supply columns and rows or the cell size.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The file is a sprite sheet, and showing its cells one after another at a chosen rate gives frame-by-frame animation.
statements.explanation: A sprite sheet stores the frames of an animation in one image, and playing the cells in sequence at a frame rate is frame-by-frame animation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A sprite sheet and a tilemap are the same thing, because both cut one image into a grid of cells that are drawn from a single texture.
statements.explanation: A tilemap places reusable tiles on a level grid to build a map, while a sprite sheet's cells are poses meant to be played in sequence.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The PNG is itself an animation clip, because the image file records the order and the duration of each frame it contains.
statements.explanation: An image holds only pixels; the order, timing and looping come from a frames resource or animation data that references the image.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A texture atlas usually packs images of different sizes into one texture and keeps a table of their rectangles.
statements.explanation: An atlas is a general packing of many images with a lookup table, whereas a classic sprite sheet relies on a regular grid of equal cells.

questions.source: What is stored: sprite sheet versus rig
questions.stem: Two teams animate the same walking hero. Team 1 ships a sprite sheet of hand-drawn walk frames. Team 2 ships a 2D cutout character: separate body-part images attached to a skeleton, with a walk clip that rotates and moves the bones. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Team 2's walk clip stores the pixels of each pose, one complete image per frame, packed together with the bone data.
statements.explanation: A skeletal clip stores transform keys (rotations, positions) over time, and the part images stay the same in every pose.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Team 1's version needs a skeleton to play, because bones are what position each drawn frame on the screen.
statements.explanation: Frame-by-frame animation needs no skeleton, since each frame is a complete picture.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Team 1's animation is mostly pixels: many drawn images, plus a clip saying which image to show and when.
statements.explanation: A sprite-sheet clip is a sequence of references into drawn frames with timing.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Between frames, Team 1's animation changes which image is shown, while Team 2's changes bone transforms and so the pose of the parts.
statements.explanation: Frame-by-frame swaps images; skeletal animation changes bone transforms and lets the attached art follow.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If Team 2 wants a longer walk cycle, it must redraw the body-part images for each additional pose in the cycle.
statements.explanation: A new or longer clip only adds keys for the bones; the part images are reused unchanged.

questions.source: Sprite sheet grid and describing it to an agent
questions.stem: A sprite sheet image is 512 × 256 pixels. It is a regular grid of 64 × 64 pixel cells with no gaps, numbered from 0, left to right and row by row, starting at the top-left cell. A developer asks a coding agent to 'play the run animation from the sheet' and says nothing else about the file. The run drawings are the eight cells of the second row. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The words 'the run animation' are enough for the agent, because the image file records which cells belong to which animation.
statements.explanation: A plain image has no record of animation names; the developer must say which cells form the run and in what order.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The sheet has 8 columns and 4 rows, so 32 cells in all.
statements.explanation: 512 / 64 = 8 columns and 256 / 64 = 4 rows, giving 32 cells.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the agent wrongly assumes 4 columns and 8 rows, it will cut cells of 128 × 32 pixels and show mis-sliced pictures without raising any error.
statements.explanation: A wrong grid still divides the image into cells (512 / 4 by 256 / 8 gives 128 × 32), so nothing fails but the slices are wrong.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Showing the eight run cells at 10 frames per second makes one loop last 1.25 seconds.
statements.explanation: Eight frames at 10 frames per second last 8 / 10 = 0.8 seconds.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Cell 19 begins at pixel x = 192, y = 128, measured from the top-left corner of the image.
statements.explanation: Cell 19 is in column 19 mod 8 = 3 and row 19 div 8 = 2, so x = 3 × 64 = 192 and y = 2 × 64 = 128.

questions.source: Memory and art cost of sprite sheets versus rigs
questions.stem: A game has one hero with 4 actions, each drawn in 8 facing directions with 8 frames per action per direction. Every frame is a 96 × 96 pixel image stored uncompressed at 4 bytes per pixel. A second plan uses a 3D model of the hero with a skeleton and one clip per action, and the model turns to face any direction by rotating. Ignore compression and mipmaps. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The sprite version holds 256 frames, which is 9,437,184 bytes (9 MiB) uncompressed.
statements.explanation: 4 × 8 × 8 = 256 frames, each 96 × 96 × 4 = 36,864 bytes, for 9,437,184 bytes, exactly 9 MiB.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Choosing the skeleton plan removes the up-front art cost, because the skeleton and the clips need no authoring.
statements.explanation: Modelling, texturing, rigging, weight painting and clip authoring are real up-front costs; they trade per-frame drawing for one-off setup.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Adding a ninth facing direction to the sprite version adds 8 frames to draw.
statements.explanation: A ninth direction needs 4 actions × 8 frames = 32 new frames.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Drawing each frame at 48 × 48 pixels instead would cut that to 2.25 MiB, a quarter of the size and not a half.
statements.explanation: Halving both sides quarters the pixel count: 256 × 48 × 48 × 4 bytes = 2.25 MiB.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A rig-based walk clip stores a full image for each pose of the walk.
statements.explanation: A skeletal clip stores transform keys per bone over time, which is far smaller than full images.

questions.stem: A studio owns a 3D walk clip authored for Character X's skeleton. Character Y has a different mesh and different limb lengths, but a skeleton whose bones (hips, spine, arms, legs) correspond one for one to X's. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: With different limb lengths, a retargeted walk can make feet slide or float, which IK or foot-contact fixes often correct.
statements.explanation: Different proportions change where the feet end up, so contact points are typically re-solved with IK.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Retargeting maps a source skeleton's motion onto a target skeleton by pairing bones, so X's clip can drive Y.
statements.explanation: Retargeting pairs source bones with target bones so the motion transfers.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A sprite-sheet walk drawn for X can be reused for Y by mapping Y's bone names onto the sheet's cells.
statements.explanation: A sprite sheet has no bones; its frames are drawings of one character and cannot be remapped to another.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A humanoid clip cannot drive a four-legged skeleton without a custom mapping, as the bones do not correspond.
statements.explanation: Without corresponding bones there is nothing to pair, so a manual mapping or new authoring is needed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Differently dressed characters that share one skeleton can share clips, because a clip stores bone motion, not pixels.
statements.explanation: Clips address bones by name or path, so any mesh bound to the same skeleton can play them.

questions.stem: A character has a walk clip and a run clip. As the player's speed rises from walking pace to running pace, the designer wants the motion to change smoothly instead of switching abruptly. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A blend weight of 0.5 between walk and run makes the character play the result at half speed, since the weight sets the rate.
statements.explanation: The blend weight mixes poses; playback speed is a separate setting.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For a rig-based character, the engine can blend two poses by interpolating each bone's transform, weighted by a blend value.
statements.explanation: Skeletal clips are bone transforms, which can be interpolated per bone to produce an in-between pose.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Mixing the pixels of two sprite frames gives a ghosted double image, not an in-between pose, so sprite sheets usually switch clips.
statements.explanation: A cross-fade of two drawings overlays both; it does not create the drawing that lies between them.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Blending suits 3D characters but not 2D cutout ones, since flat art has no bones whose transforms can be interpolated.
statements.explanation: 2D skeletal (cutout) rigs have bones too, so their poses can be blended like 3D ones.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Smooth speed changes require a separately authored clip for each intermediate speed between walking and running pace.
statements.explanation: Blending two clips by weight produces the intermediate motions without authoring each one.

questions.stem: A game ships on 1080p and 4K screens. The art lead compares a sprite sheet drawn at 64 × 64 pixels per frame with a skeletal 3D character that is drawn from its mesh each frame. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A 3D character is drawn from its mesh at screen resolution, so its sharpness is not locked to a fixed frame pixel size.
statements.explanation: Geometry is rasterized for the current screen each frame, so only the textures stay at a fixed resolution.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Switching a magnified pixel-art sprite to linear filtering makes its edges crisper by sharpening each pixel boundary.
statements.explanation: Linear filtering blends neighbouring pixels, which softens edges; nearest-neighbour keeps them crisp.

statements.label: C
statements.text: To gain real detail at 4K, a sprite sheet's frames must be redrawn or re-exported at the larger size.
statements.explanation: New detail cannot be invented by scaling; the frames must be authored or exported at the higher resolution.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A 2D cutout rig built from bitmap parts is resolution independent, because bones rescale the bitmaps without loss.
statements.explanation: The parts are still bitmaps with a fixed pixel size, so enlarging them softens or blocks them just like a sprite.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Showing 64 × 64 sprite frames larger than drawn magnifies their pixels, which look blocky (nearest) or blurry (linear).
statements.explanation: A sprite frame holds a fixed number of pixels, so enlarging it either shows the pixel blocks or smooths them into blur.

questions.stem: An animator wants a cartoon character to squash flat on landing and to show a drawn smear on a fast punch. A separate 3D character must bend an elbow without the mesh pinching. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A rig reuses one set of art and only changes its pose, so an unmodelled shape such as a smear needs extra deformation.
statements.explanation: A rig changes pose, not the underlying shapes; effects like smears need extra tools such as blend shapes or swapped parts.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A skinned mesh can take any silhouette a hand-drawn frame can, because bones can move vertices anywhere the animator wants.
statements.explanation: The silhouette is limited by the mesh, its weights and the bone motion, so arbitrary drawn shapes are not available.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Rotating the rigid body parts of a 2D cutout character around joints can open gaps or overlaps at the joints.
statements.explanation: Rigid parts rotating about a joint do not stay joined at the edges, so artists hide the joint or use deformation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Hand-drawn frames can take any shape, including squash and smear, because each frame is an independent picture.
statements.explanation: Each drawn frame is free-form, which is why exaggerated shapes are easy in frame-by-frame work.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Skinning with vertex weights lets one mesh bend smoothly at a joint instead of splitting into rigid pieces.
statements.explanation: Skinning blends the influence of neighbouring bones on shared vertices, producing a smooth bend.

questions.stem: A producer lists four animation methods in a planning document: frame-by-frame, cutout, procedural and tweening. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A procedural animation is a fixed recording, so its pose does not change with the terrain it plays on.
statements.explanation: Procedural motion responds to conditions such as terrain or forces, so it can differ from one playback to the next.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Tweening computes in-between values of a property from a start to an end value over a duration, often with easing.
statements.explanation: That is what a tween does: it generates the in-between values for a property between two endpoints.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Procedural animation is the name for any animation authored by keys on a timeline in an animation editor.
statements.explanation: Keys on a timeline describe authored animation; procedural animation is computed at runtime from rules, physics or targets.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Frame-by-frame animation depends on a skeleton to move its pieces, with roughly one bone for each drawn piece of the figure.
statements.explanation: Frame-by-frame animation swaps whole drawings and needs no skeleton.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Cutout animation needs a fresh drawing of the whole figure for the next pose, which is why its memory use is high.
statements.explanation: Cutout animation moves separate reusable pieces, such as limbs and a head, instead of redrawing the whole figure.

questions.stem: An animator keys a door's rotation to 0 degrees at 0.0 s and to 90 degrees at 1.0 s, and sets nothing else. The game renders 60 frames per second and the engine uses linear interpolation. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The clip stores 60 rotation values, one for each rendered frame in that second.
statements.explanation: The clip stores two keys; values for rendered frames are computed from time when the clip plays.

statements.label: B
statements.text: With only two keys, the door jumps from 0 to 90 degrees, since nothing is keyed in between.
statements.explanation: Interpolation produces every value between the keys, so intermediate angles are shown.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A display refreshing twice as often needs the clip to be re-authored with twice as many keys.
statements.explanation: Values are sampled from time, so any display rate works with the same keys.

statements.label: D
statements.text: At t = 0.5 s the door's rotation is 45 degrees, halfway between the two keyed values.
statements.explanation: Linear interpolation halfway between 0 and 90 degrees gives 45 degrees.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The two keys are keyframes, and the engine computes the values between them as the clip plays.
statements.explanation: A keyframe is an authored value at a chosen time, and interpolation fills in the in-betweens.

questions.stem: A menu panel slides from x = 0 to x = 300 pixels over 0.5 s. With linear motion, the fraction of the distance covered at time t is t / 0.5. With a quadratic ease-out, it is 1 − (1 − t / 0.5)². Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: With linear motion the panel is at x = 150 when t = 0.25 s, halfway through the move.
statements.explanation: At t = 0.25 s the linear fraction is 0.5, so x = 150.

statements.label: B
statements.text: With the ease-out the panel is at x = 225 when t = 0.25 s, three quarters of the way there.
statements.explanation: The ease-out fraction is 1 − (1 − 0.5)² = 0.75, so x = 225.

statements.label: C
statements.text: With the ease-out the panel moves fastest at the start and slows to a stop at the end of the move.
statements.explanation: The curve's slope starts at 1,200 pixels per second (against 600 for linear) and falls to 0 at the end.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The ease-out finishes before the linear version, because it covers more distance early.
statements.explanation: Easing reshapes the speed profile only; both versions finish at 0.5 s.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The ease-out changes the final position, since only linear motion ends at x = 300.
statements.explanation: Both curves reach a fraction of 1 at t = 0.5 s, so both end at x = 300.

questions.stem: A developer sets up a door that opens, using an engine with an animation player node and animation clips. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If a track's target is renamed or moved, the track may no longer find it and silently animate nothing.
statements.explanation: Tracks refer to targets by path or name, so a changed path can leave a track pointing at nothing without failing loudly.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A timeline is the time axis on which a clip's keys sit, and scrubbing it moves a playhead to preview values.
statements.explanation: The timeline is where keys are placed in time, and the playhead shows the current time.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The animation player plays clips: it advances time, applies values to targets, and handles looping and speed.
statements.explanation: The player node applies a clip's values to its targets over time.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A clip is data: tracks, each bound to a target such as a node property or a bone, with keys along time.
statements.explanation: A clip is a resource of tracks and keys; it does nothing until something plays it.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A clip can animate only one property of one object, so a door needs one clip for each property.
statements.explanation: A clip commonly holds many tracks, each animating a different property or object.

questions.stem: A producer tells a developer that a character 'needs a rig'. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The skeleton is visible geometry that draws the character's body on screen in the final game.
statements.explanation: Bones are not rendered by default; the mesh or parts are what appear on screen.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A skeleton (armature) is a hierarchy of bones in which moving a parent bone moves its children.
statements.explanation: Bones are parented in a hierarchy so that a shoulder rotation carries the arm with it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A rig is the full posable setup: skeleton, skin binding and often controls such as IK handles.
statements.explanation: 'Rig' names the whole setup that makes a character posable and animatable.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A skeleton alone holds no walking motion; a walk is a separate clip keying bone transforms over time.
statements.explanation: A skeleton only holds the structure and pose; motion comes from clips, code or solvers that change its transforms.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Skinning binds mesh vertices to bones so that the mesh follows the bones when they move.
statements.explanation: Skinning ties vertices to bones with weights so that bone motion deforms the mesh.

questions.stem: Under linear blend skinning, a vertex's final displacement is the weighted sum of the displacements that each influencing bone would give it. A vertex near an elbow is influenced by the upper-arm bone with weight 0.75 and the forearm bone with weight 0.25. In one pose, the upper-arm bone alone would move this vertex by (+10, 0) units and the forearm bone alone would move it by (0, +20) units from its rest position. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The vertex moves by (7.5, 5.0).

statements.label: B
statements.text: Painting vertex weights changes the keys stored in the animation clip.
statements.explanation: Weights belong to the skin binding; clip keys are separate data that move the bones.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Vertex weights are one number per bone for the whole mesh, so a bone pulls the elbow and the wrist equally.
statements.explanation: Weights are stored per vertex, so each vertex has its own mix of bone influences.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the weights were changed to 1.0 for the upper arm and 0.0 for the forearm, the vertex would move by (10, 0), following the upper arm rigidly.
statements.explanation: With all the weight on one bone, the vertex copies that bone's displacement.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A vertex's weights are normally kept so that they sum to 1, which they do here.
statements.explanation: Normalized weights sum to 1 so that the blended result stays on the scale of the bones' motion; 0.75 + 0.25 = 1.

questions.stem: A character walks down uneven stairs. The animator keyed each leg's hip, knee and ankle rotations in the walk clip. The programmer wants each foot to rest on the actual surface of every step. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: With only keyed rotations, the foot lands wherever the keys put it, so on unseen steps it can hover or sink.
statements.explanation: Keyed rotations know nothing about the stairs, so foot height follows the clip and not the surface.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Adding IK to the legs means the authored clip is no longer used for them, since IK computes the leg poses itself.
statements.explanation: IK is usually layered on top of the clip to adjust the legs, while the clip still drives the rest of the pose.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A target farther than the chain's total length can be reached if the joint rotations are solved precisely.
statements.explanation: Rotation cannot lengthen bones, so a target beyond reach is only approached with the chain fully extended.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Inverse kinematics takes a target for the end of a chain, such as a foot, and solves the joint rotations.
statements.explanation: IK works from a desired end position to joint angles.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Forward kinematics starts from the target position of the foot and works backward to find the hip rotation.
statements.explanation: That describes IK; forward kinematics starts from joint rotations and computes where the foot ends up.

questions.stem: A walk clip's root bone travels 1.2 m forward during each 1.0 s loop. A developer tells a coding agent 'make the character walk forward when I press up' and does not say whether the clip's root motion is used. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Root motion lets gameplay code choose any walking speed without making the feet slide, as the clip adapts.
statements.explanation: The feet are planted for the distance the clip covers, so any other speed from code makes them slide.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A clip authored in place carries root translation, which root motion can extract and apply to the body.
statements.explanation: A clip authored in place has no root translation, so there is nothing to extract.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In-place animation moves the character through the world by itself, because the changing pose carries the root bone forward.
statements.explanation: An in-place clip poses the limbs but leaves the character's position to code or physics.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Root motion means the clip is played in place, without moving the character through the world, so the root bone stays at the origin.
statements.explanation: Root motion is the opposite: the root bone's movement in the clip is applied to the character's position.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If root motion moves the character and code also moves the body, the character covers the distance twice.
statements.explanation: Two sources of forward movement add up, so the character moves faster than either alone intends.

questions.stem: A hand-drawn run cycle has 8 frames shown at 12 frames per second in a looping clip. The artist drew frame 8 as an exact copy of frame 1 so that the cycle 'closes'. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A ping-pong mode (forward, then backward) is a good substitute for a run cycle because reversed footsteps look the same as forward ones.
statements.explanation: A run cycle is not symmetric in time, so playing it backward makes the feet step the wrong way.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Removing the duplicate frame leaves 7 distinct frames, so one cycle lasts about 0.58 s at 12 frames per second.
statements.explanation: 7 frames at 12 frames per second last 7 / 12 ≈ 0.583 s.

statements.label: C
statements.text: On each loop, frame 8 is followed by frame 1, so the same drawing shows on two consecutive frames, a small hitch.
statements.explanation: With the last frame equal to the first, the loop repeats one pose for two frames in a row.

statements.label: D
statements.text: At 12 frames per second, each frame stays on screen for about 12 ms before the next one.
statements.explanation: Each frame lasts 1 / 12 s, about 83 ms.

statements.label: E
statements.text: For a seamless loop, the last frame of a clip must be an exact copy of the first frame, so no pose is skipped.
statements.explanation: A seamless loop needs the pose after the last frame to lead naturally into the first; a duplicated end frame causes a repeated pose.

questions.stem: Script 1 turns a fan blade by adding 3 degrees every time the engine draws a frame. Script 2 turns it by 180 degrees per second multiplied by the time since the previous frame (delta time). Both run on a machine drawing 30 frames per second and on one drawing 120. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Script 2 turns the blade at about 180 degrees per second on both machines, scaled by elapsed time.
statements.explanation: Multiplying a per-second rate by delta time gives the same movement per second whatever the frame rate.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Frame-rate independence requires the game to be locked to one constant frame rate, such as 60.
statements.explanation: Frame-rate independence means results do not depend on the frame rate, which is achieved by scaling with elapsed time and not by locking the rate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A clip played with a playback speed scale of 2 takes twice as long to finish as at normal speed.
statements.explanation: A speed scale of 2 makes the clip play twice as fast, so it finishes in half the time.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Script 1 turns the blade four times faster on the 120 frames per second machine than on the 30 one.
statements.explanation: At 120 frames per second Script 1 turns 3 × 120 = 360 degrees per second, which is 4 times 90.

statements.label: E
statements.text: On the 30 frames per second machine, Script 1 turns the blade at 90 degrees per second.
statements.explanation: 3 degrees × 30 frames per second = 90 degrees per second.

questions.stem: A sword swing clip lasts 0.6 s. The designer wants the damage hitbox on from 0.20 s to 0.35 s and a whoosh sound at 0.20 s. Option 1 starts a 0.20 s timer in code when the swing begins. Option 2 puts animation events (a method-call track) in the clip at 0.20 s and 0.35 s. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Using events means the hitbox times have to be changed by editing code, not in the animation editor.
statements.explanation: The time is a key on the clip, so it can be moved in the animation editor without touching code.

statements.label: B
statements.text: At 1.5 times playback speed, Option 2's events stay aligned with the swing, while Option 1's timer does not.
statements.explanation: Events live in clip time, which scales with playback speed, while a code timer counts real time.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An animation event calls a function when playback passes its keyed time, so the timing travels with the clip.
statements.explanation: An event is keyed on the clip's own timeline and runs when playback reaches it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the swing is cancelled at 0.10 s, the 0.20 s event of Option 2 still fires, because events are scheduled when the clip starts.
statements.explanation: Events are reached by playback; a clip stopped before 0.20 s never gets there, so cleanup such as turning the hitbox off must also happen on cancel.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Events fire at exactly 0.2000 s on the real-world clock, even at a low frame rate, because they are timer-based.
statements.explanation: Events are checked each animation update, so they fire on the update in which the playhead crosses the key, which can be a frame later.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: animate the walk
questions.stem: A project contains one image file, hero.png. A developer types to a coding agent: 'animate the character walking', without saying what kind of art hero.png holds. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The word 'walking' tells the agent how many frames the walk has and in which order the cells are numbered.
statements.explanation: Frame count is a property of the art, not of the word 'walking'.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Walking is a looping action at a standard pace, so the instruction needs no mention of looping or speed.
statements.explanation: Whether a clip loops and how fast it plays are settings the agent would otherwise choose by default.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the agent assumes the image is rigged, it may rotate bone nodes that do not exist or invent body parts.
statements.explanation: Applying skeletal techniques to flat frames produces code that targets things that do not exist.

statements.label: D
statements.text: From those words alone the agent cannot tell whether to slice frames from a grid or drive bone transforms, so it may guess wrong.
statements.explanation: Sprite-sheet and rig-based animation are built differently, and the sentence names neither.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A precise version says hero.png is a 6 × 1 sprite sheet of 64 × 64 frames, played as a looping walk at 10 fps.
statements.explanation: It states the art type, grid, frame size, loop and rate, leaving little to guess.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: reaching with IK
questions.stem: In a 3D game the character must reach for a cup that the player can place anywhere on a table. The project has one authored reach clip, keyed to reach straight ahead at a fixed height. A developer tells a coding agent: 'play a reach animation toward the cup'. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A precise instruction asks for inverse kinematics on the arm chain with the cup's position as target, layered on an idle clip.
statements.explanation: IK solves joint rotations from a target position, and it can be applied on top of other animation.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Blending several authored reach clips with a blend space is another approach, but it covers only positions between those clips.
statements.explanation: A blend space interpolates between the authored poses, so it cannot reach outside their range.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A target alone leaves the elbow direction ambiguous, so the instruction may name the chain's bones and elbow hint.
statements.explanation: Many joint configurations reach the same point, so the elbow direction (a pole or hint) and the chain's bones need to be specified.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The authored clip reaches only the one place it was keyed for, so it cannot follow a cup placed elsewhere.
statements.explanation: Keyed rotations are fixed data and know nothing about where the cup is.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Asking for forward kinematics makes the hand go to the cup, because forward kinematics starts from the target position.
statements.explanation: Forward kinematics computes the hand position from joint rotations; it does not take a target.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: tween versus clip
questions.stem: A developer asks a coding agent for two effects. Effect 1 is a pause panel that slides in from the left over 0.25 s, which the designer wants to scrub and retime on a timeline. Effect 2 is a health bar that eases from its current width to a new width every time the player is hit, where the new width is not known in advance. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Effect 2 suits a tween created in code when the hit happens, because its end value only exists at runtime.
statements.explanation: A tween interpolates from the current value to a target supplied when it is created.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Effect 1 suits an authored clip, since its values are known ahead and a designer wants to edit them.
statements.explanation: A clip is authored ahead of time, stored with the scene and editable and scrubbable by designers.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A tween is authored as keys in the scene file so that a designer can scrub it on a timeline in the editor.
statements.explanation: A tween is created and run from code, and it is not stored as editable keys.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Easing applies only to authored clips; a tween has no easing setting and moves at constant speed to its target.
statements.explanation: Tweens normally accept an easing curve like clips do.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A tween takes a duration and an easing curve, so the word 'smoothly' should be replaced by those values.
statements.explanation: 'Smoothly' leaves duration and curve to the agent; naming them removes the guess.

questions.stem: A developer describes a platformer character's behaviour as a state machine with the states Idle, Run, Jump and Fall. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A condition compares a parameter or game value with a flag or threshold, such as 'on floor is false' or 'speed is above 0.1'.
statements.explanation: Conditions test parameters or values the game supplies, and a transition fires when its condition holds.

statements.label: B
statements.text: At any moment the machine is in exactly one of those states (within one layer).
statements.explanation: A state machine has one current state at a time, which is what separates it from a set of independent flags.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Run and Jump can both be active at once, because each state is a separate on/off flag.
statements.explanation: Independent on/off flags are the nested-conditional approach; a state machine allows one active state.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Listing the four states creates the transitions between them, so no routes need to be defined.
statements.explanation: Transitions must be defined; the existence of two states does not imply a route between them.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A transition is an allowed route from one state to another, usually guarded by a condition.
statements.explanation: Transitions are the explicit connections that say which state may follow which.

questions.source: Why state machines beat nested conditionals
questions.stem: A character script tracks its animation with four independent boolean flags (is_jumping, is_attacking, is_crouching, is_hurt) checked in a long chain of nested if statements. An alternative is a state machine with five states (Idle, Jump, Attack, Crouch, Hurt) and 11 explicitly listed transitions. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The state machine removes the need for conditions, because each state decides on its own when to change.
statements.explanation: Transitions still need conditions or events that say when a change happens.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A stuck character is harder to spot in the state machine, because its state is hidden inside nested conditionals.
statements.explanation: With one explicit current state, a stuck state is visible by watching that value; hidden state is the nested-flag problem.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Four flags can combine in 16 ways, including combinations such as jumping and hurt at once that nobody designed.
statements.explanation: Four booleans give 2^4 = 16 combinations, and many of them describe situations nobody designed.

statements.label: D
statements.text: At any moment the machine is in one of 5 named states, so a bug report can name the state.
statements.explanation: The state is a single named value that can be logged, shown and reported.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Because 11 transitions are listed, the state machine has 11 possible states for the character.
statements.explanation: The 5 states are the possible conditions of the character; the 11 transitions are the allowed moves between them.

questions.source: Animation tree, state machine, blend tree and blend space
questions.stem: In Godot, the AnimationTree node plays animation clips that are stored in an AnimationPlayer, using a graph whose root can be a state machine, a blend tree or a blend space. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A state machine has no cross-fade of its own, so a smooth change from one clip to another needs a blend tree or blend space.
statements.explanation: A transition between states can carry a cross-fade time, so a state machine can change smoothly from one clip to another; blend trees and blend spaces mix clips continuously by a parameter, which is a different job.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A state machine in the tree mixes the clips of all its states by weight at all times, even with no transition.
statements.explanation: A state machine plays its current state, and mixes in another only while a cross-fade between states is under way.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The AnimationTree node keeps its own copy of the clips it plays, independent of the AnimationPlayer.
statements.explanation: The tree decides how much of each clip enters the final pose, but the clips live in the AnimationPlayer.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A blend space picks its output from a position on one or two axes, mixing the clips placed near that position.
statements.explanation: A blend space places clips at points on a line or plane and mixes the neighbours of the current position.

statements.label: E
statements.text: 'State machine' and 'blend tree' are two names for the same kind of graph in the animation tree.
statements.explanation: A state machine chooses among states; a blend tree is a graph of nodes that combine inputs by weight, and they are different nodes.

questions.stem: A character should walk, jog or sprint according to how far the stick is pushed, and should also commit to a jump once it has started, even if the player releases the button. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A speed axis between walk, jog and sprint clips suits a blend space, because speed varies continuously and smoothly.
statements.explanation: A blend space maps a continuous number such as speed to a mix of neighbouring clips.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A blend space can enforce that a jump that has started cannot be interrupted by movement input, as it decides clip weights.
statements.explanation: A blend only decides how much of each clip to show; committing to an action is the job of states and transitions.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A blend space needs a transition with its own condition between neighbouring clips on its axis, like a state machine.
statements.explanation: Blend spaces mix by position and need no per-pair transitions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Making one state per tiny speed step (walk_1 to walk_20) is better than a blend, because states are more precise.
statements.explanation: Twenty states would need many transitions and would still jump between steps; a blend gives smooth change with one parameter.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A jump suits a state, because it is a committed action with its own entry, exit and duration.
statements.explanation: A committed action is a state with defined ways in and out.

questions.stem: In Unity's Animator Controller, transitions fire when conditions on Animator parameters are met, and a script sets those parameters. Parameters can be float, int, bool or trigger. A script keeps a bool 'isGrounded' updated every frame and sets a trigger 'Attack' when the attack button is pressed. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Parameters are outputs of the state machine, written by the controller back to the script to tell it what to do next.
statements.explanation: Parameters are inputs written by the script, and the controller reads them to decide transitions.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A trigger is meant for one-time events: it is reset when a transition consumes it.
statements.explanation: A trigger is a boolean that the controller resets once a transition has consumed it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A trigger that no transition consumes stays set until consumed or reset by the script, so it can fire a transition late.
statements.explanation: Because the reset happens on consumption, an unused trigger waits, which is why stale triggers cause late or surprise transitions.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A float such as Speed suits a condition like 'Speed is greater than 0.1' and can also drive a blend tree.
statements.explanation: Floats feed numeric comparisons and blend tree parameters.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A bool keeps its value until the script changes it, so a transition conditioned on isGrounded stays satisfied while it is true.
statements.explanation: A bool is a level: it holds its value until it is changed.

questions.source: Sampling gap between physics and animation updates
questions.stem: A game runs physics at 120 ticks per second and updates its animation graph at 60 frames per second. A held jump key makes the character land on one physics tick and jump again on the very next tick. The graph's transition conditions read 'is the character on the floor' only when the graph updates. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: If the landing tick and the take-off tick fall inside the same graph update, the graph does not see 'on floor' as true, so it does not register the landing.
statements.explanation: A condition sampled only at graph updates can miss a state that changes and changes back between two samples.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The graph updates once per two physics ticks.
statements.explanation: 120 / 60 = 2 physics ticks per graph update.

statements.label: C
statements.text: One fix is a transition that also reacts to the character rising while airborne, so the graph recovers from a missed landing.
statements.explanation: A transition that depends on the airborne, rising state still fires even when the landing was never sampled.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Engines do not let the animation graph run in the physics step, because animation updates once per rendered frame.
statements.explanation: Engines let the animation update run in the physics step (for example by choosing the update or callback mode), which removes the mismatch.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The physics engine is wrong in this situation, because it should not let a character land and jump within one frame.
statements.explanation: The physics is correct; the condition is sampled less often than the state changes.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: input-driven versus state-driven change
questions.stem: While a character is stunned (a Hurt state that ignores input), the player mashes the Space key. A developer tells a coding agent: 'when the player presses Space, switch to the jump state'. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A precise version switches to jump when Jump is pressed, the character is on the floor and the state allows jumping.
statements.explanation: Naming the press plus the guarding conditions makes the transition unambiguous.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The instruction ties the state change to the key press, so the agent may jump even while the character is stunned.
statements.explanation: A press-only condition ignores whether the character can jump now.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Input must be handled inside the animation state machine itself, because animation is where input lives and the machine owns it.
statements.explanation: Input is normally interpreted by gameplay code, which then sets state or parameters for the animation.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Choosing animation straight from key presses keeps the animation in step with what the movement code does.
statements.explanation: A key press can be ignored or overridden by the movement code (stun, no ground), so the picture and the movement can disagree.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Driving jump from physical state, such as leaving the floor with upward velocity, stays consistent even for a bounce-pad launch.
statements.explanation: Basing the state on what the body is doing keeps picture and movement in agreement, whatever caused the movement.

questions.stem: A character has the states Idle, Run, Attack, Hurt and Dead. Hit reactions should interrupt an attack. Death should override every other state. Run input should not interrupt an attack. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Priority matters only if more than one state is active at once, since only simultaneous states can compete for control.
statements.explanation: A state machine has one active state; priority decides between several transitions that are valid at the same moment.

statements.label: B
statements.text: With no Attack-to-Run transition, Run input is ignored during the attack, but Attack still needs an exit, such as Idle at clip end.
statements.explanation: The absence of a transition is how a machine forbids an interruption, but an exit must still exist or the state sticks.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Giving Hurt a transition out of Attack expresses 'hit reactions interrupt an attack' explicitly.
statements.explanation: An interrupt exists only if a transition from the interrupted state to the interrupting state is defined.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A transition into Dead from all states (an Any State transition in Unity, say) expresses 'death overrides everything'.
statements.explanation: Any State is a special state that stands for all states, so one transition from it applies everywhere.

statements.label: E
statements.text: When two transitions out of the current state are both valid, the engine's ordering or priority rules pick one, so state the order.
statements.explanation: Equal-looking choices are resolved by priority or order, and an unstated order leaves the result to chance or to the agent.

questions.stem: In a playtest, after the player is hit, the character plays the Hurt animation and then freezes in its last pose, ignoring input forever. The only transition out of Hurt has the condition 'hurt_finished is true'. Nothing in the project's code ever sets hurt_finished. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: This is a stuck state: the machine sits in a state whose only exit condition stays false.
statements.explanation: A state with an exit condition that is never satisfied can never be left.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Adding a second, unconditional transition from Hurt to Dead fixes the problem without side effects.
statements.explanation: An unconditional transition would send every hurt character to Dead, which is a new bug.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because the machine has one current state, the problem is easy to see by logging the current state, which stays Hurt.
statements.explanation: The current state is one visible value, so it can be logged or shown on screen.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Making Hurt exit when its clip ends would remove the dependence on a flag that nobody sets.
statements.explanation: An exit at the end of the clip, or a condition the code really sets, gives Hurt a working way out.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The cause must be a bug in the animation clip, because clips decide transitions.
statements.explanation: Transitions come from the machine's conditions and parameters; a clip only supplies the pose over time.

questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: 'when the player presses Dodge, play the dodge animation'. The animation state machine has the states Idle, Run, Attack and Dodge. No transition from Attack to Dodge exists. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The state machine will go from Attack to Dodge on its own, since both states belong to the same machine.
statements.explanation: Reachability exists only through transitions that were defined.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A request for a state with no allowed route is refused, whether it comes from a trigger or a direct play call.
statements.explanation: Engines differ: a call that forces a state directly (for example Animator.Play in Unity) skips transitions, while a trigger or condition needs one.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The engine adds the missing Attack-to-Dodge transition the first time the player presses Dodge during an attack.
statements.explanation: Engines do not invent transitions; missing ones must be authored.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the agent plays the dodge clip directly, bypassing the state machine, while the machine is in Attack, the machine still reports Attack.
statements.explanation: A clip played outside the machine does not update the machine's recorded state, so it stays out of step with what is on screen.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The instruction does not say whether Dodge may cancel an attack, so the agent has to decide.
statements.explanation: Whether an attack can be cancelled is a design rule that the sentence leaves unsaid.

questions.stem: An attack clip lasts 0.5 s. The player presses Attack at t = 0.00, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30 and 0.40 s. Three designs are considered: (1) ignore Attack presses while an attack is playing; (2) restart the attack on every press; (3) remember one press made during the attack and start the next attack when the first one ends. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Under (2), the swing is cut off and restarted four times, so the last swing can finish no earlier than 0.90 s.
statements.explanation: Restarts at 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4 s mean the final swing starts at 0.40 s and ends at 0.40 + 0.5 = 0.90 s.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Under (3), the second attack starts at 0.10 s, as soon as the second press arrives, interrupting the first.
statements.explanation: Under (3) the press is remembered and used when the first attack ends, at 0.50 s.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Under (1), exactly one attack happens, starting at 0.00 s, and the other four presses are lost.
statements.explanation: The first press starts the attack, and the later presses fall inside its 0.5 s and are discarded.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Under (3), the character performs five attacks in a row, one for each press that was made.
statements.explanation: Only one press is remembered, so one extra attack follows, not four.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Design (1) is an input buffer, since it handles the presses that arrive during the attack.
statements.explanation: Design (1) is an input lock; an input buffer is design (3), which remembers a press instead of discarding it.

questions.stem: A game uses an input buffer of 0.15 s. After an attack, the player may start the next attack at t = 0.50 s, when recovery ends. A press of Attack is remembered for 0.15 s after it is pressed and is used if an attack becomes available within that time. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Input buffering shortens the attack clip so that the next attack comes sooner.
statements.explanation: A buffer changes when a remembered press is used, not how long the clip lasts.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A press at t = 0.40 s starts the next attack at t = 0.50 s.
statements.explanation: The press is remembered until 0.55 s, which is after the attack becomes available at 0.50 s, so it is used then.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Lengthening the buffer to 0.5 s makes the controls more precise with no downside.
statements.explanation: A long buffer lets old presses fire later and queues attacks the player did not mean, which makes controls feel unresponsive and unpredictable.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A press at t = 0.52 s starts an attack immediately, because an attack is already available when the press arrives and nothing needs to be remembered.
statements.explanation: The attack is already available at 0.52 s, so the press is used at once without being remembered; the buffer only matters for presses made before 0.50 s.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A press at t = 0.30 s starts the next attack at t = 0.50 s.
statements.explanation: The press expires at 0.45 s, before the attack is available at 0.50 s, so it is lost.

questions.source: Cooldown versus animation lock versus buffer
questions.stem: A dash lasts 0.2 s and has a cooldown of 1.5 s measured from the moment the dash starts. The player presses Dash at t = 0.0, 1.0, 1.6 and 2.0 s. A press is used at once if a dash is allowed and is otherwise discarded (there is no buffering). Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A cooldown and an animation lock are the same thing, since both only block actions while an animation is playing.
statements.explanation: A cooldown is a minimum time between uses and can outlast the animation, while a lock blocks action only while the animation plays.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The press at 2.0 s is rejected by the cooldown, which runs until 3.1 s, even though the second dash animation has already ended.
statements.explanation: The second dash ran from 1.6 s to 1.8 s, but the cooldown lasts until 1.6 + 1.5 = 3.1 s.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Exactly two dashes happen, starting at 0.0 s and 1.6 s.
statements.explanation: The first dash starts at 0.0 s and the cooldown ends at 1.5 s, so 1.0 s is rejected and 1.6 s is accepted; its cooldown then runs to 3.1 s, so 2.0 s is rejected.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The press at 1.0 s is rejected because the first dash is still in progress.
statements.explanation: The first dash ended at 0.2 s; the press at 1.0 s is rejected by the cooldown.

statements.label: E
statements.text: With a 0.15 s input buffer, the press at 1.0 s would start a dash at 1.5 s.
statements.explanation: The buffered press would expire at 1.15 s, before the dash is allowed again at 1.5 s.

questions.source: Input leniency: coyote time and jump buffering
questions.stem: Players complain that jumping 'doesn't work' when they press Jump a few milliseconds after running off a ledge, and also when they press it just before landing. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Coyote time allows a jump for a brief grace period after the character has left the ground.
statements.explanation: Coyote time forgives a press that arrives just after the character walked off an edge.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Coyote time is the delay between the button press and the start of the jump animation.
statements.explanation: Press-to-animation delay is input latency, which is a different problem.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Both techniques change the physics of the jump, making it higher or longer than normal.
statements.explanation: Both are tolerance windows for input timing and leave the jump's physics alone.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Jump buffering is another name for coyote time, as both forgive a late press.
statements.explanation: Jump buffering remembers a press made just before landing; coyote time forgives a press made just after leaving the ground.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The coyote window starts when the player presses Jump, and the jump is performed if the character lands before that window runs out.
statements.explanation: The coyote window starts when the character leaves the ground; a window that starts at the button press and waits for landing is jump buffering.

questions.stem: A sword swing clip is 0.6 s long. The designer needs (a) the damage hitbox on from 0.20 s to 0.35 s, (b) a sound at 0.20 s, and (c) the character to return to Idle when the swing ends. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Events keyed at 0.20 s and 0.35 s are evaluated only if the game draws a frame at exactly those times.
statements.explanation: Events are evaluated when the playhead passes their time during an update, so exact frame times are not required.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Keying the hitbox's enabled property on and off in the clip is another way to get (a).
statements.explanation: A property track in the clip can enable and disable the hitbox directly, with the timing stored in the clip.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Item (c) reacts to the clip finishing, commonly handled by a 'finished' signal or an end-of-state transition.
statements.explanation: Completion of a clip or state is normally signalled by a finished signal or an end-of-state transition.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the swing's playback speed is doubled, a code timer set to 0.20 s still lines up with the clip's events, since both are measured in seconds.
statements.explanation: At double speed the clip reaches its 0.20 s mark after 0.10 s of real time, so a 0.20 s timer fires late.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Items (a) and (b) sit at moments inside the clip, which is what animation events (calls keyed on the timeline) are for.
statements.explanation: Events run code at keyed times, which is how in-clip moments such as a hit window or a sound are timed.

questions.stem: In a melee game, the player's sword and an enemy both need collision shapes. A developer asks a coding agent for 'a collider on the sword and one on the enemy'. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: 'Collider' does not say which shape deals damage and which receives it, or whether either blocks movement.
statements.explanation: 'Collider' names neither role nor behaviour, so the agent has to guess both.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A sword's hitbox is typically enabled for part of the swing, while the enemy's hurtbox stays on while it can be hurt.
statements.explanation: Hitboxes are switched on for the active frames of an attack, while hurtboxes stay on while the target is vulnerable.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The hurtbox must be a solid collider that physically stops the sword, so the blade cannot pass through the enemy.
statements.explanation: Hitbox and hurtbox are usually detection shapes (areas or triggers) that report overlaps without blocking.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The sword's damage-dealing region is a hitbox, and the enemy's region that can receive damage is a hurtbox.
statements.explanation: A hitbox is the attacker's damaging region and a hurtbox is the defender's vulnerable region.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Without layer or mask filtering, a character's hitbox could overlap its own hurtbox and hurt its owner.
statements.explanation: Layers and masks decide which shapes can detect each other, and without them a body's own boxes overlap.

questions.stem: An attack clip runs at 60 updates per second and lasts 27 updates (numbered 0 to 26, which is 0.45 s). Its hitbox is enabled from update 6 through update 14, inclusive, and disabled for the rest of the clip. An enemy stays inside the hitbox for the whole active window. The game applies damage on every update in which the hitbox overlaps an enemy hurtbox, unless the attack records which enemies it has already hit. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The hitbox is active for 9 updates, which is 0.15 s.
statements.explanation: Updates 6 through 14 inclusive are 14 − 6 + 1 = 9 updates, and 9 / 60 = 0.15 s.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Recording already-hit enemies means the hitbox must switch off after its first overlap.
statements.explanation: The attack remembers which targets were hit and can keep the hitbox on for other enemies.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the attack does not record enemies already hit, one swing can damage this enemy up to 9 times.
statements.explanation: Damage on every overlapping update gives 9 hits over a 9-update window.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Startup (before the hitbox turns on) is 6 updates, or 0.1 s, and recovery (after it turns off) is 12 updates, or 0.2 s.
statements.explanation: Updates 0 to 5 are 6 (0.1 s) and updates 15 to 26 are 12 (0.2 s), which with the 9 active updates make 27.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Leaving the hitbox on for all 27 updates would not change how fair the attack feels, provided damage is counted once.
statements.explanation: A hitbox active during startup and recovery hurts enemies when the blade is not visibly there, which feels unfair.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: make the character animate when it moves
questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: 'make the character animate when it moves'. The project has idle, walk, run and jump clips. Check each statement that is true about what the instruction leaves open.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The word 'moves' fixes an exact condition, so two agents would build the same machine.
statements.explanation: 'Moves' leaves thresholds, directions and priorities undefined, so different agents will make different choices.

statements.label: B
statements.text: It does not say whether moving through the air counts, or what to play while jumping or falling.
statements.explanation: 'Moves' does not distinguish movement on the ground from movement in the air.

statements.label: C
statements.text: It does not say whether the jump clip loops or plays once.
statements.explanation: Looping versus one-shot playback is a per-clip decision the sentence leaves out.

statements.label: D
statements.text: It does not say at which speeds walking gives way to running.
statements.explanation: The speed threshold between walk and run is a number the sentence never gives.

statements.label: E
statements.text: It does not say whether clips should cross-fade or cut, or how long a cross-fade lasts.
statements.explanation: Blend behaviour and length are not mentioned, so the agent chooses them.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: specifying transitions
questions.stem: A developer must tell a coding agent how four states (Idle, Run, Jump, Fall) connect. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: 'Connect the states sensibly' leaves it to the agent to decide which transitions exist.
statements.explanation: Without a list, the set of transitions is the agent's guess.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The instruction should also say which states may be interrupted and by what, because otherwise the agent decides.
statements.explanation: Interrupt rules (who may cut whom) are design decisions that need to be stated.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A diagram of arrows between the states is as precise as a table, because the arrows carry the conditions.
statements.explanation: Arrows show which routes exist but not when they fire, so conditions and blend times are still missing.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Naming the four states without conditions is enough, because the conditions follow from the names.
statements.explanation: Names such as Fall do not say whether the condition is velocity, floor contact or something else.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A list with one row per allowed transition (from state, to state, condition, cross-fade time) leaves an agent nothing to decide about which transitions exist, when each one fires or how long each one blends.
statements.explanation: Each row fixes both ends, the trigger and the blend, so those three things are fully specified; loop settings and interrupt rules are separate decisions that still need their own lines.

questions.source: Say it to the agent: cancel windows and interrupts
questions.stem: A designer says: 'the attack can be cancelled into a dodge, but not into another attack, until its recovery phase starts'. The attack clip has startup, active and recovery phases. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: This describes a cancel window: a span of the attack during which another action may interrupt it.
statements.explanation: A cancel window is the portion of an action during which interruption is permitted.

statements.label: B
statements.text: By this rule, an Attack press during the active phase should start a second attack at once, since attacks chain freely.
statements.explanation: The rule says the attack cannot be cancelled into another attack before recovery starts.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The window should follow the clip's own time or events, not fixed seconds in code, so it tracks playback speed changes.
statements.explanation: Clip-time markers scale with playback speed, while fixed seconds in code drift away from the visuals.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Animation events at phase boundaries could set flags such as 'can_cancel' that transition conditions read.
statements.explanation: Events let the clip mark phase changes, and conditions on the resulting flags control which transitions are allowed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The sentence gives no times or frames for where the phases begin and end, so the agent needs them or events that mark them.
statements.explanation: Phase boundaries are numbers or markers the sentence leaves out.

questions.source: Single source of truth for state
questions.stem: A project already has a gameplay state machine in code (Idle, Move, Attack, Hurt). A coding agent is asked to 'add an animation state machine' and builds a second, separate machine in the animation tree that tracks its own Idle, Move, Attack and Hurt states from the player's input. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The two machines can disagree, for example when gameplay says Hurt while the animation is still in Attack.
statements.explanation: Two machines with their own rules and timing can fall out of step.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Making gameplay the one authority fixes a Hurt state whose exit transition does not fire, because animation and gameplay can then no longer disagree about it.
statements.explanation: One authority removes the disagreement between the two machines, not a state whose exit does not fire; that state stays in the gameplay machine, so stuck states still need design and testing.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A safer design makes gameplay state the single authority and lets the animation machine read it, say through a parameter.
statements.explanation: One source of truth for state keeps picture and gameplay in agreement.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A second machine reading the same inputs agrees with the first, because identical inputs produce identical states.
statements.explanation: Different rules, timing and sampling can give different states from the same inputs.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The animation machine should decide whether damage is dealt, because it knows when the hit animation ends.
statements.explanation: Damage is a gameplay decision; animation should present state, not decide outcomes.

questions.stem: A team wants automated tests for a character's animation state machine. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A test should set the state variable straight to the target state, because driving real input only tests the engine's input system.
statements.explanation: Writing the state directly skips the transition logic that the test is meant to check.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A test can press the real jump action and then check the current state, instead of writing the state directly.
statements.explanation: Driving real input exercises the conditions and transitions that connect input to state.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A passing state test proves that the motion looks right to players and also feels good to play.
statements.explanation: A test checks state and behaviour; whether motion looks right is judged by watching it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: With a finite list of states and transitions, a test can check each listed transition and that unlisted ones do not happen.
statements.explanation: States and transitions are enumerable, so each allowed route and each forbidden one can be exercised.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Checking that each state except a deliberate end state has an exit can find stuck-state errors before anyone plays.
statements.explanation: A state with no exit is a static property of the graph that a check can find without playing.

questions.stem: In Godot, a game plays background music, a menu click, and the footsteps of an enemy walking around a 3D world. The developer must decide, for each sound, whether to use a plain AudioStreamPlayer or a positional AudioStreamPlayer3D. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A plain AudioStreamPlayer plays its stream non-positionally, so how loud it is does not depend on where the camera or any other object is.
statements.explanation: The non-positional player ignores listener position entirely, which is why it suits music and interface sounds.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For a positional player, the listener is the point whose position and orientation define what is heard; in Godot 3D it defaults to the active camera unless an explicit listener node is made current.
