statements.explanation: A positional sound is heard relative to a listener; Godot uses the current camera unless a listener node overrides it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The listener is the object that emits a positional sound, so a scene needs one listener per positional sound it plays, each placed at the sound's source.
statements.explanation: The listener is the receiver (the ears), and there is one active at a time, not one per sound source.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The menu click is best played from an AudioStreamPlayer3D so that it is panned and attenuated consistently with the rest of the 3D world, keeping all of the game's sounds behaving the same way.
statements.explanation: A menu click has no place in the world; a positional player would make it quieter or pan it depending on where the camera happens to be.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Attenuation is the drop in loudness as the distance between a positional source and the listener grows, so footsteps far from the camera are quieter than near ones.
statements.explanation: Attenuation (falloff) is exactly the distance-dependent loss of level that makes far sources quieter.

questions.source: Wiring a game event to a sound
questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: "Play a click when the button is pressed." The project is a Godot game with one scene, one Button, and the default audio setup. Check each statement that is true about what must hold for the click to actually reach the speakers.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Something must call play() on a stream player that has an audio stream assigned, in response to the button's pressed signal.
statements.explanation: A sound is started by game logic: an event (the signal) is wired to a handler that calls play on a player holding a stream.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Hearing the click does not prove it was routed through the bus the developer intended, because a mistake in the routing can still leave the sound audible, only on a different bus.
statements.explanation: A sound can be audible while sent somewhere other than intended (for example, a misnamed bus can silently fall back to the default one), so audibility alone does not verify the wiring.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If the player's bus, or any bus it is routed through on the way to Master, is muted, the click is silent even though the player reports that it is playing.
statements.explanation: Level and mute are applied along the bus chain, so a muted bus anywhere on the route removes the sound regardless of the player's state.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The instruction already fixes the bus, the loudness and what happens when the button is pressed twice quickly, so a precise agent needs no further detail.
statements.explanation: The instruction names only an event and a sound; bus, level and overlap behavior are all left for the agent to guess.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Once the player's playing flag reads true after play(), an automated test has proved that the click reached the output and is audible to the user.
statements.explanation: The playing flag shows only that a voice was started; it says nothing about bus routing, level, mute, or whether a person can hear it.

questions.stem: A click sample has a peak amplitude of 0.8, where 1.0 is digital full scale (0 dBFS). In an engine, its stream player is set to -6 dB and routed to an SFX bus whose fader is at -6 dB; the SFX bus sends to a Master bus at 0 dB. Gains in decibels add along the chain, and an amplitude factor equals 10^(dB/20), so -6 dB is a factor of about 0.50 and -12 dB about 0.25. No effects are present. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The two -6 dB settings combine to -12 dB, an amplitude factor of about 0.25.
statements.explanation: Decibels are logarithmic, so gains in series add (-6 + -6 = -12 dB), and 10^(-12/20) is about 0.25.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The click's peak at Master is about 0.20, which is 0.8 multiplied by 0.25.
statements.explanation: 0.8 x 0.2512 is about 0.201 at the Master bus.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The click's peak at Master is about -6 dBFS, the level of the second stage.
statements.explanation: 20 log10(0.201) is about -13.9 dBFS; -6 dBFS would correspond to a peak near 0.50.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Raising only the SFX bus fader to 0 dB would restore the sample's original peak of 0.8.
statements.explanation: The player stage still contributes -6 dB, so the peak would be about 0.40, not 0.8.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A further -6 dB on any one stage would roughly halve the peak again, to about 0.10.
statements.explanation: Each further -6 dB multiplies amplitude by about 0.5, so 0.20 becomes about 0.10.

questions.source: Audio bus, master bus and effects
questions.stem: A game has Music, SFX and Voice buses that each send to Master, and a settings menu with one volume slider per bus. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Separate buses for music and effects let the player lower the music without changing how loud the effects are, since each bus has its own level.
statements.explanation: Each bus is an independent control point, which is the main reason to split a mix into groups.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Muting the SFX bus also silences everything on the Music bus, because both ultimately feed the same Master bus.
statements.explanation: Buses that feed a common parent do not affect each other; muting SFX removes only what is routed through SFX.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Muting Master silences only sounds that are played directly on Master; sounds on the Music and SFX buses still come through.
statements.explanation: Master is the end of the chain, so muting it silences everything routed to it, directly or through child buses.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A reverb effect placed on the SFX bus processes each sound routed to that bus and does not touch sounds routed only to the Music bus.
statements.explanation: Effects belong to a bus and apply to everything that passes through that bus.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A settings slider that runs from 0.0 to 1.0 can be passed straight to a bus as a decibel value and will behave like a linear volume knob, since 1.0 means full volume and 0.0 means silence.
statements.explanation: Decibels are logarithmic, so a linear slider value should be converted to dB; passing 0 to 1 as dB would span only 1 dB near full level.

questions.stem: A designer says: "When a character speaks, the music should get quieter, then come back up when the speech ends." The developer passes this to a coding agent as "pause the music during dialogue". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Ducking is the automatic, temporary lowering of one group of sounds while another is active.
statements.explanation: Ducking is a temporary, automatic level reduction that restores itself, which is what the designer described.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Pausing the music satisfies the designer's request, because a paused track and a ducked track sound the same to the player.
statements.explanation: A paused track is silent and frozen; a ducked track keeps playing quietly and continues in time.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Ducking can be driven by a side-chain, where an effect on the music bus reacts to the level of the voice signal.
statements.explanation: Side-chain compression is the usual way to make one bus's level depend on another's.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Ducking requires the music and the voice to be played by the same stream player node, so that one can lower the other.
statements.explanation: Music and voice normally sit on different buses and players; ducking works across them.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Calling stop() on the music and later play() again resumes the track from the position where it stopped.
statements.explanation: Stopping discards the playback position, so a later play() starts from the beginning unless a start position is given.

questions.source: Trigger versus collider for events that start sounds
questions.stem: A designer wants a chime to play when the player walks into a glowing zone, while the player keeps walking through the zone without being blocked. A developer asks a coding agent for "a zone collider that plays a chime". Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The zone must be a trigger (an Area in Godot, a trigger collider in Unity, an overlap volume in Unreal), which reports overlap as an event and does not block.
statements.explanation: A trigger observes overlap and raises an event; it does not push back on the objects that enter it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A solid collider is the right choice, because it reports contact events and also lets the player pass through while the chime plays.
statements.explanation: A solid collider blocks the player; passing through is the defining behavior of a trigger.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The chime should be started from the zone's enter event, which fires when the overlap begins, rather than from code that checks for overlap on each frame.
statements.explanation: The enter event fires once per entry, which is the moment the chime should start.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The zone should be limited, by collision layers or filtering, to the objects that are meant to trigger the chime, so that enemies or projectiles passing through do not play it.
statements.explanation: A zone reports every object that overlaps it unless its detection is filtered, so layers or masks decide which objects count and an unfiltered zone plays the chime for things the designer did not mean.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Once a chime player is placed inside the zone, the audio system detects the player's overlap itself and plays the chime with no further code.
statements.explanation: Audio never decides when to play; game logic detects the overlap and calls the player.

questions.stem: A pressure plate should play a click when the player steps on it. The agent wired the click to a trigger callback that runs on every physics step while an overlap persists (the kind of event Unity calls OnTriggerStay). Physics runs at 50 steps per second. Players report a buzzing, machine-gun click whenever they stand on the plate. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A per-step overlap callback fires about 50 times a second while the player stands on the plate, restarting the click at 20 ms intervals.
statements.explanation: 50 steps per second means one callback every 20 ms for as long as the overlap lasts, each restarting the sound.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Starting the click from the enter event instead plays it once, when the overlap begins; an exit event marks when the player leaves.
statements.explanation: Enter and exit events mark the transitions, so a one-time sound belongs on enter.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Raising the player's polyphony so the restarted clicks overlap instead of cutting each other off fixes the cause of the buzzing.
statements.explanation: More voices would let all 50 per second overlap, which treats the symptom and makes it louder and noisier.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Making the click file longer fixes the problem, because a longer sound keeps playing and is not restarted so often by the trigger callback.
statements.explanation: The trigger still fires every step; a longer file is simply restarted just as often.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A trigger can only report that an overlap is ongoing; it has no event that marks the moment the overlap starts or ends.
statements.explanation: Triggers report entering, staying and exiting; the enter event marks the start of the overlap.

questions.stem: A developer asks a coding agent: "Make the engine hum loop while the car drives, and make the horn honk once per button press." The project is Godot. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In Godot, whether a sound loops is a property of the audio stream resource, not of the player node that plays it.
statements.explanation: Godot's loop settings live on the stream (for example the WAV loop mode), while the player node only plays what it is given.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A hum recorded with a fade-out at its end makes a good loop, because the fade hides the join between the end and the start.
statements.explanation: A fade-out dips the volume once per pass, so the hum would pulse audibly; a clean loop ends at the same level and phase at which it begins.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "One-shot" describes a sound that may be triggered only once in an entire play session, after which its player is disabled.
statements.explanation: One-shot means the sound plays through once per trigger and then stops; it can be triggered again later.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Looping the hum by calling play() again from the finished handler is seamless, so it is better than the stream's own loop setting.
statements.explanation: Restarting after finished goes through the mixer's block timing and can leave an audible gap that a built-in loop does not.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Creating a new player node for each honk needs no clean-up, because a node that has finished its job leaves the scene on its own.
statements.explanation: A node stays in the scene after its sound ends; removing it, or reusing it from a pool, is the job of the developer's code.

questions.stem: In an engine whose stream player cuts off its oldest voice when play() is called beyond its maximum polyphony, a 60 ms click is triggered at t = 0 ms, t = 40 ms and t = 80 ms on the same player. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: With a maximum polyphony of 1, the first click is cut off at 40 ms, after only 40 of its 60 ms.
statements.explanation: The second trigger at 40 ms exceeds the single voice and cuts off the first, which would have run until 60 ms.

statements.label: B
statements.text: With a maximum polyphony of 1, all three clicks play their full 60 ms because each trigger starts a new voice.
statements.explanation: With one voice, each new play() replaces the running click, so the first two are truncated.

statements.label: C
statements.text: With a maximum polyphony of 2, none of the three clicks is cut off.
statements.explanation: The clicks occupy 0-60, 40-100 and 80-140 ms, and never more than two overlap, so two voices suffice.

statements.label: D
statements.text: With a maximum polyphony of 2, there is an instant at which three voices are sounding at once.
statements.explanation: At any instant at most two of the three intervals overlap, so three voices are never needed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: With a maximum polyphony of 4, the click triggered at 80 ms ends at 120 ms.
statements.explanation: The third click starts at 80 ms and lasts 60 ms, so it ends at 140 ms.

questions.stem: A rhythm game must judge whether a tap landed within 50 ms of a beat in the music. The first version advances a song-time variable by delta (the duration of the last frame) every frame. A second version asks the audio system for the music player's playback position. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Frame delta varies with rendering load, so song time summed from it can drift away from the audio actually playing.
statements.explanation: The game loop and the audio hardware run on different clocks, so summed frame times slowly disagree with the music.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Audio is mixed in blocks on its own clock, so its reported position is coarse and may need correcting for output latency.
statements.explanation: Mixing happens in chunks and the output device adds delay, so the raw position is an approximation of what is heard.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The audio playback position is exact to the sample when read and already includes device delay, so no latency compensation is needed.
statements.explanation: The position updates per mixed block and ignores device latency, so it is not exact to the sample when read.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Judging taps against the audio clock, corrected for latency, tracks what the player actually hears better than accumulated delta does.
statements.explanation: The audio clock is the one the music follows, which is why it is the reference for timing judgments.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Calling play() on a hit sound in the same frame as the tap guarantees the sound is heard exactly on the beat.
statements.explanation: Playback begins at the next mix boundary and then passes through output latency, so the start is slightly late.

questions.stem: A positional audio source follows an inverse-distance law: amplitude is proportional to 1/distance, with 0 dB at 1 m from the listener. A decibel level is 20 log10 of the amplitude ratio. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: At 2 m from the listener the level is about -6 dB, since the amplitude is halved.
statements.explanation: Amplitude 0.5 corresponds to 20 log10(0.5), about -6.02 dB.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Moving the source from 4 m to 8 m lowers the level by about 6 dB, because each doubling halves the amplitude.
statements.explanation: Each doubling of distance halves the amplitude, which is always about -6 dB.

statements.label: C
statements.text: At 10 m the amplitude is one tenth of its value at 1 m, which works out to -20 dB.
statements.explanation: Amplitude 0.1 gives 20 log10(0.1) = -20 dB.

statements.label: D
statements.text: At 16 m the level is about -24 dB, which is four doublings of distance away from 1 m.
statements.explanation: 16 m is four doublings from 1 m, and four times -6.02 dB is about -24.1 dB.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Under this law the sound reaches exactly zero at some finite distance, so no maximum distance is needed.
statements.explanation: An inverse law gets smaller forever but never reaches zero, which is why engines add a maximum distance beyond which the sound is cut off.

questions.source: Wiring a game event to a sound
questions.stem: A game plays an explosion when an enemy dies. The agent attached a stream player as a child of the enemy node. In the enemy's code it calls play() on that player and immediately frees the enemy node. Players hear nothing, or a clipped pop. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Freeing a node also frees its children, including the stream player, which ends its sound.
statements.explanation: Children live and die with their parent, so the sound disappears when the enemy is freed.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Playing the explosion from a node that outlives the enemy, such as a scene-level audio manager or a self-freeing short-lived player, avoids the cut-off.
statements.explanation: The player must belong to something that survives the enemy for as long as the sound lasts.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Raising the player's volume fixes the problem, because the sound is only too quiet to notice and the node still exists to play it.
statements.explanation: The sound is not quiet, it is being destroyed; more volume does not bring it back.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Having the enemy emit a "died" signal once, and letting an audio handler respond to that signal, separates the enemy's lifetime from the sound's lifetime.
statements.explanation: An event fires once and decouples who reacts from who died, which is the standard way to wire a game event to a sound.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Checking "health <= 0" every frame and playing the explosion whenever it is true is equivalent to a death signal, since both start the sound when the enemy dies.
statements.explanation: Polling is true on every frame the condition holds, so the explosion would be restarted repeatedly rather than started once.

questions.stem: Audio designers want to change the footstep sounds without asking programmers to edit code. Gameplay code asks for a cue named "footstep_stone" and the audio data decides which recordings play. Check each statement that is true about cues.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A cue is a named request for a sound event; which recordings it maps to can change without changing gameplay code.
statements.explanation: A cue separates "what happened" from "which files play", so designers can retune sound without code changes.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A cue can pick among several recordings and vary pitch or volume slightly, which reduces the repetitive feel of footsteps.
statements.explanation: Variation inside a cue is a standard way to avoid listener fatigue from repeated identical samples.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A cue is a bus that other sounds are routed through, letting the designers set the level and effects of the footstep recordings together.
statements.explanation: A bus is a mixing and routing channel; a cue is a named sound event that plays on some bus.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Unreal's Sound Cue asset is an example: a node graph that combines and modifies sounds, played by reference rather than by hard-coding a file.
statements.explanation: Epic describes a Sound Cue as a node graph that encapsulates sound design tasks, which fits the cue idea.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The same gameplay event can request different cues in different situations, such as stone or grass, so the cue name carries the situation.
statements.explanation: Choosing the cue name from game state, such as the surface under the foot, is how one event produces varied sounds.

questions.source: Pause, restart and the lifecycle of a player
questions.stem: In Godot, a pause menu sets the scene tree to paused. A developer asks a coding agent: "The menu's click should still sound while paused, the music should resume where it left off when unpaused, and pressing restart should reload the level." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A stream player in the default process mode pauses its stream when the tree pauses and resumes when it unpauses.
statements.explanation: Godot's audio nodes pause their streams with the tree and resume them automatically afterwards.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A menu-click player will play normally while the tree is paused without any change to its process mode, as it is a short sound.
statements.explanation: A player that follows the paused tree is paused too; a pause-menu sound needs a player whose process mode keeps it running.

statements.label: C
statements.text: After the level scene is reloaded, music players that lived in the old scene keep playing from their previous position.
statements.explanation: Reloading a scene frees the old players and creates new ones, so music restarts unless it lives outside the reloaded scene.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A sound that must survive a scene reload is best attached to the scene being reloaded, so it is reloaded with everything else.
statements.explanation: Anything attached to the reloaded scene is destroyed with it; surviving a reload requires living outside it, for example in an autoload.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Calling stop() on the music when pausing and play() when unpausing resumes it from where it stopped, as the stream remembers its position.
statements.explanation: Stop discards the position, so play() starts from the beginning; pausing the stream is what preserves it.

questions.source: Trigger zones, bus effects and event pairs
questions.stem: A cave region should add reverb to sound effects while the player is inside. The agent enables a reverb effect on the SFX bus from the cave trigger's enter event and disables it from the exit event. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Enter and exit events must be paired; if an exit is missed or the zone is disabled with the player inside, the reverb can stay on.
statements.explanation: A toggle driven by two events is only correct if both arrive, so robust code re-derives the state from where the player is.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Because the reverb sits on the SFX bus, it also colors the music, which is played on the separate Music bus.
statements.explanation: Only sounds routed through the SFX bus are processed; the Music bus is untouched.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The bus effect applies to all sounds routed through the SFX bus while it is enabled, including effects triggered far outside the cave.
statements.explanation: A bus effect is not positional, so it colors all SFX, wherever they originate.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The cave trigger must block the player's movement, or its exit event will not fire when the player leaves.
statements.explanation: A trigger detects overlap without blocking, and still reports both entering and leaving.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Reverb on a bus is the same thing as positional attenuation, since both change a sound's character depending on where the player is.
statements.explanation: Reverb adds reflections to a bus; attenuation lowers a source's level with distance from the listener; they are different mechanisms.

questions.stem: A developer moves between engines and must give a coding agent the right term for each audio idea. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: In Unity, an AudioClip is the imported sound and an AudioSource is the component that plays it.
statements.explanation: Unity separates the sound asset (AudioClip) from the component that plays it (AudioSource).

statements.label: B
statements.text: Unity's AudioListener acts like a microphone, and a scene should have only one.
statements.explanation: The listener is the receiver, and Unity documents that a scene works properly with just one.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Unity's Audio Mixer groups play the role that buses play in Godot: routing, per-group level and effects.
statements.explanation: Mixer groups accept inputs, apply effects and levels, and send a single output, matching a bus.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In Unreal, Play Sound 2D applies distance attenuation from the player's location, so it is meant for sounds that belong in the world.
statements.explanation: Play Sound 2D plays without attenuation and is intended for interface sounds.

statements.label: E
statements.text: In Unreal, Play Sound at Location is fire-and-forget at a point and does not follow an actor, so a sound that must follow a moving enemy needs an attached audio component instead.
statements.explanation: Play Sound at Location does not travel with any actor; Spawn Sound Attached creates a component that does.

questions.stem: A team reports performance in frames per second, but the engineers work in frame time, where frame time in milliseconds is 1000 divided by FPS. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A drop from 60 FPS to 50 FPS costs about 3.3 ms of extra time on each frame.
statements.explanation: 1000/50 = 20.0 ms against 1000/60 = 16.7 ms, a difference of about 3.3 ms.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A drop of 5 FPS, from 30 to 25, costs about 6.7 ms per frame, more than the 3.3 ms lost going from 60 to 50.
statements.explanation: 1000/25 = 40.0 ms against 1000/30 = 33.3 ms, a difference of about 6.7 ms, even though the FPS drop is smaller.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Equal drops in FPS, such as 5 FPS starting from 60 or from 30, correspond to equal increases in frame time.
statements.explanation: FPS is the reciprocal of frame time, so the same FPS loss costs more milliseconds at low frame rates than at high ones.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A 60 Hz target leaves a budget of about 16.7 ms for all the work in a frame.
statements.explanation: 1000/60 is about 16.7 ms, the time available to finish everything.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A 144 Hz display target leaves a budget of about 14.4 ms, the refresh rate divided by ten.
statements.explanation: 1000/144 is about 6.9 ms; 14.4 ms would correspond to roughly 69 FPS.

questions.source: Frame time distribution, mean versus worst frame
questions.stem: In a capture of 100 consecutive frames, 98 frames took 10 ms and 2 frames took 50 ms. The game targets 60 Hz, a budget of 16.7 ms per frame. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The mean frame time of the capture is 10.8 ms, well under the 16.7 ms budget.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The 99th percentile frame time is 50 ms, so it exposes the hitches that the mean hides.
statements.explanation: Sorted, the 99th and 100th values are 50 ms, so the 99th percentile catches the stutters while the mean (10.8) and the 95th percentile (10) do not.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Because the mean of 10.8 ms is under the 16.7 ms budget, the game will feel smooth.
statements.explanation: An average can sit well under budget while individual frames miss it, and players see the misses as stutter.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Each of the two slow frames overshoots the 60 Hz budget by about 33 ms.
statements.explanation: 50 ms minus the 16.7 ms budget is about 33 ms of overshoot per slow frame.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Removing the two slow frames from the capture would raise the mean frame time above 11 ms.
statements.explanation: Without the slow frames every remaining frame is 10 ms, so the mean falls to 10.0 ms.

questions.stem: A game runs at 22 ms per frame on a target phone, with vertical sync off. The developer lowers the render resolution to half the width and half the height (a quarter of the pixels) and frame time stays at 22 ms. Then the developer halves the number of AI-controlled characters and frame time drops to 15 ms. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The first result suggests the frame is CPU-bound rather than limited by pixel work on the GPU.
statements.explanation: Changing pixel count did nothing, so the time is being spent elsewhere, most likely on the CPU side.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The first result shows that fill rate is the bottleneck, since the frame time did not change when the pixel count did.
statements.explanation: Fill-rate limits would have improved when the pixel count fell by 75 percent.

statements.label: C
statements.text: If pixel work on the GPU limited the frame, lowering the resolution should have shortened it.
statements.explanation: Resolution is the standard experiment for separating pixel-bound GPU work from CPU work.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because resolution had no effect, it proves that draw calls are not a problem.
statements.explanation: Draw-call overhead is CPU work and does not change with resolution, so the experiment cannot rule it out.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The drop to 15 ms proves that AI code is the only cost in the frame and nothing else needs attention.
statements.explanation: A 7 ms saving shows AI is a large part of the frame, not that nothing else costs time.

questions.stem: In a renderer where the main thread, the render thread and the GPU work as a pipeline, a frame takes about as long as the slowest of the three. Per-frame times are: main thread 14 ms, render thread 6 ms, GPU 9 ms. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Frame time is about 14 ms, roughly 71 FPS.
statements.explanation: The slowest stage, the main thread at 14 ms, sets the pace, and 1000/14 is about 71 FPS.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Cutting GPU time from 9 ms to 4.5 ms leaves frame time at about 14 ms.
statements.explanation: The GPU was not the longest stage, so speeding it up changes nothing while the main thread is the bottleneck.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Cutting main-thread time by 4 ms, to 10 ms, brings frame time to about 10 ms, roughly 100 FPS.
statements.explanation: With the main thread at 10 ms the slowest stage becomes the GPU at 9 ms, so the frame takes max(10, 6, 9) = 10 ms.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Cutting render-thread time from 6 ms to 3 ms brings frame time to about 11 ms.
statements.explanation: The render thread is not the slowest stage, so cutting it leaves the frame at 14 ms.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Because the three stages add up to 29 ms, the game runs at about 34 FPS.
statements.explanation: In a pipeline the stages overlap in time, so frame time is the longest stage and not their sum.

questions.stem: A scene has 1,000 small props, each drawn with its own draw call, and the frame is slow on the CPU. Another scene has one mesh of 1,000,000 triangles drawn with a single draw call and runs fast. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A draw call is a command from the CPU to the GPU to draw some geometry using a particular set of state, such as a mesh and a material.
statements.explanation: A draw call is how the CPU submits a batch of geometry plus the state needed to draw it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Each draw call carries CPU overhead, so many small draw calls can cost more CPU time than one large one with more triangles.
statements.explanation: Validation and state changes make each call cost CPU time, which is why call count matters apart from triangle count.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The slow scene must contain more triangles in total, since the number of triangles is what mostly determines how long the CPU takes to prepare a frame.
statements.explanation: The slow scene need not have more triangles at all (the props can be small and few-sided), because triangle count is only one cost and per-call overhead can dominate when there are many small objects.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Merging draw calls reduces GPU shading cost in proportion, because the GPU then has fewer commands to process.
statements.explanation: Draw calls are mostly CPU and submission cost; shading cost depends on pixels covered, which merging calls does not reduce.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Draw-call overhead comes from the GPU hardware, so a call costs about the same whichever graphics API or engine submits it.
statements.explanation: The overhead is mostly CPU-side validation and driver work, which differs between APIs and engines, which is why newer APIs were designed to lower it.

questions.stem: A forest scene has 2,000 trees that use the same mesh and the same material, and 40 rocks that each use a different mesh and a different material. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Instancing can draw all 2,000 trees in one draw call, because they share a mesh and material and differ only in per-instance data like position.
statements.explanation: Instancing draws many copies of one mesh with one material, with per-instance values such as transform supplied alongside.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Instancing can also combine the 40 rocks into one draw call, because instancing works on groups of objects with different meshes and materials.
statements.explanation: Different meshes and materials cannot be drawn as instances of one mesh, so the rocks remain separate.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Batching merges geometry that shares a material into fewer draw calls, but merging copies of one mesh into a single large mesh stores the vertex data of each copy, using more memory.
statements.explanation: Merging copies into one mesh cuts calls but stores each copy's geometry separately, so memory use rises.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Giving each of the 2,000 trees its own unique material makes them easier to batch, because each tree can then be tuned separately.
statements.explanation: A unique material per tree breaks any grouping by material and makes the draw count worse.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Sprites that show different images can still share one material and be batched if the images are packed into a single texture atlas.
statements.explanation: An atlas lets different images live in one texture, so objects using different pictures can share a material.

questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: "The grass is slow. Use instancing." The grass is 50,000 blades, each currently a separate scene node with its own mesh and material resource. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: For the instruction to work, the agent must set up one shared blade mesh, one shared material, and a per-instance list of transforms.
statements.explanation: Instancing needs one mesh and material shared by all copies, plus per-copy data, so the existing per-node resources must be replaced.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The saving from instancing comes mainly from submitting one draw call for many copies of the mesh, not from drawing fewer triangles.
statements.explanation: Every copy still has its triangles processed; what shrinks is the per-call CPU overhead of submitting 50,000 separate draws.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Instancing lowers the pixel-shading cost of the grass, since the copies are drawn together in one call.
statements.explanation: Drawing copies together saves submission overhead, but every visible pixel of every blade is still shaded, so grass that is slow because of overdraw or shader cost stays slow.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Because instancing removes thousands of draw calls, it will speed up the grass, so the agent can apply it and move on without comparing frame times.
statements.explanation: The benefit depends on the platform and on where the time goes (if the grass is slow from shading or overdraw, fewer draw calls will not help), so the change is justified by before and after measurements.

statements.label: E
statements.text: The instruction is precise enough on its own, because "instancing" implies the agent will also add level of detail and culling for each blade.
statements.explanation: Instancing is a way of drawing many copies in one call; deciding which copies to draw (level of detail, culling) is a separate matter that the instruction would have to request.

questions.stem: A 1920 x 1080 screen (2,073,600 pixels) is covered by 8 full-screen semi-transparent smoke layers. Each layer is shaded in full for every pixel, with no early rejection. The game targets 60 FPS. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The layers cause about 16.6 million fragment shader invocations per frame.
statements.explanation: 2,073,600 pixels x 8 layers = 16,588,800 fragments per frame.

statements.label: B
statements.text: At 60 FPS that is about 1.0 billion fragment shader invocations per second.
statements.explanation: 16,588,800 x 60 = 995,328,000, about one billion per second.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The overdraw factor is about 8, meaning each screen pixel is shaded about 8 times per frame.
statements.explanation: Overdraw measures how many times the average pixel is shaded; eight full layers give a factor of 8.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Cutting from 8 layers to 2 layers reduces the fragment work by about one third.
statements.explanation: Two layers is a quarter of eight, so the work falls by about 75 percent, to about 4.1 million per frame.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Overdraw is a cost on the CPU, so it shows up when the CPU is waiting on the GPU.
statements.explanation: Overdraw is shading work on the GPU (a fill-rate cost), not CPU work.

questions.stem: A mobile scene has only 200 draw calls and spends 4 ms of CPU time per frame, yet runs at 14 FPS because 12 full-screen semi-transparent fog planes overlap. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Fill rate, the pixel shading work, is the likely limit, so cutting draw calls alone will not help much.
statements.explanation: The CPU side is cheap here, so the GPU is the limit, and each pixel is shaded about twelve times.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Merging all twelve fog planes into one mesh removes the overdraw, since only one object is then drawn.
statements.explanation: Merged geometry still covers the same pixels twelve times, so every pixel is still shaded for every layer.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Frustum culling would remove the fog planes and fix the problem, since most of them overlap each other.
statements.explanation: The planes are inside the view, so frustum culling keeps them.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Adding level-of-detail meshes to the fog planes would fix the problem, since LOD reduces the cost of drawing distant objects.
statements.explanation: The planes are already minimal geometry; the cost is the number of pixels shaded, not triangles.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Using higher-resolution fog textures would fix the problem, since sharper textures need fewer layers to look dense.
statements.explanation: Larger textures add memory and sampling cost without reducing the layers shaded.

questions.stem: A 3D game draws a city. Check each statement that is true about culling.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Frustum culling skips objects that lie wholly outside the camera's view volume.
statements.explanation: A view frustum is the volume the camera can see; objects wholly outside it cannot appear.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Occlusion culling skips objects that are inside the view volume but hidden behind other geometry.
statements.explanation: Occlusion culling tests visibility against other geometry, not just the view volume.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Frustum culling alone still submits a building hidden behind a large wall if the building is inside the camera's view volume.
statements.explanation: Being in the frustum is not the same as being visible, which is the gap occlusion culling fills.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Culling decides what not to draw, so it lowers the draw calls and shading work spent on the culled objects.
statements.explanation: A culled object is not submitted, saving the calls and pixel work it would have caused.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Backface culling removes entire objects that are behind the camera, which is why frustum culling is rarely needed.
statements.explanation: Backface culling discards individual triangles facing away from the camera; objects behind the camera are handled by frustum culling.

questions.stem: A character model has three versions: 20,000 triangles for close-ups, 5,000 for mid-range and 1,000 for the distance. Check each statement that is true about level of detail (LOD).

statements.label: A
statements.text: The engine switches to a cheaper version as the object gets farther away or smaller on screen.
statements.explanation: LOD swaps in simpler representations according to distance or screen size.

statements.label: B
statements.text: At a distance, using the 1,000-triangle version reduces the vertex and triangle processing for each character drawn.
statements.explanation: Fewer triangles and vertices means less geometry work for each distant character.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Storing all three versions takes more memory than storing only the 20,000-triangle version.
statements.explanation: Each extra version is additional mesh data kept in memory.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Visible popping when the version switches can be reduced by cross-fading between versions or by tuning the switch distances.
statements.explanation: Cross-fades and well-chosen transition distances hide the swap from the player.

statements.label: E
statements.text: With LOD in place, culling is no longer needed, since distant objects are cheap and cost nothing to draw.
statements.explanation: Cheap is not free; objects outside the view or hidden still cost work unless culled.

questions.stem: A developer tells a coding agent: "Pool the bullets." Currently each shot creates a new bullet object and destroys it on impact. At 20 shots per second the game stutters periodically. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Object pooling creates bullets in advance and reuses them: one is taken from the pool on firing and returned on impact.
statements.explanation: The pool trades creating and destroying objects for acquiring and releasing existing ones.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A pooled bullet must be fully reset on reuse (position, velocity, timers, hit flags), or state from its last use leaks into the new shot.
statements.explanation: Reused objects keep whatever state they had, so a missed reset makes a shot behave like the previous one.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Pooling removes the need to decide what happens when the pool has no free bullet left, since the pool has enough bullets.
statements.explanation: A pool has a fixed size, so the code needs a policy for exhaustion, such as growing, skipping the shot or recycling the oldest.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Pooling avoids repeated allocation and destruction, which with garbage collection also means less garbage to clean up.
statements.explanation: Less allocation means less short-lived garbage and fewer collection pauses where a collector is used.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Idle bullets in a pool cost nothing while they wait, since an object that is not in use takes up no memory and no processing time at all.
statements.explanation: Pooled objects still occupy memory and may cost processing unless they are disabled.

questions.stem: A game written in a language with a tracing garbage collector allocates a small temporary list every frame. After ten seconds, players see a brief freeze about once every few seconds. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Garbage is memory that was allocated and is no longer referenced, which the collector later reclaims.
statements.explanation: Garbage is unreachable allocated memory awaiting reclamation by the collector.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Collection can interrupt the game for part of a frame at times the developer does not control, which shows as a hitch.
statements.explanation: The collector runs when it decides to, and its work can take time out of a frame, which shows as a spike.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Making the temporary list larger removes the freezes, because the collector then runs less often.
statements.explanation: A larger list creates more garbage per frame, which makes collection more frequent or longer.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Lowering the display refresh rate fixes the cause of the freezes, because frames then arrive less often and the collector has more time.
statements.explanation: The refresh rate does not control allocation; the freezes come from allocation and collection.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A faster GPU reduces collection pauses, because the freezes happen at the moment the frame is drawn.
statements.explanation: Collection runs on the CPU and manages CPU-side memory, so GPU speed does not change it.

questions.stem: A 2048 x 2048 texture with four 8-bit channels (RGBA, 4 bytes per pixel) is uploaded to the GPU uncompressed. Take 1 MiB as 1,048,576 bytes. A full mipmap chain adds about one third on top of the base level (1 + 1/4 + 1/16 + ... = 4/3). A GPU-compressed format stores the same image at 1 byte per pixel. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The base level occupies 16 MiB (2048 x 2048 x 4 bytes).

statements.label: B
statements.text: With a full mipmap chain, the uncompressed texture occupies about 21.3 MiB.
statements.explanation: 16 MiB x 4/3 is about 21.3 MiB.

statements.label: C
statements.text: In the compressed format with a full mipmap chain, it occupies about 5.3 MiB.
statements.explanation: 2048 x 2048 x 1 byte = 4 MiB, and times 4/3 is about 5.3 MiB.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A 100 KB PNG file of this image occupies only about 100 KB of GPU memory.
statements.explanation: A PNG is compressed for storage on disk; the GPU needs the pixels in a format it can sample, so its size in memory follows the format, not the file.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Halving both dimensions to 1024 x 1024 reduces the uncompressed base level to a quarter, 4 MiB.
statements.explanation: Memory scales with pixel count, so halving each dimension leaves a quarter: 1024 x 1024 x 4 = 4 MiB.

questions.stem: A developer compares two implementations of a system. Version A's mean frame time (ms) in five separate runs was 8.4, 8.0, 8.2, 8.1 and 8.3. Version B's was 7.9, 8.5, 7.6, 8.4 and 8.2. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Both versions have a median of 8.2 ms across their five runs.
statements.explanation: Sorted, A is 8.0, 8.1, 8.2, 8.3, 8.4 and B is 7.6, 7.9, 8.2, 8.4, 8.5; the middle value is 8.2 in both.

statements.label: B
statements.text: B's mean (8.12 ms) is only 0.08 ms below A's (8.2 ms), far less than B's own spread of 7.6 to 8.5 ms, so the runs do not show B is faster.
statements.explanation: Variation between runs of the same code is larger than the gap between the means, so the difference is within noise.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The right conclusion from these numbers is that B is about 1 percent faster, since its mean is lower, so the team should switch.
statements.explanation: Reporting a 1 percent gain would claim an effect the data cannot distinguish from chance.

statements.label: D
statements.text: More repeated runs would help show whether any real difference exists beyond run-to-run variance.
statements.explanation: More repetitions shrink the uncertainty and show whether a consistent difference exists.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Frames from the first seconds after launch, while shaders compile and caches fill, should usually be excluded as warm-up.
statements.explanation: Start-up work is not representative of steady-state cost, so it is normally discarded before measuring.

questions.source: Measurement pitfalls: vsync, build type, hardware
questions.stem: A developer reports: "The game shows a steady 60 FPS, so it has plenty of headroom." The display refreshes at 60 Hz with vertical sync on, the measurement was taken inside the editor with debugging tools attached, and it was taken on a fast development PC rather than the target phone. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: With vertical sync on, frame rate is capped at the refresh rate, so 60 FPS does not show whether frames take 4 ms or 16 ms.
statements.explanation: A frame that finishes early waits for the next refresh, so the FPS number hides how much time is left over.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Measurements from an editor session or a debug build can differ from a release build, because of extra checks and tool overhead.
statements.explanation: Editors and debug builds add work that a shipped build does not, so release builds on the target are the honest test.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A fast development PC performs the same as the target phone, so the result transfers directly to the device.
statements.explanation: Different hardware has different CPU, GPU and memory limits, so measurements must be taken on the device being targeted.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A steady 60 FPS proves that each frame uses exactly 16.7 ms of CPU work, since a locked frame rate means the frames take the full budget.
statements.explanation: The cap means the frame can take less than the budget and still show 60 FPS.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Turning vertical sync off would make the game slower, because the display would then be waiting on it.
statements.explanation: Vertical sync waits on the display and does not make the work faster; turning it off only removes the cap and exposes the real frame time.

questions.stem: A 60 Hz game has a budget of 16.7 ms per frame and currently takes 20 ms. A profiler shows: physics 8 ms, one function update_minimap 1 ms, and everything else 11 ms. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Making update_minimap twice as fast saves only 0.5 ms, small compared with the roughly 3.3 ms that must be saved to reach the budget.
statements.explanation: Halving a 1 ms function saves 0.5 ms, about 3 percent of the frame.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Making physics four times faster would cut the frame to about 14 ms, inside the budget.
statements.explanation: Physics falls from 8 to 2 ms, saving 6 ms, and 20 - 6 = 14 ms.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Making update_minimap infinitely fast would bring the game under budget on its own.
statements.explanation: Removing the whole 1 ms still leaves 19 ms, above 16.7 ms.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The 3.3 ms to be saved should be shared out in roughly equal parts across physics, update_minimap and the remaining 11 ms of work, since each of them adds to the frame time.
statements.explanation: update_minimap costs 1 ms in total, so it cannot supply an equal 1.1 ms share; the saving has to come mostly from the large items, physics and the remaining work.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Because update_minimap is the easiest function to change, the best first step is to rewrite it, and the larger costs can be looked at afterwards if the budget is still missed.
statements.explanation: Effort belongs where the measured time is: update_minimap offers at most 1 ms of the 3.3 ms needed and cannot meet the goal alone, while physics at 8 ms offers far more, and ease of change does not alter that.

questions.stem: A developer is learning to use a profiler. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A profiler records where time or memory goes during a run, such as per function or frame stage, to find hot spots.
statements.explanation: Showing where time is spent is the purpose of a profiler.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Recording in a profiler's most detailed mode does not change how fast the game runs, so the frame times it reports can be quoted as the game's normal speed.
statements.explanation: Detailed profiling adds overhead and slows the program, which is why absolute times from a profiled run should not be quoted as normal speed.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A profiler's report points to the fix as well as to the slow part, so the developer's job is to carry out what the report indicates.
statements.explanation: A profiler shows data; deciding what it means and what to change is the developer's work.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A capture of a single frame taken at a busy moment is enough to find the bottleneck of a game whose load changes during play.
statements.explanation: One frame can be unrepresentative, so captures should span a representative stretch of play.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A profiler reports how long the CPU spends in each function, but time spent on the GPU is not measured directly and has to be guessed from the frame rate.
statements.explanation: GPU profiling tools exist in the major engines and report GPU time separately from CPU time.

questions.stem: A developer asks a coding agent to implement a guard non-player character (NPC) as a finite state machine (FSM) instead of one large function full of nested if statements. Check each statement that is true about finite state machines.

statements.label: A
statements.text: An FSM has a defined set of states, exactly one of which is current, and rules called transitions for moving between them.
statements.explanation: States, a single current state and transitions are what define a finite state machine.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Each state defines what the guard does while in it, such as patrolling or chasing, keeping the behavior for each mode in one place.
statements.explanation: Putting behavior inside states is the main structural benefit over nested conditions.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An FSM lets the guard be in the Chase state and the Patrol state at the same time, which is how it blends behaviors smoothly, such as chasing while patrolling.
statements.explanation: A finite state machine has exactly one current state; blending behaviors needs a different design.

statements.label: D
statements.text: In an FSM, the order of child nodes sets priority, and the whole structure is re-evaluated from a root node per update.
statements.explanation: Ordered children re-evaluated from a root describe a behavior tree, not an FSM.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A guard stuck in Search forever is usually caused by a missing or unreachable transition out of that state, easier to find with a transition table.
statements.explanation: A stuck state is a problem with the exits from that state, and a transition table makes missing exits visible.

questions.source: Finite state machine versus behavior tree: where transition logic lives
questions.stem: An NPC has a finite state machine with 6 states. In the worst case any state can move directly to any other, giving n x (n - 1) possible directed transitions for n states. A designer asks for a seventh state, Flee, that can be entered from every other state and can return to every other state. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: With 6 states there can be up to 30 directed transitions, because each of the 6 can lead to the other 5.

statements.label: B
statements.text: With a seventh state the maximum rises to 42 directed transitions, because each of the 7 can lead to the other 6.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Adding Flee adds 12 transitions in the worst case: 6 leading into Flee and 6 leading out of it to the other states.
statements.explanation: 42 - 30 = 12, which is 6 entries to Flee plus 6 exits from it.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Adding Flee requires editing only the new state, because existing states need no way of reaching it.
statements.explanation: Each existing state that can be hurt needs a new exit edge into Flee, so many files or states change.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A behavior tree needs the same 12 new connections to add "flee when hurt", since the other behaviors must be able to reach it.
statements.explanation: In a behavior tree "flee when hurt" can be one new high-priority branch checked first, with no edges added to the other behaviors.

questions.source: Behavior tree: selector, sequence and tick results
questions.stem: A guard's behavior tree is: Selector[ Sequence[CanSeePlayer, Chase], Sequence[HasLastKnownPosition, Search], Patrol ]. Nodes are ticked from the root, left to right. A Selector stops at the first child that does not fail, and a Sequence stops at the first child that does not succeed. On this tick, CanSeePlayer returns FAILURE, HasLastKnownPosition returns SUCCESS, Search returns RUNNING, and Patrol would return RUNNING if it were ticked. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Chase is not ticked on this tick, because the first Sequence stops at its failing first child.
statements.explanation: The first Sequence stops at CanSeePlayer, which fails, so Chase is never reached.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Patrol is not ticked on this tick, because the Selector stops at the RUNNING second child.
statements.explanation: The second Sequence returns RUNNING, and a Selector stops at a child that has not failed, so Patrol is not reached.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The root Selector returns RUNNING, passing up the result from the second Sequence.
statements.explanation: Search returns RUNNING, the second Sequence passes it up, and the Selector passes it up to the root.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The first Sequence returns SUCCESS because its last child, Chase, was skipped and did not report a failure.
statements.explanation: A Sequence that stops at a failing child returns FAILURE; skipped children do not make it succeed.

statements.label: E
statements.text: If CanSeePlayer succeeds on the next tick and the tree restarts from the root each tick, the guard switches to Chase with no exit rule in Search.
statements.explanation: The higher-priority branch is checked first on every tick, so it pre-empts Search without Search having to know.

questions.source: FSM, behavior tree, utility AI and GOAP
questions.stem: A studio is choosing how its NPCs decide what to do. Check each statement that is true about decision architectures.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Utility AI scores each candidate action with numeric considerations, such as hunger or distance, and picks the highest score.
statements.explanation: Utility AI picks by score, and because scores vary continuously the choice can shift gradually.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Goal-oriented action planning (GOAP) requires the designer to author the exact order of actions for each goal in advance.
statements.explanation: GOAP's planner finds the sequence; the designer supplies actions and goals, not fixed orders.

statements.label: C
statements.text: GOAP describes each action by its preconditions and effects and searches for a sequence of actions that reaches a goal state.
statements.explanation: Preconditions, effects and a search over action sequences define GOAP.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A behavior tree stores its transitions as edges between states, in the same way as a finite state machine does.
statements.explanation: A behavior tree has no state-to-state edges; its logic is in the order and type of its nodes.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A finite state machine re-ticks from a root node per update, so higher-priority behaviors pre-empt lower ones as it runs.
statements.explanation: Re-ticking from a root with ordered priority describes a behavior tree; an FSM only checks the exits of its current state.

questions.source: Saying it to the agent: a precise NPC behavior instruction
questions.stem: A developer needs a guard that patrols between waypoints, chases the player when it sees them, and searches the last place it saw them when the player is lost. The developer wants an instruction to a coding agent that can be built and tested without the agent guessing. An instruction counts as precise enough only if it gives, as numbers, the distances and times that a test would check. Check each instruction that is precise enough for that purpose.

statements.label: A
statements.text: "Make the guard intelligent: it should patrol between waypoints, notice the player, chase them and then search for them, react in a believable way and feel fair to play against, using the AI approach that works best, and tune the distances and timings so that the encounters feel natural and not cheap."
statements.explanation: It names no states, conditions or test hook, so the agent decides everything and the result cannot be checked.

statements.label: B
statements.text: "Build a finite state machine with the states Patrol, Chase and Search. The guard chases when it notices the player within about 10 m and searches when it loses them, then patrols again after a while. Use sensible timers, and keep the code tidy."
statements.explanation: "Loses" and "a while" are undefined, only one distance is given, "sensible timers" gives no times, and nothing lets a test read the state.

statements.label: C
statements.text: "Build a finite state machine with states Patrol, Chase and Search. Patrol to Chase: player within 10 m and visible by a line-of-sight check. Chase to Search: player beyond 14 m or hidden for 2 s. Search to Patrol: 5 s at the last seen position. Expose the current state name as a read-only property."
statements.explanation: It gives states, numeric transition conditions, a timer and a readable property, so it can be built and tested as written.

statements.label: D
statements.text: "Use machine learning so the guard learns to catch the player over many games, rewarding it for closing distance and for catching the player, and make sure that it does not get stuck or lose the player's trail."
statements.explanation: It names no states, conditions or test hook, leaves the training setup unspecified, and promises an untestable guarantee (not getting stuck).

statements.label: E
statements.text: "Write a behavior tree whose root is a selector trying Chase first, then Search, then Patrol, with a blackboard for the last known position. Give the Chase and Search branches condition checks (Chase when the player is within 10 m), and expose the other distances and timers in the editor with the values left for the designers to fill in later."
statements.explanation: It names the structure and gives one distance, but the other distances and every time are left for the agent to invent, so no test can say what correct behavior is; there is also no readable state to check.

questions.stem: A guard enters Chase from any other state when the player is within 10 m, and leaves Chase (entering Search) only when the player is farther than 14 m. The player's distance at five consecutive decisions is 9, 11, 9, 11 and 9 m. A second guard uses a single radius of 10 m both to enter Chase and to leave it for Search: it enters Chase from any other state when the player is within 10 m and enters Search from Chase as soon as the player is farther than 10 m. Both guards start in Patrol. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The two-radius guard is in Chase after all five decisions and does not leave it, because 11 m is not beyond 14 m.
statements.explanation: The first decision (9 m) enters Chase, and 11 m is not beyond 14 m, so the guard stays.

statements.label: B
statements.text: The single-radius guard is in Search after the second decision, because 11 m is outside its 10 m radius.
statements.explanation: At 11 m the single-radius guard is outside its 10 m radius and leaves Chase.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The single-radius guard stays in Chase through all five decisions, because it only leaves Chase when the player is out of sight.
statements.explanation: It leaves Chase at 11 m and re-enters at 9 m, so it alternates.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The gap between 10 m and 14 m is called hysteresis, and its purpose is to make the guard move faster.
statements.explanation: Hysteresis means different thresholds for entering and leaving a state; its purpose is to prevent flickering at the boundary.

statements.label: E
statements.text: After first entering Chase, the two guards change state the same number of times over the five decisions.
statements.explanation: The two-radius guard makes no further changes, while the single-radius guard changes four more times.

questions.stem: Check each statement that is true about steering behaviors and pathfinding for an NPC.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Pathfinding computes a route through the level as a list of points; steering turns it into per-frame motion by adjusting velocity.
statements.explanation: Pathfinding is the global planning step, and steering is the local, per-frame motion that follows it.

statements.label: B
statements.text: For seek with velocity (2, 0), a target straight along +y and maximum speed 4, desired velocity is (0, 4) and the steering change is (-2, 4).
statements.explanation: Desired velocity is the direction to the target at maximum speed, (0, 4); subtracting the current (2, 0) gives (-2, 4).

statements.label: C
statements.text: Seek alone is enough to get an NPC around a wall that stands between it and its target, because steering knows the layout of the level.
statements.explanation: Seek heads straight toward the target and has no knowledge of walls, so it pushes into the wall.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Arrive is seek that slows down as it nears the target, so the NPC stops on it instead of overshooting.
statements.explanation: Arrive reduces speed inside a slowing radius so the NPC stops at the target.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Pursue steers toward the target's current position, which is the same thing as seek, since the target is a point in space.
statements.explanation: Pursue predicts where a moving target will be and steers toward that point, whereas seek steers toward where the target is now.

questions.stem: A developer asks a coding agent to make a flock of 200 birds. Each bird follows three local rules: steer away from very close neighbors (separation), match the heading of neighbors (alignment), and steer toward the average position of nearby neighbors (cohesion). No code describes the shape of the flock. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The coordinated movement of the flock is emergent behavior: it arises from simple local rules and is not written down as a global behavior.
statements.explanation: Global patterns that come from local interactions, not from code that describes them, are what emergent behavior means.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Because the rules are simple, the exact shape of the flock can be predicted without running the simulation.
statements.explanation: Simple rules can produce complex outcomes that are hard to predict without simulation.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Each bird only needs to look at nearby neighbors; no central controller directs the flock.
statements.explanation: Each bird uses only local information, which is why the behavior scales to many birds.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Changing the weight of one rule, such as cohesion, can change the flock's overall behavior a lot, so emergent systems need tuning and playtesting.
statements.explanation: Parameter weights shape the collective result, so designers must test and tune.

statements.label: E
statements.text: Emergent behavior means the AI is defective, because it does something the designer did not code directly, so the rules must have been wrong.
statements.explanation: Emergence is often the goal, as in flocks and crowds; it is only a defect when the result is unwanted.

questions.stem: A developer needs enemies to navigate a level with walls and furniture. Check each statement that is true about grids, A* and navigation meshes.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A grid and a navigation mesh are two ways of representing walkable space, while A* is a search algorithm that can run on either.
statements.explanation: Grid and navmesh describe the space; A* is the algorithm that searches over a graph built from either.

statements.label: B
statements.text: A navigation mesh covers walkable surface with polygons, so open floor needs far fewer nodes than a grid: 128 x 128 is 16,384 cells.
statements.explanation: A grid stores one node per cell (128 x 128 = 16,384), while a navmesh stores polygons, so open areas are cheap.

statements.label: C
statements.text: A navigation mesh is baked from level geometry and the agent's size, so it must be rebuilt when static geometry changes.
statements.explanation: The mesh is generated from geometry, so it goes stale when walls move unless it is updated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: A larger agent radius shrinks the walkable area of the navigation mesh so the agent's body does not clip walls.
statements.explanation: Navigation meshes are shrunk by the agent radius so a path keeps the body clear of obstacles.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A* is a representation of walkable space, in the same sense that a grid is, since both are used to store the level and A* does so as a graph of nodes.
statements.explanation: A* is a search method, not a data structure for the world.

questions.stem: On an empty grid, an NPC at (0, 0) wants to reach (7, 5). A* picks nodes by f = g + h, where g is the cost so far and h is a heuristic estimate of the remaining cost. An admissible heuristic never overestimates the true remaining cost. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: With 4-direction movement at cost 1 per step, the Manhattan distance of 12 equals the true cost and is admissible.
statements.explanation: Without obstacles a 4-direction path needs 7 + 5 = 12 steps, matching the Manhattan distance exactly.

statements.label: B
statements.text: With 8-direction movement (diagonal about 1.414) the true cost is about 9.07, so the Manhattan distance of 12 overestimates and is not admissible.
statements.explanation: Five diagonal steps plus two straight ones cost about 5 x 1.414 + 2 = 9.07, which is below 12.

statements.label: C
statements.text: An admissible heuristic lets A* return a shortest path.
statements.explanation: If h never overestimates, A* cannot skip past the best route.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Setting h to zero everywhere makes A* behave like Dijkstra's algorithm, which expands nodes by cost so far with no sense of direction.
statements.explanation: With h = 0, f equals g, which is Dijkstra's ordering.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A heuristic that overestimates lets A* find shorter paths faster, because it pushes the search toward the goal.
statements.explanation: Overestimating can make A* faster but it can return a longer path, because it may expand the wrong nodes first.

questions.stem: In Godot, a developer says to a coding agent: "Use a NavigationAgent2D so the enemy walks to the player." Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The agent computes the path; the body's own movement code, such as a CharacterBody2D velocity, must follow the next path position.
statements.explanation: The class reference says the calculation can be used by the parent node to move it; the parent does the moving.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Once the agent has computed a path to the target, the enemy counts as having arrived, so its movement code can stop.
statements.explanation: Having a path is not the same as having arrived; the body still has to move along the path, and arrival is judged by how close the body has actually come to the target.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The navigation system applies new navigation data a step after it is added, not instantly, so a path requested in the same frame the level is built can come back empty.
statements.explanation: The navigation system batches changes and synchronises them at the end of the physics frame rather than at that instant, so a query made before that can find no path because the map is still empty or not updated.

statements.label: D
statements.text: Calling get_next_path_position() once when the target is set is enough, because the path does not need updating afterwards.
statements.explanation: get_next_path_position() is meant to be called once every physics frame to keep the path logic updated.

statements.label: E
statements.text: NavigationAgent2D moves its parent body along the path by itself each physics frame, so no movement code is needed in the enemy's script.
statements.explanation: The agent does not move the body, so without movement code nothing moves.

questions.source: Perception: sight cone, range and line of sight
questions.stem: A guard faces along unit vector f. Its vision is a cone with a total field of view of 90 degrees (45 degrees to each side of f) and a range of 12 m. For a unit vector d pointing from the guard to a target, the target is inside the cone angle when dot(f, d) is greater than cos(45 degrees), about 0.707. Target X is 8 m away and 30 degrees off f. Target Y is 8 m away and 60 degrees off f. Target Z is 20 m away straight ahead. Assume there are no walls. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: The guard sees X, which is inside the cone and within range.
statements.explanation: cos(30 degrees) is about 0.866, above 0.707, and 8 m is within 12 m, so X is seen.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Y is inside the cone because it is within the 12 m range and nothing blocks the view.
statements.explanation: Being within range is necessary but not sufficient; the angle must also be inside the cone.

statements.label: C
statements.text: Y is outside the cone, because dot(f, d) is about 0.5, which is less than 0.707.
statements.explanation: cos(60 degrees) is 0.5, below the cone threshold, so Y is outside the field of view.

statements.label: D
statements.text: The guard sees Z because it is straight ahead, in the middle of the cone.
statements.explanation: Z is centered in the cone but 20 m exceeds the 12 m range.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A complete sight check also needs a line-of-sight test such as a raycast, since cone and range ignore walls.
statements.explanation: Range and angle say nothing about obstacles, so a raycast or similar test is needed for walls to block sight.

questions.stem: A guard hears a thrown bottle break 15 m away and out of sight. Designers want the guard to walk to the sound's origin and then return to patrolling. The agent stores the noise position in a blackboard entry named last_known_position. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: A blackboard is shared memory that behavior nodes read and write, such as last_known_position, so one node can record what another uses.
statements.explanation: A blackboard is a store of facts that nodes share, which decouples the node that senses from the node that acts.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Hearing is usually modelled as an event with a position and loudness that nearby NPCs may react to, not a continuous scan.
statements.explanation: A noise event carries a location and loudness, and listeners within hearing range react to it.

statements.label: C
statements.text: The blackboard is the logic that decides whether the guard searches or patrols, based on what is stored in it.
statements.explanation: The decision logic lives in the states or tree; the blackboard only holds data.

statements.label: D
statements.text: If the guard can read the player's position directly from the player object at all times, it is perceiving the player fairly and nothing is being cheated.
statements.explanation: Reading the player's position directly makes the NPC omniscient, which is why perception systems limit what an NPC can know.

statements.label: E
statements.text: A stored noise position remains valid after the guard has checked it, so the guard does not need to clear or expire it.
statements.explanation: Knowledge goes stale, so it should expire or be cleared once the guard has checked it or a timer runs out.

questions.stem: A developer asks an agent for "random terrain". The agent fills a height array by giving every cell an independent random number, and the result looks like static. Check each statement that is true.

statements.label: A
statements.text: Independent random values per cell are white noise: neighboring cells are unrelated, so there are no smooth hills.
statements.explanation: White noise has no correlation between neighbors, which is why it looks like static.

statements.label: B
statements.text: Coherent noise, such as Perlin, simplex or value noise, returns similar values for nearby coordinates and so gives smooth variation.
